Three cabled reports reached the Agency from Mexico City on 22 and 23 November 1963. They told of photos of an unknown man at the Cuban and Soviet embassies there. They also listed air exits by three men who might have been Lee Harvey Oswald. The memo states plainly that the man in the photos is not Oswald. Named look-alikes include Lee Martin, Wilford Oswalt, and William Oswald, with flight dates given.
cia-crest-cia-rdp11s00229r000201630001-7:
Economic reform in China is summed up in a Directorate paper dated 19 April 1985. The past year is called a turning point for the reform drive, with Deng Xiaoping backing key steps. New rules cut central planning and lean more on market signals, the summary states.

Farm reform leads the account as the drive's chief gain since 1978. The commune system was phased out and farm families gained use of land for set terms of 15 years. Farm output value grew at an 8 percent yearly rate from 1979 to 1983. Wage, price, and tax changes fill later pages. Findings are framed as the paper's assessed view of Beijing's course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100200005-7:
Staff matters fill a file catalogued with a report on the teeth of Hitler and Goebbels. A memo dated 8 July 1946 treats the case of Erwin Hirschberg, Jr. and promotion blocks in the signals arm. Signals staff, it argues, were trained above Army norms yet held back by frozen promotion slots.

Hirschberg was sought by OSS on 26 June 1945 and reported on 30 July 1945, the memo states. Training at Area O ran to 29 November 1945 with no promotion in that span. Later pages hold a 3 January 1944 note urging that Major Watts Hill be raised to lieutenant colonel. David K. E. Bruce signs that note from the European theatre desk.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100210004-7:
Archduke Otto von Habsburg heads the catalogue line for a very large wartime file. Other heads listed name ties with British intelligence, work with OSS, and response to the loss of the ship Struma. Letters on the Foreign Nationalities Branch also figure in the catalogue line.

One readable memo urges a propaganda drive aimed at the French navy. Two naval vessels would carry the broadcasts, one placed at Gibraltar and one at Bathurst or Freetown. The Gibraltar ship would reach French ports in the Mediterranean and North Africa. Time on United States short-wave stations was too short for the plan, the memo argues. Early pages hold a garbled profile of a church figure and funds lost in mines.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100270008-7:
German labor after defeat is watched in a file catalogued with two further studies. Other heads listed name a study of how German thought is organized and moves to reach Catholic groups in Germany. Those moves aim to keep social order once German arms fall, the catalogue line states.

A covering note sends a labor memo to the President as of keen interest. Local union growth is spotty, the memo reports, with some Kreis-level unions rising fast. A strong pull runs toward one single union movement in place of many, it states. United States and Soviet methods clash in the account, one building from the shop floor up. The scan is rough in stretches but the labor account reads clear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100070078-7:
Aerial photos of Russia are urged as a rare chance in a memo dated November 1954. The memo, marked TS 15018, goes to the Director with a summary attached. It argues that peace rests on knowing what a great power does inside its own borders.

Russia can study United States bases and industry freely, the memo states. The United States lacks the same view in return and must guess at Soviet plans. Flight over Russia had been too risky with past planes, it grants. A task force is urged to test the plan within a few weeks. If tests pass, a lasting force under cover would buy a matched Lockheed system and fly high overflights.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200170012-7:
Surfacing the OXCART program is planned in an Office of the Secretary of Defense paper dated 16 January 1963. Tab A holds the first plan: show Congress that manned strategic aircraft are not being dropped. The craft would be shown as an X-21, a multi-use plane now ready for test.

Its low radar cross section is the one trait that must stay secret, the plan states. Secretary McNamara and Director McCone agreed he would read a set statement to cleared members. No copies would change hands, and the program would stay in the black. Later pages weigh the B-70 question and the range cost of tanker stops.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200190029-7:
Flight test plans fill an agenda memo dated 1 October 1956 from C. L. Johnson to R. M. Bissell. One test aircraft can clear all known work by 1 February 1957, the agenda states. Tests that need no special gear shift to training aircraft instead.

The J-2 compass gives way to a new type in all aircraft for far north flight. Autopilot ground checks worked out in September look sound, the memo states. Defogging tests use a water vaporizer to mimic hot, wet air in the lab. Each B camera must fly two full missions to prove itself, it adds. A first C camera should be ready for flight test near 1 November.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200270020-7:
Base support for a secret project is set at a conference held 4 October 1956 at USAFE headquarters. Lt Col O. W. Karthens called the meeting in Room 228, Building B15. Only open matters were aired, since some men present lacked project clearance.

Housing built for the unit stands done and is being furnished, the record states. It should serve by about 15 October 1956. Mess halls can take the added men at once, it adds. Supply lines run from the 1st Weather Squadron to the 7030th Support Group. A 29 seat Ford bus and a Volkswagen wagon are sought for off-duty runs. Staff cars may rise to two, with Mercedes named as the pick.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200440003-7:
Budget guidance for NRO accounts is sent in a 1969 memo from Alexander H. Flax. The memo goes to the Director of CIA Reconnaissance Programs. FY 1970 program and FY 1971 budget drafts are its twin subjects.

Drafts are due by 5 May 1969, the memo states. One account is fenced to U-2R investment costs alone, new or spare gear only. The Agency must compile gear needs for itself and SAC alike, it adds. Color film use on CORONA flights is set by set rules in the attachments. Airborne collection and countermeasure work is split into named cost heads.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300090119-7:
Keeping mission knowledge tight heads staff meeting minutes dated 18 November 1958, CHAL-0413. Mr. Bissell and Col. Burke lead the session in the copy held here. Some airlift messages should go in cipher, the group agreed.

Practice on pre-mission knowledge lags behind policy, Bissell noted at the meeting. Col. Burke was tasked to check the point across the headquarters. Lockheed crews for Detachment B rise from three in December to five by mid-January. Dual oxygen work at Lockheed still lacks a firm plan, the minutes state. CORONA clearances in ARDC had just been cut to four men in all.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300150040-7:
Four operational missions mark a commander's report dated 4 April 1962, IDEA-0738. March 1962 is called the most productive month to date in its pages. Mission GRC-106 drew cheers on both sides of the unit, the commander writes.

Twenty-one sorties gave 68 hours 35 minutes of flying in the month. A late ferry flight forced a 100 hour check on aircraft 352 at the site. Repeat AC generator failures draw sharp concern in the report. Broken wires at terminal lugs are blamed, with fresh harness on order. A flame-out fault on climbs through the Badlands is flagged for study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400050040-7:
Memorandum to Dr Charyk from the Director of Special Projects, a major general, submits a program concept for LANYARD, document TS L-0001. LANYARD is defined in the objective section as a joint Air Force and CIA covert satellite program: high resolution stereo photography over high priority targets in denied areas. Thirteen launches are planned, beginning in early 1963.

Sections cover the technical approach, security, procurement in both overt and covert forms, operations, and communications nets. Annexes add a configuration control board, contractor clearance procedures, and a covert procurement plan with its own organisation needs. The covering note asks Charyk to approve the concept so it can go to CIA for concurrence and joint action, under the April 1962 management exchanges cited as references.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400060012-7:
Memorandum dated 17 August 1963, numbered 3123-63 and sent to the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence, lays out management relations problems between CIA and the Defense Department under the NRO concept. It opens with the U-2 era: control of covert reconnaissance over denied territory rested with CIA, and Richard M. Bissell ran the whole project as a one man show. The Air Force gave bases, fuel, transport, and ground support under Colonel Geary.

Since then the load has changed in kind. The U-2 now stands beside its A-12 follow-on, a family of satellites, and much larger processing and countermeasures work. The memo counts the many directors and offices now sharing direction, and presents that spread of control as the core problem the NRO structure created.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400290008-7:
Briefing paper prepared ahead of the Executive Committee meeting of 13 November 1968 warns that the Bureau of the Budget will try to scuttle the IDEALIST program there. It was written to alert the addressee and arm CIA spokesmen for rebuttal, with a facts memorandum and a Black Book of data on missions flown and yearly costs. Comments on the briefing book are invited, and a decision is sought on presenting it to Mr Helms.

Signs are then listed. Budget Bureau men have said for two years they mean to raise the program's future, and one urged Doctor Flax in strong terms to halt IDEALIST pending a study. Mr Nitze has also asked the Air Force, the Joint Chiefs, and others for a paper by 1 November weighing reconnaissance choices, among them the drone, the U-2, and the SR-71.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400320013-7:
Memorandum dated 29 April 1964, numbered 2711-64 and sent to the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence, reports the status of System 12 and NRO actions on SAC U-2 aircraft. It flags a clash of timetables: a message from Colonel Geary asks for two aircraft changed in four weeks. A 27 April paper from the NRO Director instead allows thirty days to configure five SAC aircraft.

The stock picture is tight. Thirteen System 12 sets exist in the United States inventory, designed and modified by CIA, and helping SAC would drain at least five of them. Building twenty more sets would take a crash program of at least ninety days for the first delivery. The memo pins its hopes on tests of the improved System 12A, with range and azimuth display, serving both fleets better.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500060020-7:
Memorandum IDEA 1749, dated 17 February 1964 and sent to the Operations Order Panel, attaches a resume of proposed IDEALIST operations from a United States Navy carrier. The target country is left redacted. A joint headquarters survey team is to visit the carrier on 24 February 1964. Panel members are asked to send in their questions by close of business on 19 February. The team can then carry as many as possible.

The attached concept runs in four phases. A detachment and one U-2G move aboard the carrier and deploy from Hawaii. The photographic sortie is flown, results are confirmed, and the ship returns to Hawaii. Then the detachment comes home. Flying at about 68,000 feet with range extension methods, the carrier could stand at least 800 nautical miles from the target area. One pass with the B camera is expected to cover the whole area of interest.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500070001-7:
Memorandum for the record records an ISINGLASS briefing given to Dr McMillan at Headquarters on 13 July 1965. General Ledford opened, and technical progress was under review when McMillan began a long run of questions. He asked whether flight paths had been analysed in detail, with launch points and landing sites, and whether targets per flight had been matched to stated requirements.

His doubts run through the record. A claimed quick reaction is tested against hours of B-52 flyout, an hour of mission time, and twelve hours to bring film back. Throwaway boosters, the source of the 7,000 nautical mile range figure, and a smaller 5,000 mile vehicle launched over the Mediterranean and recovered over the Indian Ocean all come up. He is also quoted calling the vehicle an excuse for a pilot to fly over the Soviet Union.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500120005-7:
Memorandum COMIREX-D-33.4/1, dated 6 August 1968 and sent to the Committee on Imagery Requirements and Exploitation, transmits a summary of non-conventional film systems. It grew from an 18 July briefing by OSA/DDS&T, after which the committee chairman asked the EXRAND chairman to report on dry processing and other unusual systems known to his group. The attachment compares new film materials that sit at varied stages of development.

Colonel Sowers is quoted stressing that the survey, while real, is not complete: it reflects only major developments EXRAND has been watching. Further reports in the same format are promised as more data comes in, building a running comparison. The distribution list runs to fifty-nine copies across the services and agencies, and an attachment sets out the Kodak BIMAT transfer process step by step.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500120032-7:
Kodak technical booklet on the BIMAT Transfer Processing System explains a way to process film with no free liquids. Standard processing, it notes, runs develop, rinse, fix, wash, and dry, a chain found cumbersome in many uses. The BIMAT method yields a high quality negative and, at the same time, a positive transparency, with simple technique and practical gear.

Materials are described first: special transfer films on a polyester base, carrying a gelatin layer with development nuclei, and the imbibant solutions they must be soaked in. Pre-soaked films, ready to use, are offered for most systems. A process summary then walks through the four needs (transfer film, chemicals, handling gear, and the exposed negative) and the pressing together of the two films that does the work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500160001-7:
Study of the utilisation of National Reconnaissance Program U-2R aircraft sets out the fleet as it stands and the problem pressing on it. The Director of the NRO, through CIA's Office of Special Activities, keeps six U-2R aircraft for covert photographic and signals missions. Strategic Air Command keeps six more, and ten older U-2C aircraft sit in the inventory, most in flyable storage.

Since September 1968 the deployed aircraft have been held twenty miles off the China coast, and each month's flying needs a fresh request to the 303 Committee. Only three overflights were flown in 1968 against seven peripheral missions, and none had been authorised in 1969 at the time of writing. Sections on determinations, survivability, alternate postures, and program costs follow, with statements from DIA and the Office of Scientific Intelligence attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040120-7:
Getting a U-2R ready for flight is timed out in Detachment H SOP H-45-11, dated 10 August 1970. The schedule covers all Materiel work for operational, training, and functional check flights. Section chiefs for maintenance, avionics, and special equipment must see that the schedule is kept on every mission the unit flies.

Alert word should arrive at least twenty-four hours before takeoff. The Director of Materiel then tells section chiefs the aircraft number, takeoff time, gear needed, and fuel load. Attached tables break the work down by shop and hour: avionics fitting and checks, tracker camera work, driftsight and autopilot preflight, and final steps ending with engine start, taxi, and takeoff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600050075-7:
Index ATTG Reg 0-2 lists the current regulations of the 1130th group, with number, date, title, and the office in charge of each. Entries run from 1969 into the early 1970s, judging by the dates printed beside them in the scan, which is rough in places. Subject groups open with indexes, publications, and written communications, including cable policy and deployment reports.

Later groups cover duty officers, travel, leave, uniforms, overtime, supply, fire safety, telephones, and radio services. Safety entries include accident reporting and traffic control near the runway. The last pages list current supplements to Air Force regulations and manuals, plus a table of obsolete group regulations and what replaced each one.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700010005-7:
Bound file opens with a shipping invoice for mission C925C, listing boxes of processed film and tape sent in January 1966 to Yokota, project headquarters, and other named points, with weights noted. Past that form the file gathers Project Headquarters operations directives for IDEALIST, the U-2 program name used throughout these papers.

One directive, 50-10-15 dated 15 December 1969, covers weather support for detachments. Another, 50-10-12 dated 8 November 1967, sets emergency notification steps for IDEALIST controllers. Later pages deal with message handling for mission notices, with set precedence and copies kept for quick reference. Together the papers show the paperwork that moved film and flight word between detachments and headquarters.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700050001-7:
Project Headquarters directive 50-3055-4, dated 15 June 1964, sets emergency steps for non-operational A-12 flights. It replaces an August 1962 version. Four cases are covered: emergencies in flight, an accident or loss inside a named boundary, an overdue or missing aircraft, and accident inquiry and reporting. Support bodies named include NORAD, the FAA, and the Air Rescue Service.

Headquarters duties include alerting the base where an A-12 will land, or seeking the most security possible when it lands elsewhere. A pre-recovery team is sent to help. Attachments hold pilot instructions and letters of introduction to base commanders. Monthly reports of accidents and incidents are required, even when there is nothing to report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800020003-7:
Summary and progress report for 1 January to 31 March 1969 opens with OXCART costs. The Pentagon office named AFIGOS asked Lockheed for A-12 cost data for fiscal 1970 and 1971 budget work. Three costing choices were requested. The first was basic upkeep of the stored fleet. The second added the cost and time to make one A-12 ready to fly. The third gave the full cost and time for five aircraft in that state.

IDEALIST sections follow, with U-2R flight test and training totals through 31 March. A drag reduction program is reported. NASA Ames wind tunnel results backed earlier Monterey findings of fifteen to twenty percent induced drag cuts. But Lockheed found the best shape unsound for the U-2R structure, so a redesign was needed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800030002-7:
IDEALIST quarterly report for 1 October to 31 December 1972 is sent 16 January 1973 by Wendell L. Bevan Jr. Its flight table records 176 flights and 573.8 hours for the quarter across aircraft 051, 053, 054, and 055. Operational and development sections divide the report, as in the other quarters of this series.

Payload news is mixed. The new lens in H configuration serial 002 gave poor results in flight test. It went back to the contractor in early December for study. Life support pages note a display opened at CIA headquarters in October 1972 on the Cuban Missile Crisis. The display showed the full life support assembly worn by agency U-2 pilots on early Cuba missions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800100004-7:
OSA Quarterly Review for the second quarter of fiscal 1972 is built as briefing slides, with sections on operations, materiel, and a funding summary. Its IDEALIST pages first look back at Detachment G flying from 1 July to 30 September 1971. Film tests in the U-2R took three sorties. Hurricane baseline photography over Gulf Coast areas took three more, for the Office of Emergency Preparedness.

Resolution tests, at eight sorties, set baselines for varied cameras at set altitudes. Four sorties qualified the new System 13C Mod D, and one tested a Q-bay hatch blower. Forecast slides then look ahead: System 13C flight tests continue, H configuration gains a new gyro and a sixteen pound weight cut, and radio interference kits are on order.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800220001-7:
Memorandum dated 27 November 1968, to the Comptroller, Special Activities, sends a revised program call for research, development, and engineering work for fiscal years 1971 to 1975. It answers a request of 15 November 1968. All research staff needs are placed under Management Support, as the program call directs, covering project officers and related staff costs for collection systems work.

No entry is made under Collection of Intelligence, though the office states it gives technical support to OSA operational programs. Staff figures for an advanced aircraft project in fiscal 1973 to 1975 rest mainly on OXCART manning. Attached pages review sensor work, including side-looking radar interest and in-house studies of methane fuel for reconnaissance aircraft.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800250017-7:
Research and development quarterly report for July, August, and September 1967 is sent 5 October 1967 to the Director for Operations, OSA. Opening items are briefings: Dr. Flax, Director of the National Reconnaissance Office, and two Bureau of the Budget staff were briefed on general research items proposed for the fiscal 1968 budget. The first flight of the U-2R is also listed among the quarter's opening points.

Life support changes fill the middle pages. A battery heat pack for visor defogging during bailout passed its tests and entered BLACK SHIELD parachutes. All suit controllers gained solid piece oxygen hose fittings, to stop breakage in buffeting or ejection. A closing table gives A-12 flying by aircraft number, with 2,570 flights and 4,222 hours 56 minutes in total.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800300020-7:
Memorandum IDEA-0397, dated 26 July 1961, to the Chief, Security Branch, Development Projects Division, voices grave concern over briefing policy officials on DPD work. Getting political permission for operations now requires more of these briefings. The writer points to the Black Book presentations that grew up with the IDEALIST program, once handled in one or two copies by the Director or his deputies in person.

That practice is spreading. For Project TACKLE, staff had to make no less than nine Black Books for a White House meeting on 14 July, each holding priority targets, cover story, and program detail. Once one member of a policy body gets a book, all others demand the same. The writer asks for views on stopping the drift toward circulating full operations orders.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800340008-7:
Memorandum for the record 3712-63, dated 23 November 1963, compares how long three aircraft programs took to reach set milestones. Charts and tables set the A-12 beside the B-58 and the B-70. For the A-12, twenty-six months of early design studies came before the contract go-ahead. Fifty months since go-ahead had passed by the date of the memo, the text states.

Milestones for the A-12 follow: rollout at twenty-nine months, first flight at thirty-one, first Mach 2 flight at thirty-seven, and first Mach 3 flight at forty-six. The B-58 section opens with thirty-two months of design studies. A chronological table at the end gives milestone dates for all three aircraft, from first design competition wins to engine test completions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800340026-7:
Memorandum 2083-67, dated 12 January 1967, to the executive secretary of the DDS&T Historical Board, answers a call for extra studies beyond the OSA narrative history. The office reports that it has reviewed its records and sees no need for outside studies at this time. Its own staff, with long experience of the office, can cover the history from the documents already held.

A draft outline is attached for information, with shifts in emphasis still possible as study proceeds. Outline entries run from background and management through pilot recruiting and training, air force U-2 follow-on work, and detachment histories. The file is a short administrative reply, not the history itself, and its second half is a filing slip for the memorandum.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02416a000400140030-7:
File gathers successive versions of Project Headquarters directive 50-10-24 on operational hazard reports. The first version is dated 7 February 1966, the second 1 February 1967, and the third 1 October 1973. Each version keeps the same core. A hazard is any state or act that may affect the safety of project aircraft or people. Detachment commanders must report it at once and look into it.

Reporting rules are spelled out in each version. Hazards go to headquarters by immediate precedence or higher. The message format lists aircraft number, pilot or operator, and the main system at fault. It also asks for a narrative of the hazard, and corrective action taken or planned. Later versions add a ground or air marker as the first field, showing how the form grew with the program.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030002-7:
Memorandum dated 6 January, to the Chief, Services Branch, reports a survey of the Reproduction Division. The survey follows the path of Form No. 36-2, the reproduction requisition, under the procedure then in use. It then sets out a proposed new procedure for handling and scheduling the same work. Present practice is described step by step: the form arrives in duplicate, the control clerk stamps it and assigns a job number, and the blue carbon copy goes back to the requester.

Log book entries are listed in full, from type of work and number of originals to delivery dates asked for and met. The proposed scheme keeps the log in Room 202, North Building. A specimen requisition form closes the file, with boxes for process, paper, fastening, and delivery receipt.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050163-7:
Bureau of the Budget Circular No. A-8, revised and dated 19 July 1946, sets allowances payable to federal officers and employees stationed in foreign countries. From the first pay period after 30 June 1946, staff abroad are paid quarters and cost of living allowances under these rules, replacing the older living and quarters allowances. The revision cancels the 1943 circular and its supplements and appendices, the preamble states.

Parts A and B govern quarters and cost of living allowances. Long appendix tables grade posts by country and city, from Guatemala City and Port-au-Prince to Tehran, Rome, and Monrovia, and set maximum rates by pay grade. A closing table for Rumania, dated 31 December 1946, gives maxima by grade and sets reductions where quarters are obtained at low daily cost, falling to zero above three dollars a day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050181-7:
Public Law 600, 79th Congress, approved 2 August 1946, authorizes certain administrative expenses in the government service. Its first section sets the core rule for staff transfers. A civilian officer or employee moved between official stations for permanent duty is covered, when the move is authorized in the travel order. Travel costs for himself and his immediate family are then paid from government funds. Packing, crating, storage, drayage, and unpacking of household goods and effects are also paid.

Weight limits are fixed in the text: seven thousand pounds uncrated, or eight thousand seven hundred and fifty pounds crated. Later sections govern advertising for government sales, witness fees and mileage at departmental hearings, and definitions of government and appropriation. Sections 1 and 2 took effect on the first day of the third calendar month after enactment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050190-7:
National Intelligence Authority directive dated 8 February 1946 lays down policies and procedures governing the Central Intelligence Group. It rests on the President's letter of 22 January 1946 naming the undersigned as the Authority. The group is to be organized and run as a cooperative interdepartmental activity. The State, War, and Navy Departments take part on a fair basis. The Army Air Forces are represented like the Army and Navy.

The group will furnish strategic and national policy intelligence to the President and the State, War, and Navy Departments. It will also serve the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee and the Joint Chiefs of Staff, as fitting. The Director must furnish the Authority a secretariat, to prepare agendas, circulate papers, attend meetings, and keep minutes. The President's letter is enclosed, signed Harry Truman, and closes with the duty of fully protecting intelligence sources and methods.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200070170-7:
Memorandum of agreement sets out the same signal property procedures as the draft bound in this slice under a 29 December 1948 executive memorandum. Accountability records rest with the Storage and Issue Section, Supply Division, Services Office. The Communications Division, OSO, keeps a parallel memorandum record of stock, posted from requisitions as they arrive. Copies of debit and credit vouchers go to that division for information, keeping both records in step.

The catalogue section requires a joint review of all signal equipment on hand. Correct names will be fixed for each item, and a catalogue carrying them will be issued and distributed by the Services Office. Receiving copies of purchase orders stay put until a Communications Division inspector signs the file copy. For shipments, the cargo request must show priority, shipment date, and place, coordinated with the Transportation Section.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200100004-7:
Monthly report of operations for the period ending 31 July 1953, from the Chief, Records Management and Distribution Branch. This is the first month of the fiscal year in the report form, so to date totals start from July 1953. Leave figures are high: twenty-four in Mail Control, thirteen in Records Management, and six at the Records Center. Pending reassignment stands at fifteen, all in Mail Control. Three new applicants were interviewed, all recruited by Personnel.

Administration items report a records survey of the Office of Operations. The survey of that office's headquarters records had been completed for the areas named. Project 5-53, the Correspondence Manual rewrite, saw no action this month, its analyst being on other priority work after finishing the Basic Intelligence Course on 10 July. Filming totals 6,088 images in the month, split 3,777 rotary and 2,311 flatbed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00355a000100020015-7:
Memorandum dated 19 August 1952 closes S/PP Project 52-33, Space for O/TR Expansion, on paper. The project grew out of Project 52-18, a staff study on training for new personnel, which had centered on the Career Service Committee report and the Basic Intelligence Course. A large rise in enrollment looked likely, and with it an urgent need for more space. Several studies and two full alternative plans were presented on an informal basis from June 1952.

Late in July the Director of Training gave overall space planning to the new head of the Support Staff, and S/PP shifted to a consulting role. Enrollment guesses drive the close: two Personnel officers put flow at one hundred a month, four times the rate handled so far. The memo advises waiting for clearer prospects rather than taking space that could become a white elephant.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100050040-7:
Paper by Eliot S. Berkley proposes a program for bringing college and university social science staff into government work. In a long defense crisis, he argues, well formed proposals from people outside government often never reach the officials who could use them. Personal contacts ease the gap for a few, above all for those who served in government before, but no general channel exists. The loss falls on policy making across the government.

Two elements make up the program. First, careful proposals from social science faculty would be gathered in an orderly way and passed to the right agencies. Second, agencies could hand universities set problems and projects they want worked on, a step toward contract research. As more schools join, staff at different campuses working the same problem could pool their efforts and meet agency staff jointly, the paper concludes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100140004-7:
Course catalog describes the training offered by the Communications Training Branch for staff of two offices. Courses qualify a student for the radio and cipher duties of his assignment. Subjects span staff and secret radio operating and theory. They also cover teletype and power gear upkeep, teletype procedure, covert watch work, and cipher systems and practice, staff and secret alike.

The staff radio course runs twelve weeks, with classes entering on a rolling basis. It teaches sending and receiving of Morse code, radio theory, and care of agency gear. Signal plans and procedures are taught, with on the air practice included. Teletype courses cover message sending and the cipher devices used with the machines. The secret cipher course has no fixed length. It depends on the student's ability, past experience, and the assignment ahead, and students are normally taught one by one.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100140013-7:
Management Training Program of the Management Analysis Office is laid out in stages. An opening stage covers machine methods, records work, and the groundwork of organization and methods study. Office accounting machines are among its topics. The trainee learns enough of each field to spot problem areas in an office under study. Records work is stressed as one of the most significant phases of the whole training, the text states.

Stage two puts the trainee on real surveys, under the close eye of a senior examiner, for about four months. Stage three is research training, built on a required reading list. Titles include the Hoover Commission reports of February 1949, Budget Bureau bulletins on process charting and work measurement, and Army Service Forces manuals of 1943 and 1945.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00011a000100020114-7:
Briefing points, dated 1 October 1952, tell trainers what to cover when instructing supervisors in the use of the Personnel Evaluation Report. The form grew out of the Career Service Committee's work. Its final report reached the agency in June 1952, after more than a year of study by many committees. The form was built by one of those committees, as part of the CIA Career Service Program.

Numbered points walk the supervisor through the form, item by item. Due dates and the period covered are set by the central Personnel Office. Hard questions go to the Evaluations Officer, the channel for all word on the program. Supervisors should settle a steady policy on showing the finished form to the person rated, the notes advise. Staff meetings are the place to settle it. The close ties good morale to trust in the organization, and to full use of a person's abilities.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00011a000100070010-7:
Memorandum dated 5 January 1953, to Training Liaison Officers, announces area and language programs at non-CIA facilities abroad. The programs were built for headquarters staff. They are strictly training: no operational work, and no official tie with the Agency or its staff, is allowed during the training period. All letters and calls must name the programs by letter, as Program A and so on. Security on a need to know basis is required of everyone for whom training is asked.

Basic qualifications are the same for all programs: a bachelor's degree or its equal, ability to do graduate study, and above average language aptitude, Program E excepted, plus a Top Secret clearance. One program detailed is a Near East course of thirteen weeks, full time, from about 1 July 1953, with an agency quota of fifteen and requests due 15 March 1953.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00037a000200030006-7:
Memorandum dated September 1953 asks the Director of Training for training material for an Air Force program. The Air Force is revising its psychological warfare staff officer training and is charged with building the course. Staff officers trained for that work will act in ways parallel to covert activity in aims and targets, the memo argues. They should therefore know the covert phases of such work, and unity of action makes the point essential.

Material is asked on two heads: the training given to staff in the techniques of propaganda, and the fullest information the Agency can give on propaganda requirements. It may stay at the level of general principles, doctrine, and methods, with no data on current operations. Receipt forms bound with the memo route the papers to the Chief, Psychological Warfare Division, Headquarters USAF, with signed receipts returned to the Agency's central records.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00037a000200070020-7:
Test tables record radio test results in two sets. Table number 1 covers ground to ground tests, with five marked columns of results. Range is given in miles, from 0.2 to about 1.6. The ground between transmitter and receiver is described. Entries name cleared flat area with straight line of sight. They also name flat terrain with a small patch of trees in the way, and rolling terrain with heavy woods.

Table number 2 adds altitude. Tests run from short ranges at fifty feet up to thirty miles at 3,000 feet, with result marks in the same five columns. The marks mix X signs, circles, and bracketed signs, with no key in the pages. The file is data only: no narrative or findings text accompanies the tables.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100020006-7:
Official report on the Eighth Agency Orientation Course covers the program of 18 to 21 November 1952 in the Department of Agriculture Auditorium. It was the fourth course under the regulation for one every three months. The material was split in four, under the pattern that worked at the seventh course: Background, Support and Coordination, the Production Function, and the Impact of Intelligence. The split aims to cut duplication and give the course a consecutive flow, the report states.

Evaluation praises panels where preparation showed, the Economic Intelligence Panel among them. Better microphones around the panel table are wanted for future courses. Attendance tables close the file. Total attendance is given as 521. Old employees, in the agency over six months, numbered 368, or 74.5 percent; new employees numbered 133, or 25.5 percent. Grade tables show most of the house in the middle grades.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100020015-7:
Address headed Members of the Faculty and Students opens by refusing two easy paths. The speaker will not paint a gruesome picture of intrigue or a web of cloak and dagger thought. Neither will he give an evasive talk about a field the nation knows too little of. Much of that ignorance comes from a false idea of security: a hush-hush cover over all intelligence work. The process loses by it: trust is not won from those whose help is needed.

Blame follows the same error. When the function is not understood, intelligence offices become a dumping ground for blame that belongs elsewhere. The speech then traces the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group, from the service secretaries' plan to President Truman's order of 22 January 1946. The close is a plea: policy must rest on fact, not rumor.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100030017-7:
Memorandum from August 1952 on allowances rules. It went to the Deputy Director for Administration. The sender was the Chief, Administrative Staff (Special). A paper of 25 June 1952 raised the same subject. The aim was one set of Agency rules. Those rules should match the standard government rules. Running them well was a second aim.

Work listed covers several tasks. Agency policy was to be restated. The kinds of allowances were to be sorted. Each kind was to be defined anew. Central steps for granting payments were planned. Checking those payments was planned too. Faults found include split power over grants. Chiefs of mission and headquarters shared that power. The split bred confusion and uneven grants. Rules also blurred two kinds of payment. Some were due as of right. Others needed a claim first.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020073-7:
Proposal dated 6 August 1953 for a new division. The Chief, Language Training and Programs Divisions, sent it. It went to the Director of Training. A deputy director was the route used. Three drafts were attached to the memo. One stated mission and functions. One gave a descriptive table of organization. One was an organizational chart.

The new body would be a Professional Training Division. Its chief would plan and develop training. Internal and external training both fell in scope. Fields named include area and language work. Staff, management, and technical fields appear too. Industrial and other subject training is covered. Agency career staff growth is the stated end. Leaner staffing also gets frank treatment. Four area studies coordinator posts would go. Most planned internal area programs would end. A few area courses could still run.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020091-7:
Functions and activities statement, Assessment and Evaluation Staff. The staff runs professional psychological services for training. It advises the Director of Training on such work. Programs and facilities sit inside the United States. Overseas programs get staff help and supervision. Other Agency parts may request help too. The Director of Training must consent first.

An Assessment Branch sits inside the staff. It studies referred people in depth. Fitness for critical or sensitive posts is the question. It builds a staff able to do such work. It studies what makes people succeed in intelligence. Methods are checked and refined over time. A Training Evaluation Branch sits beside it. That branch builds records of student learning. Traits shown in training are recorded too. The Professional Selection Panel uses those records. Supervisors use them for career planning as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000080001-7:
Negotiated Agency contract number KH-95 with Eastman Kodak Company. The company sits in Rochester, New York. It was incorporated in New Jersey. The contract amount reads as 150,000 dollars. Inspection point was the contractor's New York site. The parties signed on 15 March 1956. The contractor must furnish facilities under the deal. It must deliver supplies and perform services too.

The attached schedule sets out that work in detail. Rights and duties are governed by the schedule. General provisions govern them as well. Where the two conflict, the schedule controls. That rule is stated on the contract face. Corporate authority pages follow the signatures. An officer certified the signing for the company. He acted within the scope of corporate powers. Later pages turn to labor and pay terms. Job classifications carry set rates under them. Air courier duties appear in the terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000080100-7:
Memorandum dated 20 March 1956 on project security personnel. Training for those personnel is the subject. An outline of major personnel actions was requested. Nine Agency project security men were on board. They were scheduled to attend the training program. Three to five more men were expected soon. Others would join in the period ahead.

The training course would begin on 26 March 1956. It would end on or about 24 April. The first two weeks held normal duty training. Orientation covered organization in that period. Italian language study formed part of the plan. A presentation on project operations was expected. On completion, the new men would be dispatched. Their destination is redacted in the text. Arrival there was expected around 25 April 1956. A long set of contract provisions follows the memo. Payment withholding caps appear in that text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000090046-7:
Memorandum on ground exploitation equipment for three systems. Systems number one, three, and four are named. Earlier Agency memoranda are cited in the head. Those memos date from March and April 1956. Film analysis equipment is the main topic. One bench item would sit in the Washington area. It would be held there after its work ended. Deliveries were set for June 1956.

System one analysis gear has three pieces. A playback unit is the first piece named. An event indicator is the second piece. A third indicator unit completes the set. The playback unit has three heads on it. Playback, stop, and record are those heads. Speeds of three, seven, and fifteen inches per second are given. Nineteen such units had been requested in total. Display equipment for a later system is noted. It notes signals at four times normal speed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000090226-7:
Agency memorandum for the record dated 14 April 1956, number SAPC-4802. Observations at Watertown on photographic equipment form the subject. Simulated operations ran from 8 to 14 April. Configurations A-1 and A-2 were observed in use. Both were built for AQUATONE. The photographic unit of Detachment A was observed too. A judgment opens the memorandum text.

Equipment and personnel show limited capability, in that judgment. That capability could grow materially with reasonable effort. Better equipment and more training are the paths named. Maker representatives would be needed at the base. Hycon and another firm are named for that role. They would ensure approved procedures were followed. Cameras observed include a Hycon tri-metrogon type. Its focal length is four inches. A 24-inch K-38 camera is listed. A tracker camera and drift sight complete the set.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000100080016-7:
Accomplishments and objectives statement for Training (General). Fiscal year 1952 was its first full year. Courses planned in late fiscal 1951 were run. Their organization and administration are claimed as gains. A Career Service Program was designed that year. It grew through the Agency Career Service Committee. Courses were tied to office requirements as well.

Course aims are listed in the statement. Indoctrination of Agency personnel comes first in the list. Mission, functions, and organization of CIA are covered. The language and process of intelligence follow. Professional training forms the next stated aim. Later sections treat language training demand. Demand stayed constant in fiscal 1953, the text states. Office requests drove that steady demand. Defense schools and colleges get a section too. Picked civilians train at those schools. Their grasp of service functions improves there. Coordination between services and CIA is promoted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000100090015-7:
Program booklet for the Arthur S. Flemming Awards. The year covered is 1953, the sixth annual program. Outstanding young men in federal service are honored. The Junior Chamber of Commerce of the capital runs it. Its purpose is threefold, the booklet states. Recognition goes to young men with outstanding work. Their deeds are publicized to draw others in. Confidence in government is promoted by the program.

The Civil Service Commission supported the program warmly. The Federal Personnel Council assisted it as well. Eligibility rules are set out in the booklet. Any civilian male officer or employee may be nominated. He must not reach forty before 1 January 1954. Justification must cite facts, not opinions. Examples and details must support each nomination. Three pages is the limit for that justification. Presentation rules close the visible text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000200090005-7:
Progress report number one for research project number five. The project studies what the intelligence officer's work demands. Talks were held with Agency training staff members. Those members had field experience in their careers. Early working terms came out of those talks. Case officer job needs were the focus. The report discusses those early working terms. More research work is urged in it.

Uses of a needs statement are reviewed first. Such a statement is basic to testing assessment. Judgments of job performance must be exact and clear. A fair sample of officials is needed. Accounts of effective case officers were built up. Accounts of weak ones were built up too. Those data built an early needs list. Notes were taken during each talk. A written summary followed each talk later. Proposed uses shape what the statement must bear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000200100003-7:
Qualifications lists for seven main Agency staff classes. Research specialists are treated first in the pages. Age carries no limits for that class. A bachelor's degree is highly desirable for it. Fields favored include education and world affairs. Political science, history, and scientific method are named. Linguistics skill is favored as well. Two years of research project charge are asked.

Two years of overseas intelligence work are also asked. Other traits are spelled out in plain terms. The specialist must be mature and steady in temper. Intelligence should sit in the upper ten percent. A liking for endless detail is expected. Instructor background appears in the later pages. A college degree or equal background is asked. Courses inside military or government structures are specified. Teaching time in service schools is asked too. Informal academic settings count toward that time.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000200110011-7:
Attachment containing a long Phase III training critique. The writer states intense interest in training results. Honest disappointment with those results is admitted. Little demonstrable gain in performance is seen. Understanding of Agency responsibilities seems weak too. That weakness shows in staff who finished training. The critique covers eight years of observation. Field and headquarters work both inform it.

Supervision of case officers sharpened the writer's view. Inadequacies of courses stand out in that role. A summary of recommendations opens the critique proper. The stated objective of Phase III is weighed first. Some aspects partly achieved their objectives, it finds. The course pinpointed key regulations for officers. Desk and case officers both gained that much. Relating the course to new staff is the hard problem. Active thought inside the course context is needed. Without it, real benefit is hard to reach.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100030009-7:
Organization and Methods survey report on central processing of travelers. Duplication of effort is the problem it tackles. Two branches shared the traveler work. The Central Processing Branch sat in the Personnel Office. The Passenger Movement Branch sat in Logistics. Meetings were held in April and June 1953. Determinations from those meetings are attached. A joint committee worked out the details.

Processing of travelers should sit with one branch. Overseas and domestic travel both fall in that plan. The Logistics Office keeps staff responsibility for transport. Technical aspects stay with the Passenger Movement Branch. Personal effects handling is named among those aspects. Unaccompanied baggage, household goods, and automobiles are listed. The Transportation Division chief holds matching responsibility. His role mirrors the general duties of his office. Attachments carry the agreed duty split.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100100001-7:
Office memorandum dated 30 March 1953, a follow-up report. The Agency Top Secret Control System is its subject. The Organization and Methods Service sent it. It went to the collection and dissemination chief. The CIA Top Secret Control Officer was the route. Accomplishments to date were to be reviewed. Actions to finish installation were to be set.

A final report had gone forward in May 1952. Seventeen reports preceded that final one. Twenty-six control areas and sub-stations were covered. Meetings followed between the control officers involved. Recommendations in the reports were accepted in principle. Ways of carrying them out were developed. Inspection and Security staff attended meetings on request. They approved the security side of the plan. Two objectives bound the system proposed here. Control of documents moving between areas is one. Inventory of all Top Secret documents is the other.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100190011-7:
Tab B summary of table of organization reductions. A survey of budget and fiscal work stands behind it. Area divisions of the plans directorate are covered. Senior staffs of that directorate are covered too. Their budget elements sit in the right places, it finds. Economic and efficient performance is the test used. Exceptions to that finding are noted below it.

Personnel needed for essential functions can fall materially. That fall depends on adopting the listed recommendations. Travel voucher preparation should end in the divisions. Staff employees should use the Central Processing Branch instead. Travel order preparation should be withdrawn as well. That work should move to a single assigned place. Job duty text fills the later pages. Contract and project personnel duties are described. Table of organization development duties follow them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100260004-7:
Study file on an Agency personnel and training section, opening with action tables. SF-50 and SF-52 actions for one area division are counted. June, July, and August 1953 are the months covered. Appointments numbered eight in the visible table. Reassignments numbered thirty-six across the period. Promotions numbered sixteen in the same table. Conversions and name changes numbered two each.

Records kept by the section are catalogued next. Individual personnel files lead that catalogue. Their folders divide into four groups of documents. Personnel actions, travel and finance, and training appear. General correspondence forms the fourth group there. A position inventory record is described as well. It is a typewritten list of table slots. Incumbents are written in as actions occur. Study conclusions close the file text. A smaller table of organization is contemplated there. Acceptance of two recommendations drives that outcome.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200070013-7:
Memo to the Deputy Director, Administration. A merger of the Real Estate and Construction Division is proposed. The Chief, Procurement and Supply Office, sent it. Division functions would fold into his office. Present and future workload drives the proposal. Facts bearing on the problem open the body. Transfer to procurement came on 20 August 1952.

General Services had held the unit before that move. The unit provides all real estate needs across the Agency. Construction needs of the Agency are also its charge. Certain headquarters space functions stay with General Services. Maintenance functions there are likewise left out. Policy direction comes from the office above. Technical work remains the unit's own charge. Staff and operating functions both sit in it. A register of holdings is discussed later. Records for many holdings are incomplete there. Formal report rules are planned in the text. Reporting forms and steps would follow them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200090002-7:
Survey report on the Organization and Methods Service. It is presented to the Management Officer. Work proceeded under the Comptroller's authorization and guidance. Purpose, functions, and capability of the service were surveyed. Relations of the service were examined as well. Immediate improvements were the first aim. Future action for wider Agency service was the second.

Background covers substantial change over two years. Philosophy, purpose, and organization all shifted in it. Functions and staff of the service shifted too. Approach moved from authoritative to consultant style. The pendulum may have swung too far, it notes. The incoming officer inherited low morale a year earlier. Prestige was impaired and customer relations weak. Steady progress since then is recorded in the report. Mission, authority, and functions have been clarified. Three assistant management officers were appointed in reorganization. A booklet drafting task for the Deputy Director appears.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200100019-7:
Procedure notes for routing and processing security requests. A status table opens the released text. Items are marked tested, analyzed, or accomplished. Differences in reporting periods head the problem list. Non-receipt of basic records is the second problem. Delays in delivery of accounting forms follow. Month-end periods made those delays worst. Lack of full coordination is the fourth problem.

Procedures for requesting clearances were established in response. Procedures for reporting clearances came with them. An exhibit carries the full procedure text. Case file control is being standardized as well. Unnecessary controls, logs, and records would end. A standard three by five control card was designed. Operations Staff and Special Referral Group would use it. Agency field offices would use the same card format. Basic case data is reproduced on the card. A ditto master produces the needed copies. Meetings with two offices expedited processing that July.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150005-7:
Interim report on a machine indexing project. The Agency's correlation mission opens the summary. Information within very broad fields must correlate. Large numbers of records need organization for specialists. Documents must answer a wide range of subjects. Many situations cannot be predicted at receipt. The document library should act as memory.

Mere recording of information is not enough there. Quick recall must serve changing intelligence requirements. Recall should rest on new associations of ideas. Specific situations as they arise set those associations. Russian views of the problem appear in an appendix. First steps toward the memory function came in March 1947. Punch card work began at that point historically. Scanning mechanics fill the technical middle. A plugboard can condition the scanning pattern. Selection occurs only when every pattern is detected. Four patterns combine as a logical product.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150014-7:
Part nine of the Agency indexing study covers files and steps for code growth. An indexing system for electronic gear is the goal. The problem is called practical here. Theory can contribute much of importance. The trial path must be taken. Best results within a fair time require it. Two paths ran at once on terms.

One path used Intelligence Subject Code terms. Its terms are of a more general nature. The other drew more terms together. Subject heading lists supplied many of them. Classing systems and textbook indexes supplied more. Science and technology formed that general field. Semantic factoring based code construction in both paths. A record file analyzed the code terms. Each heading line was punched on its own card. The new scanning machine searched that file. Terms like radiation were searched one by one. Basic English received consideration in the work. Its words fit everyday situations narrowly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200200009-7:
Staff policy study copy on Agency dealings with employees. The scan of this copy is rough in places. Its problem matches the policy question on services. Rules should govern use of Agency services. Employee selection, training, and handling are covered. Placement and effective use of each person are named. Termination of employees completes the stated problem.

Assumptions mirror the policy framing. Staff administration is no different in rule here. Single actions must flow from set policy. Many-sided policy is ruled out by the text. Efficiency is a duty in the Agency. Needless or duplicating costs must be avoided there. Facts name forces outside staff jurisdiction again. Medical and psychiatric forces lead that list. Psychological force stands outside the pale as well. Security handling forms the third named force. Psychologists assist in selection work later. Objective and consistent reports are their product. Deep testing services are described there.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200200045-7:
Untitled memorandum of May 1951 on psychological staffing. A Division of Psychology was requested on 8 March 1951. The Agency Director of Training's office would house it. Approval for the division had not been given. Its exact status is unknown. One branch would be Aptitude Appraisal.

That branch would embrace three teams in all. A Field Testing Team forms the first. A Headquarters Testing Team forms the second. An Assessment Team forms the third team. A memorandum of 10 May 1951 is studied closely. It presents needs for the Assessment Program. College graduate Candidate Trainees are its subjects. Grades requested may be a little excessive. Positions requested draw the same question there. Approving them might exceed the Assessment Team alone. Workload figures for senior psychologists follow later. A day between assessment days is needed. Reports and future cases consume that day. Four intensive cases weekly is the capacity. Covert cases take two days each.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00259a000200090002-7:
Memo dated 18 October 1954 on a teacher overload. It went to the Agency Chief, Operations Instruction School. Critical situation in Phases II and III is the subject. Many talks had already covered the problem. A memo of record was now wanted. The Training chief and his deputy would consider it. Easing of the overload is the decision sought.

Reports over recent months confirmed the problem upward. The load's being is assumed agreed by all parties. Policy matters are set aside in the memo. Seriousness touches teachers' lives in several ways. Several senior teachers hold Reserve Officer rank. Keeping that rank in force grows difficult. Relief staffing receives attention in later pages. One new teacher could start in early January. Another might be ready at that time. No plans staff stand ready to join the school. Qualified field staff must be obtained for teaching. Lowering teacher standards would be a grave mistake.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100020004-7:
Staff study dated 31 October 1949 on CIA participation. Foreign information programming and wartime control are its field. Admiral Roscoe Hillenkoetter is the addressee as Director of Central Intelligence. The writer served as CIA representative on two staffs. Combined SSC-A and NSC-43 staffs are meant. A table of contents frames four problems. Combining two council papers poses the first.

Language must legally express CIA's role and mission. That wording for the new paper is problem one. Organization and functions form the second problem. A Joint Intelligence Committee request poses the third. Its request dates from May 1949 originally. A letter from Mr. Armstrong poses the fourth. That letter reached the Director on 7 October 1949. Analysis sections discuss each problem in turn. Conclusions follow for all four problems separately. One answer awaits resolution by planning offices first. A draft letter to Armstrong is suggested later.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100070009-7:
National Science Foundation guide for reporting research spending pledges. Data covers federal science research and growth work. Non-profit institutions are where the pledges fall. The Bureau of the Budget compiled earlier statistics. Fiscal years 1946, 1949, and 1950 were covered. Funds pledged at colleges and universities were measured. The Foundation was asked to take over this tally.

Duties set by law ground that ask in the text. General interest in the field supports it too. Scope and classes were changed for use. Information is asked for two fiscal years. Pledges in 1951 and 1952 are wanted. Federal agencies incurred those pledges at non-profits. Data is limited to research in the sciences. Classes to be used are explained in detail. Trouble with basic research terms appears later. Program and nonprogram splits cause such trouble. Drive behind work is hard to tell. Applied research and growth pose similar trouble.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100140001-7:
Agency field trip report covering 9 September to 1 November 1953. The station visited is redacted in the release. A power line transfer fills the opening pages. Engineers had built the plant and transmission system. Transfer to a public company was asked for locally. The Civil Administrator would create that company. The Army would then lease the system back.

The Commanding Officer sought help drafting an endorsement. Study and consultation preceded that drafting work. The Post Engineer and Construction Engineer were consulted. Civil affairs and district offices cleared it informally. A conference then produced a conclusion agreed by all. Direct transfer was better on two grounds. Accounting and security both favored that route. Funds transfer at department level was the alternative. Power for Washington action was given in writing. Quarters fittings appear in the later report pages. Rugs and window coverings outweighed other fittings there.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100150091-7:
Paper on the background of central intelligence. The idea grew out of World War II years. Lack of joining hurt the military effort badly. Departmental and other services worked separate then. A presidential order set up the organization. Its date was 22 January 1946 in the account. Long study by interested departments preceded it.

A draft order was agreed in beforehand by all. The Secretaries of State, War, and Navy agreed. Sending to the President came on 7 January 1946. A War Department committee shaped the draft. Assistant Secretary Lovett headed that committee's work. Wide hearings ran during October 1945. Many proposals on future work were received. The Strategic Services Unit submitted one such proposal. Its reasoning for the central idea was clearest. On-the-job hazards receive warning treatment later. Unjoined clandestine work would increase those hazards. Departments with great duties cannot put them first. Special means like training and financing are needed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100190024-7:
Memorandum for the record dated 15 January 1952. Legislative problems of the Psychological Strategy Board are recorded. A 5 January 1952 memorandum is referenced first. Charles Norberg of the Board wrote that reference. Liaison with Congressmen was its subject there. Houston and Pforzheimer met Board staff on it. The Board's problems divide into three categories.

Budget problems form the first category named. Personnel problems form the second category. Substantive problems form the third category listed. Financing comes from three budgets equally shared. State, Defense, and the Agency each contribute. The figure of 188,000 dollars apiece is given. A single appearance per committee is preferred there. Defending the budget three times is the alternative. Senate interest gets attention in later pages. Two Senate committees share responsibility there. Mutual Security Agency workings draw that joint interest.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100190051-7:
Memorandum dated 11 July 1951 on the Psychological Strategy Board. The General Counsel wrote to the Deputy Director, Administration. Lawrence R. Houston signed the memorandum. A presidential directive ordered a salary payment. Mr. Gordon Gray was to receive 16,000 dollars yearly. No agency but this one can pay that. Specific statutory authority is lacking elsewhere government-wide.

Gray is not an employee of this Agency though. Paying him stretches even this Agency's authority. Specific presidential instructions should cover such payment instead. A draft letter to that effect is attached. Tab A carries that draft letter text. The Bureau of the Budget would route it. Presidential signature on it is the recommendation. An alternative exists if signature is declined. A White House request by an authoritative spokesman suffices. Mr. Donald Dawson is named as such a spokesman. Tab B would serve in that case.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100230029-7:
Writing on 21 July 1950, the Assistant Director for Collection and Dissemination told the Management Officer that a plan to split liaison work would do more harm than good. The plan, sent to all assistant directors on 10 July, would move liaison duties out of one office. He argues it would take three liaison officers to do work now done by one. Other offices would need full-time staff just to keep contact with the Pentagon and the State Department.

The memorandum warns that papers other agencies least want to share are often the ones CIA most needs. Pressure, steady contact, and one clear channel are presented as the means to get reports and cables sent across. It is a defence of central liaison, written while the young Agency was still fixing who spoke for it to the rest of government.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400060007-7:
Categories of CIA personnel form the problem in a memorandum dated 25 February 1953 for the Chairman of the CIA Career Service Board. Two linked tasks are set: fix the main staff groups the Agency needs, and state the basic tie between the Agency and each group. A sound answer, the paper says, rests on how far the Agency may direct a person's work. It also rests on how lasting the need for that person's service is likely to be.

A second aim is a clear line between career staff and all other staff. The paper says the lack of set groups had slowed work on wider staff policy. It frames group labels not as paperwork but as the base on which the whole career program would stand.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400120028-7:
An Agency notice sets out the principles that govern how authority is used and handed down inside the organisation. Sound running of a large body, it argues, needs power spread to officials in a clear chain. Some powers call for formal grant and formal proof of that grant. The notice gives two reasons for care: written proof is a legal need in some cases, and it is sound practice in the rest.

Size and complexity also drive the rule, since one task may need several powers used in step. Clear records show whether those powers were used in proper order. Crossed wires and gaps in who may act are the faults the notice aims to prevent. The scan is worn, but the notice's stress on written delegation comes through plainly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500030009-7:
Payment of home leave travel for overseas personnel who are changing station for good to the continental United States is tested in an office memorandum dated 6 November 1952. It runs from the Comptroller's office to the Office of the General Counsel. Three earlier papers are listed as raising the question, two from the Finance Division in April 1952 and one from the Assistant Comptroller in May. Their topics were grants of home leave and shifting dependency and residency reports.

Counsel then works from the statutes and rulings that define home leave and its travel rights. The hard point is fit: leave rules were written for staff returning to a foreign post, not for staff ending overseas service. How the two sets of orders meet decides whether the fare home is a public cost.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500050007-7:
S. 1507, printed with House Report Number 3013, would amend section 10 of the Act of 2 August 1946 on drawing two kinds of government money. The act passed the Senate and reached the House in June 1949, going to the Committee on Armed Services. It was reported with an amendment in August 1950. Italic text in the print marks the part to be inserted.

The subject is pay, allowances, and travel costs for a person already drawing a pension, disability allowance, disability compensation, or retired pay. Naval Reserve and Marine Corps Reserve members are named first in the new wording. The change would let such members take later service without the older bar working in the same blunt way.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500060033-7:
An appendix gathers the court and official rulings that gloss sections 58, 69, and 70 of Title 5, the dual-pay statutes. A contents page lists six court cases first, from Woodwell against the United States onward. A Court of Claims decision and an Attorney General opinion follow. Many Comptroller General decisions are cited across the closing pages.

The first case study gives agreed facts in numbered points. Woodwell, paid two thousand dollars a year by the Treasury to inspect electric light plants, was ordered to work on a lighting and heating plant for the Interior Department. He did that work, some nine hundred hours, outside his normal hours. Summaries like this let lawyers see quickly which side won each dual-pay fight.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500080059-7:
Benefits for hazardous service are sketched in a general proposal whose surviving pages open in mid-scheme. Cases of death, injury, or illness abroad would reach the Board through the proper personnel office. Supervisors of staff who might qualify are drawn into the reporting chain. For those who qualify, a death gratuity equal to one year's salary heads the list.

Only base salary counts toward that sum, leaving out allowances, differentials, overtime, and hazard pay itself. The money goes to the beneficiary the worker named in writing, or to the estate if none was named. It is not to be set against benefits under the Compensation Act, nor counted as a choice between schemes. Practice in the Public Health Service is cited as a model for the benefit.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500090003-7:
Senate Report Number 2265, ordered printed on 10 August 1950, backs H.R. 7824 on running performance-rating plans for federal staff. Mr. Frear sent in the report for the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. The committee favoured the bill with amendments and urged that it pass. A statement section explains that the bill builds a performance-rating system to stand in place of the old one.

The older efficiency rating system sat in Title IX of the Classification Act of 1949. Parts of the new plan had appeared in S. 2111, a bill drawn to carry out reform advice. The report then compares the two measures and lists the changes made. It is the Senate half of the paper trail behind the Performance Rating Act of 1950.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500090030-7:
A Personnel Director memorandum dated 29 December 1950 tells the General Counsel how the Performance Rating Act of 1950 will bind the Agency. Public Law 873, passed on 30 September 1950, takes effect that day. It ends the civil service efficiency rating system. In its place, each department must build its own performance rating plans for judging the work of its officers and employees.

Named bodies such as the Tennessee Valley Authority, the Foreign Service, and the Atomic Energy Commission sit outside the act. The Central Intelligence Agency is not on that exempt list, so it must count itself fully covered. The memorandum then examines what the Agency should build. A secret agency grading its own staff under a public law is the tension running through the advice.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500120045-7:
A proposed Agency notice on leave draws a short General Counsel reply dated 13 August 1953. Counsel returns the concurrence sheet to an aide of the Deputy Director for Administration. With one exception, there is no legal objection to issuing the notice as drafted. The exception is paragraph 2, which deals with a change in the Annual and Sick Leave Act.

Counsel had talked over a revised wording with a named officer, whose name is redacted. The aim is to sharpen the contrast between the earlier law and the amendment on fixing the leave year. A suggested redraft of the paragraph is attached, along with a question-and-answer sheet on the leave year. The file shows lawyers polishing a staff notice before it went out.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500120135-7:
A Comptroller General decision, file B-95570 of 15 June 1951, answers the Administrator of the Housing and Home Finance Agency. His letter of 14 June 1951 had asked how section 1212 of the General Appropriation Act of 1950 applies to payment for unused leave. That section, in Public Law 759, bars use of funds to pay for annual leave built up during 1950 and still unused at the close of business on 30 June 1951.

Two carve-outs are quoted with the bar: staff posted outside the continental United States, and sums due as direct pay for leave in named cases. The decision then works through the questions put. Leave earned in the rush of 1950 hiring was a government-wide money worry, and this ruling fixed who could still be paid for it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140007-7:
Standard Form Number 1152, in its October 1950 edition, is the designation of beneficiary for unpaid compensation of a deceased civilian employee. A warning heads the sheet: read the instructions on the back of the duplicate before filling it in. The employee first gives name, date of birth, and the department, bureau, and division of employment. Signing the form cancels every earlier designation the worker had made.

The named beneficiaries are to receive unpaid compensation due under the Act of 3 August 1950, Public Law 636. The form stresses that it touches nothing payable under any retirement act. It stays in force until cancelled or replaced. A single sheet like this decided where a worker's final pay cheque went, so the wording is careful and plain.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000800140004-7:
An audit report on Contract Number PSC-50-UNV, held by an engineering company whose name is redacted, tests the contractor's charges to the Agency. Except for one class of cost, salaries and wages were checked against cancelled payroll checks. Disallowed items total a stated sum made of California sales tax, cash discounts kept back, and duplicate billings. Each charge was traced to the first invoice and the cancelled check that paid it.

Overhead spread across the contractor's jobs by share of direct labour cost is examined next. It bears a ratio of 52.50 per cent to the allowable wage bill. The contract's Article 2(e)(3), a style the Agency no longer used, allowed the contractor to bill an overhead allowance. The auditors measure that allowance against what the paper allowed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000800170001-7:
Section 8 of Public Law 600 is read against Confidential Funds Branch practice in a General Counsel opinion of April 1949. The branch chief had asked on 15 March 1949 for a reading of the section. The practice in question concerns sale or exchange of non-expendable equipment, with automobiles as the standing case. Sales money had been pooled, and the whole cost of purchases charged to the fund where total sales passed total purchases.

Single sales were not tied to single purchases, because swaps inside the branch caused trouble and cost. One new car, the branch argued, can replace more than one old car in worth and service. Counsel tests that pooling habit against the words of the 1946 act. The answer matters for every unvouchered purchase the branch made.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000020031-7:
Statutes on espionage, sabotage, and subversion, with the Delimitations Agreement, are summarised for the Director of Central Intelligence in a memorandum dated 20 November 1953.
