Tab A carries a digest of the statutes. Tab B carries the agreement itself. Enforcement of the laws belongs in the first place to the Department of Justice. Presidential directives, however, led the investigative bodies to divide the field by agreement among themselves.

Four parties made that division: the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Army's Intelligence Division, the Office of Naval Intelligence, and the Air Force Office of Special Investigations. The agreement dates from 23 February 1949. Under it the Bureau answers for cases involving citizens and foreign nationals in the classes named. This copy prints the summary in cleaner type than its twin in the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000020077-7:
A proposed omnibus bill revising the espionage laws is flagged in an office memorandum of 16 September 1948 from the Assistant General Counsel to the Acting Director. The bill concerns the internal security of the United States. It revises the espionage laws and related statutes in one package. The Director's comments on it went to Mr. Eberstadt in a letter of 14 September 1948, the memorandum notes.

Origins trace back to spring 1946 meetings of a joint committee drawn from G-2, the Office of Naval Intelligence, and the FBI. Their proposals reached the Attorney General from Secretary of War Robert B. Patterson on 27 June 1946. State, Treasury, and the Federal Communications Commission later commented. CIA had never been formally asked for its views, though it held an early copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000020095-7:
An amendment to Title 50, Section 31 is proposed under the heading Recommendation I in a paper on the espionage statutes. Offences in clauses (d) and (e) should stand without proof that the accused meant the information to harm the United States. Judges, the writer fears, might import the intent element from the earlier clauses. The change is framed to block that construction in advance.

Clause by clause, the text under review is then set out. One clause punishes going upon or flying over defence works to obtain information. Another punishes copying, taking, or obtaining sketches and photographic negatives for that purpose. A third reaches anyone who receives or tries to obtain such material. This copy of the recommendation matches its twin in substance, with its own type and spacing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040002-7:
Senate Report Number 1675, ordered printed on 18 May 1950, reports Senate Resolution 270 on Reorganization Plan Number 18 of 1950. Mr. McClellan sent it in for the Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments. The committee reported the disapproval resolution without recommendation. Passing it would stop the plan from taking effect.

The plan's purpose is stated early: move building and space work to the Administrator of General Services. Leasing and assigning general-purpose space would pass from the many agencies holding it. Running, maintaining, and guarding office buildings would pass as well. Central control of the government's roof space is the aim. For an agency housed in borrowed buildings, who held the keys and leases was no small matter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040011-7:
House Report Number 670, filed 24 May 1949, reports H.R. 4754 in favour with a long list of amendments. Mr. Dawson sent it in for the Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments. The bill would simplify procurement, use, and disposal of government property and reorganise certain agencies. Amendments begin with small edits: adding cataloging to a title heading on page 2, and striking a word after public on page 3.

Numbering fixes follow, turning roman marks into plain figures in the contents. The bulk of the report then prints the amended bill with a section-by-section account. At over two hundred thousand characters of scan, this is the largest of the property act papers in the file. It carries the House committee's full hand on the measure.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000050001-7:
Foreign Service Serial Number 1202, sent from the Department of State on 2 December 1952 by unclassified air mail marked urgent, compares two nationality laws. It sets the Nationality Act of 1940 beside the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952. The new act takes effect at 12:01 Eastern Standard Time on 24 December 1952. Only the important changes are treated; the serial does not claim to cover every shift.

Discussion follows the section order of the 1952 act, and copies had already gone to all posts. Consular officers are told to raise questions on the new law only where a live case needs a ruling. Loss and keeping of American nationality drive most of the changes. Officers abroad would apply this guidance at the window within weeks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000070009-7:
A public notice of the Federal Communications Commission, numbered FCC 51-304 and dated 28 March 1951, covers recording devices on telephone service. The underlying case, Docket Number 6787, asked whether devices for recording conversations could ride on interstate and foreign message toll lines. The Commission's final report was adopted on 24 March 1947. Orders of November 1947 and May 1948 set and adjusted the effective terms.

From 30 June 1948 the use of such devices stood authorised, subject to stated safeguards. Notice to all parties on the call sits at the centre of those safeguards. This file copy runs to the same length as its twin and prints the same statement. Agencies whose work touched telephone lines kept the ruling where lawyers could reach it fast.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000070063-7:
Who should watch licensed amateur radio stations is the question in a secret memorandum of 16 January 1948 for the Chief of the Administrative Staff. A December 1947 note from the USCIB secretariat had asked the Director's view. The activity in view is any amateur traffic that matters to United States communications intelligence bodies. Four parts to the problem are drawn out at the start.

Monitoring licensed operators is one part, and hunting clandestine transmitters is a second. Doing each for home security or law enforcement is a third, and doing each for foreign intelligence gathering is a fourth. The bulk of the work, the paper argues below, falls in set quarters. The memorandum sorts duty among agencies before a turf fight could settle the question by default.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000100005-7:
Treasury Department Circular Number 577, dated 13 August 1937, gives the regulations for claims under the Government Losses in Shipment Act. It issues from the Accounts and Deposits office of the Secretary of the Treasury. Heads of departments, agencies, government companies, and Federal Reserve Banks acting for the United States are all addressed. The rules rest on section 6 of the act, Public Number 192 of the 75th Congress, approved 8 July 1937.

Terms in the regulations carry the same meanings as in the act. General instructions open the text, aimed at speeding reports of loss, destruction, or damage to valuables. Proofs of claim for relief get their own steps. Anyone shipping government valuables, from cash to securities, worked under this circular for years.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000120021-7:
Circular Number 3301 of the Justice Department sums up rulings on section 9(a) of the Hatch Act. Doubt had arisen in case after case, and the Department was asked to rule. The circular aims only to gather those rulings for staff and the public. It warns that it does not list every post or act the law may reach. The law itself is then quoted in its pertinent part.

In general scope, the act bars officers and employees of the executive branch from taking any active part in political management or campaigns. A few prominent exceptions stand out from that bar. The rulings that follow sort borderline cases: holding party office, working at polls, and the like. For a young agency hiring fast, the circular drew the line on politics at work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200020002-7:
A letter of 18 February 1953 from Group Hospitalization, Inc. sends the Government Employees Health Association a detailed comparison of health cover. Pages 1 and 2 of the comparison sum up the chief differences between the two kinds of protection, cost included. The writer flags a few facts first. Group Hospitalization and Medical Service are community, non-profit bodies whose trustees and officers serve without pay.

No commissions are paid, and about ninety-two cents of each dollar goes to care, the letter states. The sender writes from the Transportation Building on Seventeenth Street in Washington, under a charter from Congress. The enclosed chart, printed as a sister record in this file, then sets benefits side by side. The letter is a sales pitch, but a restrained one aimed at fellow servants of the government.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200020011-7:
A benefits comparison chart, matching a sister sheet in this file, sets Group Hospitalization's offer against the Government Employees Health Association's present plan. Hospital services fill the first block of rows. Group cover has no dollar limit: semi-private rooms, meals and special diets, nursing, and listed medicines are all marked covered in full for twenty-one days per confinement. The GEHA column marks several of the same rows limited instead.

Maternity benefits spell out nine dollars a day for eight days, with full service benefits for named grave cases. Laboratory work is limited to a first urinalysis and blood count in one column. Sera, oxygen, operating room, and recovery room each get a row. The chart's blunt covered-versus-limited marks made the sales case at a glance.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001300070006-7:
The Chinese Communist legal system is described in a State Department research paper dated 10 November 1949, from the Division of Research for Far East. It opens with Tung Pi-wu's report on drafting the organic statute of the Central People's Government. His words set out the ruling theory: democratic centralism stands against the old separation of powers. The parliamentary system, in that account, lets one part of the bourgeoisie talk while those in power rule.

Judicial independence, the paper quotes, likewise serves the ruling class in fact. Article 17 of the new statute is then brought in as the discussion turns to courts and law. The study is an early American reading of the legal order of the People's Republic, weeks after its founding. It reports the system's own stated theory first.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100040004-7:
Report of the Civil Aeronautics Board on the role of competition in commercial air transportation was printed on 24 November 1952. It appeared as Subcommittee Print number 9 for the Subcommittee on Monopoly of the Senate Select Committee on Small Business. The Board's letter of 29 August 1952 to the committee chairman explains that the study was made at the committee's request, and the file runs to a long printed volume.

Inside, the Board weighs how much rivalry the air system should allow, including scheduled carriers and irregular or supplemental services. A later section sets out an inquiry into added and supplemental service. The limits include a set number of flights between the same points, high load factors, or casual and infrequent flights. Readers get the early 1950s policy debate in the Board's own terms, with the questions left open for parties to answer.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100160001-7:
Compilation titled Statutes Relative to Conflicts of Interest gathers the federal criminal sections that bar officials from taking pay or favors tied to government business. It is kept in a Central Intelligence Agency legal file. A note points readers to a treatise on the subject by Frank X. Brown in the Office of the Secretary of Defense and to a related file on outside employment pay.

Sections are quoted in full, with fines and terms stated. Section 216 covers an officer, employee, or member of Congress who takes money or a thing of value for helping to get a government contract. The stated penalty is a fine of up to ten thousand dollars, up to two years in prison, and loss of office. Later sections cover pay for work in matters that affect the government and a bar on officials acting as agents in claims against the United States.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100300005-7:
Trusteeship Agreement for the former Japanese mandated islands is printed in full as an agreement with numbered articles. It was approved at the one hundred and twenty fourth meeting of the United Nations Security Council. Its recitals cite the United Nations Charter and the League of Nations mandate confirmed on 17 December 1920 for the former German islands north of the equator. They also note Japan's loss of authority there after the Second World War.

Article I names the Pacific islands formerly held by Japan under mandate as a strategic area under the trusteeship system, called the trust territory. Later articles name the United States as the administering authority, with full powers of administration, legislation, and jurisdiction. They set duties to foster political growth, promote education with a system of elementary schooling, and guard freedoms of conscience, speech, press, assembly, and worship. Those freedoms are subject to public order and security.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200090017-7:
Memorandum dated 18 June 1953, from the Assistant Comptroller to the Comptroller, the General Counsel, and the Director of Personnel, is titled Salary Differential Due Detailed Employees. New State Department rules for government civilians in foreign areas change how a post differential is counted and paid. An employee on temporary duty away from his post may be owed more or less. The memo sees no practical way for the Agency to control payments under those rules.

Facts cited include rules issued 6 June 1953 under the Foreign Service Act of 1946 and Executive Order 10000, effective with the pay period that began 7 June 1953. Staff detailed sixty or more days to a higher rated post are due the higher rate, backed by a personnel action, a travel order, and a completed itinerary. Later pages weigh reporting burdens, tax forms, and a claim based path for increases.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200100015-7:
Copy of a decree of the Bundesgerichtshof, the Federal Court, is dated 16 February 1954, file number 1 StR 576/53. It cites Article 1 of the Basic Law and sections 136a and 81a of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Its syllabus holds that examination with the polygraph, or lie detector, violates the freedom of decision and will of the accused. It is not allowed in trials or early inquiries, even with the consent of the accused.

The attached case was tried by the First Criminal Senate on appeal from a district court sentence of 11 June 1953; the verdict was set aside and a new trial ordered. The defendant, a bookkeeper, was accused of taking 5,760 marks and faking a burglary to cover the act. Reasoning stresses that the machine records bodily reactions the person cannot control, so it draws out statements beyond a normal hearing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300030085-7:
Memorandum on the TASS News Agency, dated 6 November, in a Central Intelligence Agency legal file, describes the agency and its United States bureaus. TASS at Rockefeller Center, New York City, is identified as the American bureau of the Telegraph Agency of the USSR. Its sub bureau sits in Washington's National Press Building. It is described as the central information gathering body of the USSR under its Council of People's Commissars.

A registration statement filed 17 April with the Department of Justice, number 1460, is described. It was filed under the Foreign Agents Registration Act of 1938 and signed by the then manager. It names him as an agent acting on the instructions of the Soviet ambassador. Later pages set out the agency's duties in its own charter terms. They include naming correspondents, sending special correspondents across the USSR and abroad, and running bureaus in foreign countries under a managing director.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130048-7:
Case notes on Cole v. Young, decided by the Supreme Court on 11 June 1956, work through a discharge on loyalty grounds. The portion shown opens in mid analysis. It notes that the Civil Service Commission declined to hear Cole's appeal and that the Act of 26 August 1950 was held to supersede the Veterans Preference Act. That left whether the 1950 Act authorised the discharge as the sole question.

The notes record that the Court assumed, for the decision, that the act had been validly extended to the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare. They note that personnel laws allow dismissal for cause that promotes the efficiency of the service, and doubt as to loyalty was accepted as such a cause as early as 1884. Discussion weighs risk from staff in sensitive posts against summary dismissal of staff in other posts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130147-7:
Note dated 21 March 1956 is titled Building: Use of CIA Appropriation for Survey and Acquisition of Right of Way for a Parkway. It asks whether Agency funds could be used for a survey and for land needed for a parkway near Route 123. The scan is partly garbled in its figures, but the course of talks with planning and county officials can be read.

A survey must come first, before land can be acquired, and delay for lack of funds is treated as a real risk. The writer reports checking the language of the act that authorised the work. Later passages quote terms for advancing federal funds for roads, with repayment of half the cost, without interest, within not more than eight years. The terms rest on an agreement with Maryland or Virginia or a local body.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100010023-7:
Printed act H.R. 7391, in the Senate of the United States on 10 April 1952, read twice and sent to the Committee on Appropriations. It makes appropriations for the Department of Defense and related independent agencies for the fiscal year ending 30 June 1953. The 82nd Congress, second session text runs to a long act with sums stated heading by heading.

Title I begins with the National Security Council, with one hundred fifty thousand dollars for salaries and expenses. The sum covers services at rates not over fifty dollars per day for individuals and use of voluntary services. The National Security Resources Board follows. Later titles carry the large service sums. Air Force items cover obligations under earlier contract authority and maintenance and operation of Air Force activities, aircraft, transport of things, and rents at the seat of government and elsewhere.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100020059-7:
War Department General Staff Circular number 5-10, dated 18 September, year partly garbled in the scan, sets out the organization of the Legislative and Liaison Division in a tentative three page draft. The Chief of the division, on the War Department Special Staff, is responsible for starting and supervising all War Department relations with Congress and for liaison with certain federal agencies.

Duties listed include supervising preparation and processing of legislation of War Department interest. They also include keeping liaison with Congress on bills, investigations, and matters of interest to individual members. Liaison with agencies such as the Federal Works Agency and the Civil Aeronautics Authority is included. The division also clears correspondence and reports to Congress for the Secretary of War or the Chief of Staff. Subdivisions follow: a Legislative Branch, a branch handling evidence requested by Congress and committee investigations, and a Liaison Branch.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100030003-7:
Collection titled Excerpts from Editorials Commenting on the McCarran Anti-Subversive Bill Passed by the United States Senate gathers short passages from newspaper editorials. The editorials are from September 1950, each credited by paper and date. The Wilmington Journal-Every Evening of 13 September 1950 is quoted as saying America was losing its sense of proportion on communism, a danger to the liberties of all Americans.

The Washington Post of the same date is quoted as saying anticommunism had proved stronger than Americanism and that the bill would hit distinctive American liberties. An earlier Post excerpt argues the bill would penalise men for their opinions and help rather than hurt Communists by blurring the line between them and loyal Americans. Later excerpts include the Rocky Mountain News of 15 September 1950. They argue the bill's provisions would do no injury to spies and saboteurs but grave injury to rights of expression.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100150082-7:
Committee print of the report of Subcommittee IV of the Committee on the Judiciary, House of Representatives, 79th Congress, second session. The report was made under House Resolution 430 and printed by the Government Printing Office in Washington in 1946. The subcommittee, chaired by Sam Hobbs of Alabama, was directed to investigate the disposition of charges of espionage and possession of documents stolen from secret government files.

The report opens by quoting its charge to make a thorough investigation of all the circumstances. A section on the law cites Gorin v. United States, Supreme Court, 312 U.S. 19, for the point that whether information is connected with national defense is a question of fact for the jury. A further finding notes that most of the classified items in question were copies, with few if any original documents among them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100180007-7:
Department of State instruction on CODEL Harris, the trip to Europe of the House Committee on Interstate and Foreign Commerce, gives travel facts for a congressional party, in a garbled scan. Twelve members of the committee planned to depart the United States on 8 October for Europe and return about 1 November, with hotel reservations handled through posts abroad.

The group is listed by name, led by Representative Oren Harris of Arkansas as chairman. Members come from Louisiana, Mississippi, Illinois, Massachusetts, Texas, New Jersey, Minnesota, Iowa, and New York, plus a staff member and an airline representative. References are to telegrams from Stockholm and Oslo on hotels. A later itinerary shows legs by air, including an Air France flight, arrival in London and return to New York. Tickets as far as Stockholm were booked through Scandinavian Airlines, with work with that airline and Intourist on onward reservations to Vienna.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100240073-7:
House speech titled Revolution in Russia, shown here from a point inside the address, attacks a State Department recommendation to admit certain delegates. The speaker argues that the Department is hampering work to expose the truth about international communism and conditions behind the Iron Curtain, and the world menace faced at home and abroad.

The speaker states he is not crying treason and not accusing the National Council of Churches, of which his own church is a member, or the State Department of Communist infiltration. He charges instead that persons in authority in both are blinded by naivete and persist in a course of non-realism and peaceful coexistence. A quoted speaker of 9 July is cited on coexistence with an outlaw conspiracy. Later pages discuss the NTS symbol traced inside Russia as a vote against the regime and a growing political force beyond government control.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100240082-7:
Memorandum dated 2 July 1954, from Walter L. Pforzheimer, Legislative Counsel, to the Chief of the Graphics Register, sends photographs for copying and prompt return. A note above it records that the Director had also shown willingness to testify before the Jenner Task Force on strategy and tactics of world communism if an appropriate occasion arose.

Staff of the Senate Internal Security and Immigration Subcommittees, long interested in Communist penetration in Cuba and in ties they believed existed between General Batista and the Communists, supplied the pictures. Figure 1 in the larger photograph is alleged to be President Batista, and figure 2 Blas Roca, described as an alleged Latin American Communist Party organizer. A second picture allegedly shows Batista with communists in Cuba, at about the time Cuba broke relations with the USSR. Copies were also offered to Staff C and the WH Division.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200030002-7:
Memorandum for the Director dated 16 December 1953, marked confidential, proposes a program of weekly congressional lunches, to start at once. The aim is that key members of Congress can be apprised of pertinent matters concerning the Agency. A dated invitation schedule follows, guest by guest, with a short note on each man's committee place and value to the Agency.

First listed, for 21 December 1953, is Congressman John M. Vorys of Ohio, ranking Republican on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who had asked to come and had not lunched at the Agency since the 82nd Congress. For 11 January 1954 the guests are the three Republican House Appropriations members who handled the Agency budget for fiscal 1954. For 18 January comes Senator Leverett Saltonstall of Massachusetts, Armed Services chairman, before whose committee a Joint Committee on Intelligence proposal lay.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200110003-7:
Memorandum for the record dated 23 May 1952, on standard form, is titled Some Legal Problems Relating to the CIA Corporation and opens with summary conclusions. First, there is some basis in law for a general exemption of Agency corporations from government wide restrictions, by two alternative lines of approach.

One line rests on Totten v. United States, 92 U.S. 105 (1875), recognising spending of contingent funds for covert work without explicit congressional authorization, so the CIA Act should not be read as a limit on deeply covert work. The other treats government corporations as separate legal personalities, and Agency corporations, with their unusual features, as possibly wholly non-governmental. A second conclusion finds considerable basis for exempting certain phases of corporate activity, noting the Comptroller General does not read the Agency's broad authority to cover ordinary administrative problems. Later argument weighs that intelligence is a field traditionally part of government.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100130013-7:
Printed bill H.R. 4513 was introduced in the House on 1 March 1955 by Mr. Celler and sent to the Committee on the Judiciary, in the 84th Congress, first session. Its title is to prohibit wiretapping except by a court authorised federal officer engaged in the investigation of crimes against the security of the United States.

The bill adds a new chapter 119, Wiretapping, to part I of Title 18. Section 2501 covers interception of telephone communications. Whoever, without prior authorization from sender or recipient, willfully intercepts or attempts to intercept a telephone communication by common carrier is liable to a stated penalty. The penalty is a fine of not more than five thousand dollars or ten years in prison, or both, with a proviso following. Later sections limit use and divulgence of intercepted matter and admission of such evidence in federal courts to prosecutions for crimes specified in the bill.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100130022-7:
Third copy in the file of H.R. 4513, Mr. Celler's wiretapping bill of 1 March 1955, adding chapter 119 to Title 18. The penalty in section 2501 is a fine of not more than five thousand dollars or ten years in prison, or both, with a proviso that qualifies the bar on interception.

The middle of this copy gives the use limits in full. Evidence obtained from telephone line interceptions under the act is admissible in federal courts only in prosecutions for crimes specified in subsection (c). Any use or divulgence of information obtained by a duly authorised interception is then regulated. A bar on receiving such matter in any court or agency proceeding, absent compliance, appears just before.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100210005-7:
Public Law 413 of the 80th Congress, chapter 65, second session, H.R. 1366, is the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947 as enacted. Its title is to facilitate procurement of supplies and services by the Departments of the Army, the Navy, and the Air Force. The Coast Guard and the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics are also named, with other purposes.

Section 2(a) makes the act apply to all purchases and contracts for supplies or services made by those agencies, to be paid from appropriated funds. Declared policy in section 2(b) is that a fair proportion of total government purchases and contracts be placed with small business concerns. Publicity rules apply for contracts over ten thousand dollars made by negotiation without advertising. Later sections cover advance payments, with terms that may create a government lien, paramount to all other liens, on the supplies contracted for.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670005-7:
Committee print of the 84th Congress, second session, printed for the use of the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, is an analysis of S. 2628 and H.R. 7619, bills to increase rates of compensation of the heads and assistant heads of executive departments and independent agencies. The committee membership is printed under Chairman Olin D. Johnston of South Carolina.

Contents list tables of positions by department or agency. They cover the ten executive departments, then the Executive Office of the President, including administrative assistants, the Bureau of the Budget, Central Intelligence, the Council of Economic Advisers, and Defense Mobilization. Legislative and judicial matter follows. A middle passage discusses commissioners of the Court of Claims. Their salary adjustment went over in 1948 and was taken up in the Executive Pay Act without a full presentation of their status and work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670014-7:
Senate Report number 2642, Calendar number 2687, dated 18 July 1956, from the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, submits a report by Mr. Johnston of South Carolina to accompany H.R. 7619, on adjusting compensation of heads of executive departments and certain other federal officials. The committee reports it favorably with an amendment and recommends passage.

The amendment strikes all after the enacting clause and substitutes a new bill, printed in italic. Title I sets new rates of basic compensation for heads of executive departments and other officials. Title II covers organization of the Civil Service Commission. Title III covers establishment and classification of a variety of positions in the executive departments, with a section on federal staff matters. Later sections work through retirement changes: section 8, on deferred retirement, notes that a transferee to a post outside the Retirement Act keeps only refund rights under existing law.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670023-7:
Printed bill S. 2628, Report number 1257, Calendar number 1274, was introduced in the Senate on 25 July 1955 by Mr. Johnston of South Carolina, for himself and Mr. Carlson, by request, and reported with amendments on 29 July 1955. Its title is to increase rates of compensation of the heads and assistant heads of executive departments and independent agencies.

Title I is cited as the Executive Pay Act Amendments of 1955 and amends the Act of 15 October 1949, Public Law 359 of the 81st Congress. Section 102 rewrites rates, starting with the head of each executive department, the Secretary of Defense, and the Director of the Bureau of the Budget. A middle provision amends a Foreign Service Act provision of 26 August 1954, striking fifteen thousand dollars a year for the salary rate for Assistant Secretaries of State. Title III carries Classification Act amendments.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670032-7:
Reported print of H.R. 7619 under Report number 2642, a long bill text running past one hundred pages in the scan. The heading traces the bill from the Senate calendar of 2 August 1955 through referral on 5 January 1956 to the report of 18 July 1956 by Mr. Johnston of South Carolina, with the Senate amendment struck through and printed in italic.

Title I, Basic Compensation for Heads of Executive Departments and Other Federal Officials, opens the rates. It sets twenty five thousand dollars a year for the head of each executive department and the Secretary of Defense. The next tier follows. Deep in the print, retirement matter governs credit for Members of Congress. Credit is allowed only for periods of military service not exceeding five years. Service performed on leaving office during a war or national emergency proclaimed by the President or declared by Congress is also covered.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670041-7:
Congressional Record, House, pages carry House business of the 84th Congress in a long daily volume. Items at the head of the portion shown include concurrent resolutions authorizing the Joint Committee on Atomic Energy to print forty thousand additional copies of a hearing. A progress report on radioactive isotopes is also covered, and a resolution authorizing a correction in an enrolled bill appears.

The item headed Compensation of Heads of Executive Departments, Civil Service Retirement prints a conference report and statement submitted by Mr. Murray of Tennessee on H.R. 7619, Conference Report number 2935. The committee of conference reports on the disagreeing votes of the two Houses on the Senate amendment to the bill adjusting compensation of heads of executive departments and other federal officials. Pages deeper in the volume carry unrelated tax matter, with amendments stated to apply to service performed after 1954 and to taxable years ending after 1954 and 1955.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100680022-7:
Revised Outline of State Department Proposals on Executive Pay Legislation lists, under Title I, the State posts to be included beyond the Secretary, Under Secretary, and Assistant Secretaries. Those officers fall under the title at the proposed rates on their own. Named additions include the Director of the International Cooperation Administration.

Each Deputy Under Secretary of State is put at twenty three thousand five hundred dollars, and the Legal Adviser and the Counselor of the Department at twenty two thousand five hundred dollars. A note weighs whether ten Assistant Secretaries warrant specific reference under Title I at a higher rate. Title II explains the proposals. Reorganization Plan number 7 of 1953 authorises two offices at sixteen thousand dollars and four at fifteen thousand. A middle passage raises a rate from twelve thousand to sixteen thousand dollars.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100690003-7:
Bill text of the Overseas Allowances Act of 1955, dated 14 June 1955. It would consolidate and revise the laws on added compensation for civilian federal employees stationed outside the continental United States and in Alaska. Its stated aims are to ease recruitment, cut turnover, and pay for the extra costs and hardships of overseas assignments.

Section 101 declares the objectives: codify the provisions compensating United States citizen employees overseas into one act. It would give uniform treatment to staff of all agencies so far as conditions justify, build a basis for fair and efficient administration, and aid recruitment. Title I then sets definitions and general provisions. Near the middle of the file, amendments to the Act of 20 June 1949 rewrite paragraphs on packing, transporting, and storing household effects of an officer or employee of the Agency. The work is done while he is absent from his post of assignment, at government expense.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100690030-7:
Second copy of H.R. 3819, Mr. Corbett's Overseas Allowances Act of 1955, introduced 8 February 1955 and sent to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. Section 101's objectives open Title I: codify the laws compensating United States citizen employees stationed outside the continental United States, and give uniform treatment across agencies.

An education passage in the middle covers transport of an employee's minor dependents when adequate schools are not available at his post, to the nearest place where they are. Travel grants follow for an employee who has served in foreign areas more than five years. They go toward moving his minor dependents to and from the nearest port of entry in the continental United States or a Territory. The bill's title adds the aims of easing recruitment, cutting turnover, and paying for extra costs and hardships of overseas assignments.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200060001-7:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel, headed Legislative Proposals Affecting Military Personnel, reviews three referenced bills: S. 912, on a set retirement date for authorized retired lists of federal staff; S. 913, to ease settlement of accounts of deceased members of the uniformed services; and a third bill giving benefits to reservists who suffer disability or death on active duty or training duty.

The memorandum concludes the proposals may interest military staff detailed to the Agency but have no direct bearing on the Agency's staff work. No further action by the Legislative Counsel's office is desired. Attached bill prints include the settlement bill's order of payment for sums due a decedent. Payment goes first to the widow or widower, then, if none survives, to the children or their issue. Routing marks close the memorandum.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200150001-7:
Office memorandum dated 9 April 1956, from the Director of Security to the Legislative Counsel, raises a question on Legislative Bill number H.R. 9619. The bill provides for a Commission on Civil Rights and would authorize the Commission to subpoena witnesses and documentary evidence.

That power, the memorandum notes, raises a question whether the Director's responsibility for protecting intelligence sources and methods might be affected. The responsibility is imposed by the Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949 and the National Security Act of 1947. If so, action should be proposed to prevent any lessening of those responsibilities, and the Legislative Counsel is asked to consider the point in reviewing the bill. A routing slip carries the memorandum to the Legislative Counsel at 335 Administration Building. The bill print in the file also covers a joint committee of Congress on civil rights legislation, with vacancies filled as in the original selection.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200330001-7:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel, dated 5 July 1956, comments on H.R. 10731, a bill to establish a plan and procedures for the promotion of employees of the Government on the basis of merit. The plan, for the classified civil service, would be run on an organization or service wide basis.

Unassembled examinations would yield numerical ratings based on experience, length of service, and shown capacity for greater responsibility. Eligible lists would be built from them, and selections made from the top three names. A like procedure is proposed for the Postal Field Service. The measure covers only posts under the Classification Act of 1949. Posts exempt from that act, and those excepted under Schedules A, B, and C, are outside it, and the Agency is exempt from the Classification Act. Bill text bars an employee from an examination without the set qualifications.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200420001-7:
An internal CIA memorandum to the Legislative Counsel examines H.R. 5204, a bill on withholding state and local income taxes from federal pay. Maryland and the District of Columbia were pressing for tighter revenue controls. The bill would let the Treasury Secretary make withholding agreements with state and local governments covering civilian employees' salaries.

Within the Agency, the burden would fall mainly on the Comptroller, who would run the program, and on Security, which would need a safe way to report deductions. The memo lists the listing and external reporting of employees as both an administrative and a security problem, given frequent changes of assignment. It also warns that Maryland's view of tax jurisdiction, based on where income is earned, could bring litigation over domicile and place of employment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100230015-7:
A CIA memorandum of 11 January 1955 reports on air conditioning for the South Building. The Chief of Logistics wrote it for the Deputy Director (Administration). It answers a November 1954 request for units in that space. It also answers later questions about funding. By then, 56 window units and one package unit were being installed.

The work ran through the General Services Administration. A contract was awarded on 30 June 1954. The Public Buildings Service, Region 3, drew the specifications. The same job order covered a tunnel between the two buildings. It also covered work on the South Building's east elevator. A January 1955 review with GSA confirmed the legal frame. A 1942 law put air conditioning in government buildings under GSA control. Only GSA funds could pay for it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100250004-7:
A CIA memorandum puts a dispute over GEHA life insurance up for decision. It went to the Acting Director of Central Intelligence. Paragraph 6 holds the recommendations. GEHA, the Government Employees Health Association, runs the Agency's group insurance. Agency representatives held that GEHA cover reaches every employee. That includes the Mutual of Omaha policy. It applies whatever hazards the duties carry. GEHA's board took the other view. For extra-hazardous missions, the Agency itself should carry the burden.

The history section explains how GEHA began. The Agency set it up to build a program meeting its needs for protection and security. Any employee may apply for membership. The dispute sharpened after deaths on one project. The first death was a pilot's accident. Board members then asked whether the men were true staff employees. They also asked whether such hazardous work was ever meant to be covered.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100270039-7:
A CIA legal paper lays out the background, responsibility, and authority of the Agency. It was prepared for the Task Force on Intelligence Activities. The paper warns that law here is mixed with history and policy. Its conclusions, though, stay legal. The opening section traces the Agency's structure to two wartime lessons.

The first lesson was Pearl Harbor. The facts needed to predict the attack existed. But no system ensured they reached the President and his advisers. No single official bore blame for the failure either. The second lesson was the Office of Strategic Services under William J. Donovan. From those roots the paper moves to the National Security Council. It holds that Council intelligence directives have the force of law. They bind the agencies they cover.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200010009-7:
A CIA legislative file opens with a brief guide to cited laws. It identifies the public laws and House bills its lawyers kept citing. Public Law 724 is the CIA Act of 1949. Public Law 22 is the Foreign Service Act of 1946. Public Law 233 is the Annual and Sick Leave Act of 1951. Public Law 413 is the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947. Notes on recent bills and their sponsors follow.

The bulk of the file analyses proposed CIA legislation for 1956. It walks through a bill amending the CIA Act, section by section. Each change is compared with existing law. Early sections revise which parts of the procurement act the Agency adopts. They also update organisation titles. And they align section 5 benefits in Public Law 110 with Foreign Service rules.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200240095-7:
A CIA paper takes up allowances for independent contractors. Much of the scan is garbled, so only the broad lines can be read. The paper asks which allowances may be granted to contractors who are in fact treated like employees. It names out-of-area costs among the items. It also names added payments to reflect the true nature of a post.

One passage cites section 213(1) of the Internal Revenue Code. A class of civilians of the United States, stationed outside the continental limits, may be exempt from taxation. Cost of living allowances abroad are treated in that light. The paper also sorts contractors into types. Some are in fact staff in all but name. For them, a Government claim to a tax exemption might hold. A final point concerns what the memorandum style for such cases should be.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200330220-7:
A CIA administrative instruction sets up rewards for superior accomplishment. Its legal basis is the Classification Act of 1923, as amended by the Federal Employees Pay Act of 1945. Those laws allow within-grade pay increases as rewards. The rules follow Civil Service Departmental Circular No. 540 of 5 October 1945. A CIA Committee on Superior Accomplishment is created to run the scheme.

The committee reviews all recommended rewards and advises the Director. Its members include the Executive Director and the Executive for Administration and Management. The chiefs of the Management and Personnel branches sit on it too. So does a representative of the Assistant Director concerned. Eligibility turns on set conditions. Funds must be available, and the accomplishment must meet the standards. The person must be below the top rate for his grade. Sustained work of at least three months is one qualifying test.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300220005-7:
A CIA memorandum of 2 August 1956 reports advice on delegating firing power under Executive Order 10450. It went to the General Counsel. The writer first asked the Civil Service Commission. Mr. Meloy there said the question belonged to the Attorney General. So the writer called Assistant Attorney General Tompkins's office. His assistant, Mr. Doherty, answered on 1 August.

Doherty's view was clear. An agency head cannot delegate the final power to terminate. He may delegate final review. So the head need not read the whole file. He may decide on a summary of the salient points, prepared by subordinates. The Director of Personnel could sign the notice to the employee. The notice would state that he was terminated by direction of the Director. That assumes a real decision by the Director, passed on verbally. A June 1956 memorandum on the same question is attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300220014-7:
Notes for a discussion with the Committee on the Loyalty and Security Program set out the CIA case-handling system in outline. The first head is the investigatory function. The Civil Service Commission handles non-subversive checks. The Bureau handles all subversive investigations. Its first checks are judged adequate, and its special checks thorough but slow. Agency checks are rare, used mainly where a case has overseas aspects.

The second head is preparation. The Office of Security documents each case, and its papers set the tone for later steps. It presents facts for and against, and judges only the security question. The General Counsel reviews the whole case and advises the Director on the law. A board of senior staff then evaluates loyalty, security, and suitability. Later heads cover counsel for the subject, limits on investigations, and the finality of Agency action. There is no effective appeal system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300240120-7:
A CIA legal memorandum examines the power of congressional committees to investigate the Agency. It notes that the issue has never been tested in the courts. Political history, though, holds many cases of presidents and department heads refusing information to committees. Where the President backed the refusal, the papers were withheld. The reason given was always the public interest.

The memo quotes former President William Howard Taft. The President must give Congress information on the state of the Union. He may recommend measures. But that duty does not let Congress draw out confidential information he holds for his own duties, if disclosure seems imprudent. The memo adds that classified information has often been furnished anyway, in a spirit of comity. No power compels it. An appendix recounts a hearing episode involving Mr. Hoover, who refused to testify on matters the President had directed him to keep silent.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300240148-7:
A State Department memorandum of 15 April 1948 sorts departmental records for congressional requests. Ernest A. Gross wrote it. It answers how the Department should meet demands from congressional committees, by subpoena or otherwise. The records fall into three classes. Some must not be produced. Some may be produced or withheld at discretion. Some must be produced.

The first class is set out in detail. The President's directive of 13 March 1948 covers loyalty program files. Requests for them from unauthorised sources must be declined and referred to the President. Departmental security rules add a second bar. Material from another department or agency may not be produced without that agency's consent. Section 161 of the Revised Statutes supports the rule. Loaned material is protected the same way. Later pages warn against disclosing FBI reports. Much of that information comes in confidence, and naming sources could endanger informants.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100010001-7:
A CIA memo of May, from the Director of Communications to the Director of Training, reports a study of emergency communications. The place names are redacted. The Office of Training had asked for a preliminary study of an emergency link between two redacted sites. This office agreed to supply recommendations, cost estimates, and security reactions.

Landline teletype is not recommended. In a real disaster in the greater Washington area, wire service cannot be counted on. An idle line kept for emergencies also brings recurring charges. Microwave and very high frequency are also rejected. Their capacity far exceeds the need, and their costs are prohibitive. Microwave equipment alone would cost over $85,000, with two relay points. A radio teletype circuit is recommended instead. Most of the needed equipment is already installed. A few added components would let the present installation serve as a terminal.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100080004-7:
A CIA study examines success and failure in the Basic Orientation Course. A pre-training testing program was proposed in September 1952. The idea was to plan courses around the known abilities of students. The A&E Staff has since studied links between test scores and course performance. Its conclusion is firm. Success rests mainly on verbal ability and on skill in analysing material quickly.

Three items predict performance with unusual assurance. They are level of education, vocabulary level under speed conditions, and ability to abstract from charts and graphs. The course, the study says, is more academic than most college courses. Students without a college background are handicapped by weak learning skills. Verbally unskilled students are also embarrassed by competing in a weak area. Many start their Agency careers with a poor record that could have been foreseen.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100140007-7:
A CIA memo of March 1955 transmits an analysis of a training report. The report covers Area, Language and External Training from 1 July to 31 December 1954. The analyst wrote for the Director of Training, through the Chief of the Language and External Training School. A copy went to the Chief, HRS. The memo suggests presenting a summary to the Training Liaison Officers.

The analysis draws general conclusions from the figures. About 40 percent of fiscal 1955 requirements should appear in requests from this period. Area training cost $28,467.88 in total. Travel and per diem for six people came to $6,250, or 22 percent. In those six cases, travel alone equalled half the cost. That sum could have trained 13 more people at external facilities. The memo offers to extend the study, comparing costs of language training across Agency, private, and government facilities.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030050-7:
A CIA memorandum for the Director analyses manpower across the Agency. A House committee request prompted the study. The Inspector General led a special task force. It held two representatives each from the DD/I, DD/P, and DD/S. The Management Staff assisted, and an IG staff member served as secretary. The committee's letter aimed chiefly at a ten percent reduction.

The Director's reply had warned that a cut might not serve the national interest. The Agency is new, and demands on it exceed present manpower. So the task force looked wider. It examined how an arbitrary cut could be made. It hunted duplication inside CIA and between CIA and other agencies. It also asked what requirements present manpower cannot fill. The paper then works through each deputy's area, question by question.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100010021-7:
A CIA memorandum for the record is dated 4 February 1957. It reports a conference at the National Science Foundation. The subject was a proposed register of area-language specialist personnel. The meeting was held on 30 January 1957 at 1520 H Street, N.W. Representatives came from the Defense Department, the Army, the State Department, USIA, ICA, and others. The CIA writer attended as an observer only. Dr. Tom Mills of the Foundation chaired.

National registers now exist only for the sciences. They cover physics, earth sciences, life sciences, meteorology, psychology, and some engineering fields. Their aims are threefold. They serve as a standby tool for canvassing resources in an emergency. They support a statistical review of specialist manpower. They aid business and government in mobilization only. The State Department, the memo notes, leans on its own training program. Some 300 students are enrolled in it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410009-7:
A status table lists Geography Division projects as of 1 October 1957. Far East entries lead. A geography of Ningsia, Suiyuan, Chahar, and Shensi is drafting its resources chapter. A compiled map of agricultural areas will strengthen its land-use presentation. The Tibet geography remains delayed. A Northeast Thailand draft is being read by a representative of another office, redacted here.

Assistance to the Office of Training appears as a project. Staff lectured to the Intelligence Orientation Course on geographic intelligence. A country course lecture on China drew an invitation to return. USSR entries include a territorial-administrative division study meant to revise GR-63. Its materials still sit in the Machine Division. An urban area study of Magadanskaya Oblast is in abeyance. Map numbers accompany many entries.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410018-7:
A Cartography Division project status list is dated 1 July 1957. The USSR-Satellites Branch leads. A USSR industrial regions map is complete for June in first revision. Rumania's ferrous metal industry follows. New projects are starred. They include USSR administrative and economic regions for 1957 and guided missile ranges. Hungary entries cover soil, precipitation, sunshine, and frost sheets.

Bulgaria and Rumania industry sheets remain in the list. USSR entries cover oil and gas pipelines, cities over 100,000 population, and railroad construction from 1946 to 1950. A Sino-Soviet Bloc sheet locates geomagnetic observatories. Moscow and Leningrad chemical science locations appear again. Population distribution sheets close the branch list: total population, and urban population by regions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490010-7:
Minutes record NIS Committee Meeting No. 244 of 14 May 1957. The committee reviewed Chapter I on NIS 12, Finland. The draft was approved with certain changes. The Task Group was asked to review agency comments. This chapter was published without control. It was released only to the United Kingdom.

The Army member praised the terrain base maps in the chapter. They were prepared by CIA's Cartographic Division. The chairman voiced his own gratitude for the agencies' thorough reviews. Control policy for Chapters I came next. Members must apply controls realistically, he said. Some agencies still impose mandatory controls on chapter comments against NIS policy. Controls should rest on the fundamental considerations in NIC 206/29, not on automatic practice. Contributor statements for sections and Supplement II follow in the record.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200110001-7:
An annual report tabulates inter-agency procurement for January to December 1957. The tables count maps and publications received, by country and region. A Europe table leads. France accounts for thousands of maps and publications. Germany, Great Britain, and the USSR also run high. Far East tables follow. Japan leads with some 4,000 maps. Hong Kong, Korea, and the Philippines appear as well.

Near East tables cover India, Iran, Israel, and their neighbours. A summary breaks receipts down by source agency. One channel accounts for about 90 percent of the 64,804 total items. Publications total 6,758. A closing table lists material received from the Inter-American Geodetic Survey by map series. Brazil, Chile, and Colombia lead that list. The tables carry no narrative beyond their headings.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100030059-7:
A legal memorandum of 22 January 1949 addresses the Chairman of the Munitions Board. It supplements a memorandum of 12 November 1948. The subject is legal considerations in government service by members of private industry. Six situations are posed. An employee may draw pay from both industry and the government. He may be on paid leave from industry while serving. His government pay may be supplemented by industry money. Or he may serve as a per diem consultant while fully paid by industry.

On the first situation, the opinion is permissive with a limit. Private employment and income are no bar to government appointment. But the duties must not create a conflict of interests. A statute, 5 U.S.C. 66, bars salary supplements for government service. Attorney General opinions are cited.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100090035-7:
A CIA legal memorandum of 5 January 1956 concerns an overpayment of terminal leave to a staff agent. It went to the Assistant Controller. A proposed dispatch would advise how to collect the sum. The writer concurs in the first paragraph. Periodic payments seem the only logical way to collect a large sum. The employee could not pay it at once.

The writer cannot concur in the rest. The second and third questions turn on tax law. A cash-basis taxpayer who repays excess salary cannot report net salary for the year of repayment. He cannot reopen the prior year's return either. His only relief is an itemized deduction in the repayment year. That costs him the standard deduction. The memo ends by directing new wording, in line with an opinion of 10 December 1953 on staff agents' annual leave.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100130003-7:
A CIA legal file digests two court decisions on discharging federal employees. The first is Scher v. Weeks, decided 19 January 1956 by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. Scher, a Commerce Department employee, was discharged under section 304 of the Commerce Appropriation Act of 1953. That statute closely matches the DCI's own termination authority. The court upheld the statute and the discharge.

The second case is Service v. Dulles, decided 16 June 1956. It upheld the discharge of John Stewart Service. Earlier loyalty boards had found no reasonable doubt as to his loyalty. The Civil Service Loyalty Board later ruled the other way. A footnote in Scher notes his discharge implies neither disloyalty nor security risk. The file quotes the Director's termination power: employment may end whenever he deems it necessary in the interests of the United States.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100150010-7:
A memorandum dated January 13, 1956, to the Deputy Director (Support) frames a problem of rates. It asks how the Agency should set per diem and mileage allowances for travel inside the continental United States. The rates must sit within the maximums set by law. They must cover a traveller's necessary costs on official business. They must also follow the basis Congress used when it raised those maximums.

The discussion traces Public Law 189, enacted July 28, 1955. That law raised the top per diem and mileage rates. It rested on the principle that federal employees should not pay official travel costs from their own pockets. The conclusions reject one tempting approach. Keeping current cost data for every place in the country, and setting each trip's rate from it, would be costly and cumbersome. It would still not be effective.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00538a000100010007-7:
A study dated September 29, 1955, weighs a possible merger of the Cable Secretariat and the Signal Center. The memorandum to the Chief of the Management Staff responds to a request from the Deputy Director (Support). The request was made on September 15, 1955. The office pledges full cooperation. It places its personnel and complete organizational records at the study team's disposal.

The attached material describes the Agency secretariat's work in depth. It covers the message center duties and the career program for staff. One passage warns about any promotion system. It must make room for the few people ready for higher grades out of turn. It must still give the great majority a fair chance to advance. Their skill and morale decide how well the office runs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00538a000100150002-7:
A survey report on the Personnel Section of the Agency's FE Division administration staff goes to the Chief of Administration, DD/P. The survey covered the personnel and training table-of-organization positions in the division. Its two aims were to find the best organizational home for the essential personnel functions, and to estimate the smallest number of people needed to perform them.

The report builds on an earlier management study of the Personnel Section rendered on January 21, 1953. Among its findings, some of the section's work could be taken over by branch personnel, which would remove the need for a full-time GS-7 personnel officer on that activity. The related files and records, it suggests, could be kept by a staff secretary or by the personnel section's own transactions and records unit.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200010034-7:
Questions prepared on September 21, 1956, by a special assistant list what should be raised with the Training Office about its briefing at the next SSA-DD/S staff meeting. The first asks whether case officers can be required to take Operations Support, so they learn the services the Agency's support functions offer. The second tackles a scheduling problem with the Operations Familiarization Course.

Because key staff are hard to spare, the paper asks whether that course could be split into three sections, with credit given two weeks at a time. A third question asks for the course's required book list to go to division training officers in advance, so employees can read ahead. An attached note records an invitation for the Director of Training to address the DD/P support chiefs on October 11.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200020006-7:
Lecture notes prepared for a War Planners Conference on Tuesday, January 29, 1957, set out a plan. They state what the Agency's Office of Training should put before the planners. Suggested items include the office's current responsibilities. Those are written in the Training Annex to the Global War Plan. They also appear in Annex G, the war training annex to the European Theater area war plan. Current training programs that bear on war planning are included as well.

The notes quote the Global Plan's training appendix on preparation before D-Day. It calls for training all personnel for their wartime responsibilities, so far as feasible. The notes also record headquarters duties. They include issuing technical guidance to commands on the selection and development of training sites. They include handling requirements for training materials stockpiled at home or abroad.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200070001-7: An attendance list for the Agency's Project Useful No. 4 records the names, ranks, and services of those who attended, but the scan is so badly garbled that nearly every name is illegible. What can be read confirms the document's form: a roster arranged by name, rank, and service branch, followed by course material. No attendee can be named with confidence from this copy, and the list's value lies in showing the joint, multi-service character of the group rather than in any single entry.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200100016-7:
Detailed comments from the clandestine services on the Foreign Language Development Program regulations reach the Agency's Director of Training in October 1956. They are transmitted by memorandum. The memorandum follows an exchange running through the year. It began with an ad hoc committee's report to the Director on February 17, 1956. An interim reply followed on August 17. Further comments came on September 25. The services' views had been promised in more specific form after recent discussion.

The comments work through the draft regulations point by point. They mark where no change is wanted and where wording should shift. One shift adds a single word, training, before standards. A distinct section treats the Reserve Foreign Language Specialist Program. Under it, people with proven language and functional skill would be nominated for a standing reserve.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030013-7:
Weekly Activities Report number 31, dated August 7, 1958, goes from the Chief of the Language and Area School to the Agency's Director of Training. File studies and interviews were under way. They prepared for the next week's Qualifications Review Panels. The usual August flood of panels was expected, perhaps thirty of them. Counseling had been given to two people. Their subject was academic study of Korean and Soviet affairs.

A security item follows. The Navy's Bureau of Personnel had asked to pass on some information. It was apparently derogatory security information about a local commercial language school. The school chief accepted, and invited the Security Office to join a meeting set for August 8. Arabic students, the report adds, were being encouraged to continue. A Classical Arabic Reading Workshop was planned for October.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030022-7:
Weekly Activities Report number 22, dated June 5, 1958, comes from the Chief of the Agency's Language and Area School. It looks first at the monthly roundtable. The roundtable was meeting June 6 at the Navy Language School. The next session was set for July 24 and 25, with the Office of Training as host. The school had also defined the qualifications expected of language training personnel. They covered staff and contract people, across grades GS-5 to GS-15.

With those definitions in hand, the school had begun classifying its contract personnel. It aimed to regularize their pay and encourage their professional growth. It also aimed to give regular criteria for advancement. A course note reports French students gaining real facility. They were learning the language of public affairs. The dramatic events then unfolding in France served as a live problem for their study of modern history.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300050011-7:
Weekly Activity Report number 32, from the Deputy Registrar's office, covers August 6 to 12, 1958. A letter dated July 11 had come from the Armed Forces Staff College. It allocated the Agency two spaces in its Twenty-fifth Class. The class would run from January to June 1959. An acknowledgment was being prepared for signature. Demand for the Operations course is counted next. There were forty-four applications for Operations number 7. Only twelve of them were not from junior officer trainees.

Earlier runnings are compared. Operations number 5 drew thirty-two DD/P employees other than trainees, out of fifty places. Operations number 6 drew only fourteen. The report also clips a newspaper account. It covered Senator Henry M. Jackson's proposal for an Academy of National Policy. The writer calls the idea fast growing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300050039-7:
Weekly Activities Report number 4, from the Registrar's office, covers January 22 to 28, 1958. Its first item is a placement dispute settled in person. At the request of the WE training officer, two men met on January 23. They were the Deputy Registrar and a member of the Assessment and Evaluation Staff. They met with a supervisor and the training officer. The dispute concerned a GS-3 applicant for the IOC course.

The supervisor came away accepting the original decision. The employee would go into the Admin Procedures course instead. Later items deal with clearances and nominations. Talks with the National Security Agency on its requirements would stay limited. They would wait until proper clearances arrived. The matter was pressed again after months of waiting. Nominating procedures for junior officer trainees were also taken up with the office concerned.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300110005-7:
Weekly Report number 5 comes from the Agency's Assessment and Evaluation Staff. It covers January 29 to February 4, 1958. The chief had a full week of explaining the staff's work. He gave a presentation to the DD/S staff meeting on the assessment process itself. He gave another on the findings of a study of ORR analyst personnel. The second audience included senior NSA officers. A discussion with NSA followed, about the two organizations' mutual testing program. It agreed that cooperation on developing common tests would continue.

One personnel judgment is recorded in passing. The chances of a young woman from DD/P succeeding in the IOC course were discussed with the Registrar. Her prospects of performing satisfactorily or better were considered quite good.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000300100005-7:
An agenda for a meeting of the Agency's Career Service Committee in April 1952 is built around the working groups' latest papers. The committee would first take up the minutes of its meeting of April 7. It would then take up three memoranda. They came from the Working Group on Career Benefits, dated April 10, and the Working Group on the Personnel Development Program, dated April 11. The third came from the Working Group on Trainees, dated April 10.

Members were told which papers to have at hand. They included the progress report to the Director dated January 22, 1952. They included his March 7 memorandum on adjustments to the program and a special strength report of March 7. They included the final reports on rotation and career benefits from January and February. An attached tab sets out the composition of the career service boards. It includes a non-voting secretariat that supports each board and advises its head.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400120002-7:
Accomplishments in the Junior Officer Trainee Program for calendar year 1956 are reported to the Director of Training. The report is dated December 7, 1956. A favorable Inspector General report heads the consequences. His survey of the program brought an unequivocal recommendation. The program should be established on a firm basis and expanded. The program office also took over administration of the Junior Career Development Program. A representative of the Director of Personnel was placed in its office. He had full authority to act for him.

Recruiting experiments fill later items. Former trainees were being sent back to their home areas and former colleges. They went as recruiters for the program. The effort began that December, with no results yet in. An intensive push on recruiting had been developed by the Office of Personnel. It was helped by a fall in the Agency's need for professional staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100040006-7:
A study for the Deputy Director (Administration) asks one question. How can a better working relationship be built? It would join the DD/P area divisions and the Operations and Liaison Branch of the Finance Division. Two gains are wanted. The first is more effective financial support to the Clandestine Services. The second is a faster flow of financial documents, dispatches, and cables. They would flow between the divisions and the branch that services them. The facts show where the weight lies.

Seventy percent of the unvouchered funds obligated by the plans side of the Agency were obligated by the area divisions themselves. The study's answer is direct. Reorganize the branch, and physically relocate its sections closer to their customers. One guard is kept firm. The Comptroller's auditors and certifying officers must stay under his jurisdiction. Their objectivity must survive the move.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100080002-7:
A statement of functions dated December 2, 1957, defines the working branches of an Agency office. It begins with its Budget and Fiscal Branch. That branch prepares the office's budgets. It controls its spending against allocations. It scrutinizes every voucher for correctness and fitness. The standard is government, Agency, and office rules. It runs periodic financial audits and property surveys at headquarters. It controls and distributes salaries and reimbursements. It initiates travel orders for the office's people.

The Records and Services Branch, defined next, does the office's memory work. It does continual research on persons and organizations of interest to the Agency. It keeps complete, current records and indices of security information. Those records cover all but covert personnel and organizations. It also reviews proposed changes in assignments between major components. The review is made from a security standpoint.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100090029-7:
A request for management assistance is dated June 5, 1955. It comes from the Agency's Acting Director of Logistics to the Chief of the Management Staff. Two systems at the Printing and Reproduction Division's plant had been in use for about eighteen months. They were the production cost accounting system and the work scheduling system. No organization outside the division had reviewed them since they were installed. A review of their effectiveness was now thought desirable.

The request asks for an organization and methods examiner from the Management Staff. He would review the plant's work reporting system and its scheduling system. He would review the related procedures by which production is controlled. Price schedules attached to the file price the plant's output line by line. They run from multilith and ditto pages to photographic work such as photostats.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100130006-7:
A survey of Agency overtime practices opens with the law. Public Law 763 of the 83rd Congress amended the Federal Employees Pay Act on overtime. Time and a half had once applied only to those paid 2,980 dollars a year or less. A hard ceiling of 10,000 dollars capped total compensation. The amendments restated the limits by grade. Time and a half now ran up to the minimum rate of a GS-9. That rate is given as 5,410 dollars. Higher grades were paid at the GS-9 overtime rate, under a maximum.

The survey then goes office by office with a questionnaire. On recording, one practice is reported. Offices that grant compensatory time reported it credited on the official time and attendance records. The survey notes another practice as well. Informal records were kept in subordinate units. They covered overtime worked without formal authorization. Such records were probably customary in at least some places.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100150004-7:
An Agency Finance Division work measurement system, dated November 9, 1954, was built by the Management Staff at the Deputy Comptroller's request. Its aim was practical: a way to measure the division's work as an aid to manpower use, supervision, operations, and budget building. One fact made the job possible: practically all of the division's work consists of handling papers or forms, and paper can be counted.

The system therefore identifies work units, sets a way to count them, and records the time spent on them, so that standards can be set in man-hours per unit. Performance, stated as a percentage, is the standard man-hours divided by the actual man-hours. Daily work records feed a monthly picture that includes the units still on hand at the period's end.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100160003-7: A paper headed Program Analysis, dated September 3, 1957, survives in a scan that is heavily garbled and cut by redactions. Its tables and numbered recommendations can be seen in outline. Its fragments concern analysis work at the Agency-wide level. The wording of its findings, though, cannot be recovered from this copy. No claim in it can be stated with confidence beyond its subject. It is a 1957 staff paper on program analysis in the Agency's comptroller organization, preserved in poor condition.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100160012-7:
Comments on a November 1955 memorandum about program analysis are addressed to the Special Assistant to the Agency Director. They lay out what program analysis is and is not. Efficient management of a large organization, the comments argue, requires four primary functions. The first is fixing the objectives to be attained. Those objectives become the yardstick for results. The second is keeping a current plan to reach those objectives within set time limits. The third is a system of periodic reports on progress, in the same terms as the plan. The fourth is a system for review and analysis.

Against that frame, the budgetary process fails the test. It is not a program analysis system in the broad meaning of the term. The budget process exists to compile the data needed for policy decisions. It then builds the document that secures funds from Congress.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100240068-7:
A statement of functions covers a Finance and Fiscal Branch. The office's name was removed in review. The statement puts its Finance Officer under the Executive Officer's general direction. He works inside the approved policies of the Office of Training and the Agency. The officer must establish a system of records and accountings, and keep it current. It would show allotments of funds for the office's operations. It would show obligations against them, actual expenditures, and unencumbered balances.

Money may not move without him. Every instrument that will result in spending funds must reach him before approval for action. He assures that a proposed expenditure does not break the rules governing public funds. He certifies each instrument as to the availability of funds. He informs the Executive Officer at once of anything irregular.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200170001-7:
Phase II of a Management Staff survey maps personnel records held by the CIA and the Department of State, though the scan's OCR is rough in places. The survey describes the official distribution of chosen personnel forms inside the Agency, with extra copies found in parts of the intelligence and plans directorates. State Department personnel files are also described, covering convenience files, overseas personnel files, and efficiency reports, along with career histories for Foreign Service staff.
