Five forms anchor the work. They are the Personal History Statement, the Fitness Report, the Profile, the Request for Personnel Action, and the Notice of Personnel Action. The phase also traces where Agency personnel files sat before a central personnel office existed, and asks whether the official file could be split among a third echelon of offices.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200190009-7:
A mission and functions statement for the CIA Library, under the Office of Collection and Dissemination, defines the library as the Agency's central collection and reference service. It receives, processes, files, and passes on incoming classified documents and CIA-produced foreign material, builds indexes and bibliographies, and buys publications that research and operations offices need. Loan requests are served from its own files or through inter-library loan.

Further duties include strict control of top secret and registered documents, and upkeep of an Intelligence Subject Code used to analyze incoming papers by subject and area for a central machine index. English and foreign language books and periodicals are cataloged. A Book Branch section follows, covering buying, cataloging, a monthly index of intelligence publications, and clipping from English language newspapers and periodicals.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300010017-7:
Printed House hearings from 10 June 1959 record testimony on bills to improve how the United States runs its overseas activities. The Subcommittee on Civil Service of the House Post Office and Civil Service Committee heard H.R. 5007 and H.R. 5099, plus H.R. 5178 and H.R. 5238, which dealt with health and medical services for civilian staff overseas and their dependents. The volume was printed for the committee's use in the Eighty-sixth Congress.

Witnesses and members work through allowances and conditions for staff posted abroad. In one exchange, a witness explains that his system matches the Foreign Service practice of a flat allowance. Military personnel, he notes, follow a different system that still tries to relate sums to set rates. The hearings give a full public record of how overseas pay, health care, and administration were debated together.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300030060-7:
A memorandum for the record dated 15 April 1959 sums up Senate hearings on S. 94, an early health benefits bill. Hearings were set for 15, 16, 21, and 23 April, and Chairman Senator Neuberger said the committee was not wedded to the bill and wanted suggested changes. Elmer Staats of the Bureau of the Budget backed some bill, ideally on no more than a fifty-fifty cost split, with a start no earlier than 1 July 1960.

Roger Jones of the Civil Service Commission brought a new attachment listing eighteen principles for a sound bill, then compared S. 94 with a broader Commission plan. Jones put likely coverage at four and a half million employees and dependents, with sample costs quoted. The writer's own view closes the memo: both plans look very liberal and may break down under their own weight.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020001-7:
A functions sheet dated 31 December 1958 lists what the Office of the Chief, Geographic Research Area, did inside the CIA research structure. Two chief-level duties open the sheet. One is supervising and coordinating the area's research and support work, costed at three manyears. The other is exercising central administrative control and guidance, costed at two and a half manyears. Blank fields for authority, funds, and date of establishment frame each entry. Division sheets follow the same pattern.

The Geography Division, prorated at eight and a half manyears, coordinated community contributions to the National Intelligence Survey program. It also produced special area studies for clandestine and joint use, covering unconventional warfare, border crossing, targets, routes, and towns. Map work includes town plans and special-subject maps for clandestine operations, one line dated from December 1955.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020010-7:
A monthly report for the Cartography Division covers November 1958 in the CIA geographic research structure. The summary counts map and chart requests accepted during the month, split between the Agency and the Department of State. It breaks Agency requests down by office, with the Office of Research and Reports the largest source. Completions, cancellations, and work still in hand are also counted, though some figures are garbled in the scan.

A separate passage follows the National Intelligence Survey map coordinator, who routed jobs to reproduction for final printing, color proofing, and reruns, and logged what came back. Other notes record a courtesy visit by a guest from an outside center, by invitation after a recent visit there, and good progress on a city plan map program. Staff and branch notes round out the month.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020047-7:
A monthly report headed for September covers Cartography Division work, with the body reporting August figures and a footer dating the report September 1958; the heading year is garbled in the scan. Requests accepted came to 121 maps and charts, 118 for the CIA and three for the Department of State, with research and scientific offices the largest sources. The division completed 133 maps and charts, ten of them for State.

The survey map coordinator handled seventy-five job requests and sent ninety jobs to reproduction, ending the month with a backlog of sixty-one requests. Maps and charts held in the division at the end of September came to 407. Later notes report advanced preparations for a Far East trip by an office chief, expected around 15 October, and favorable progress on a city plan project, with a final prototype in preparation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00442a000100060016-7:
Weekly Activity Report No. 20 from the Chief, Overseas, Operations School, dated 20 May 1959, reports no significant items and turns to trainee handling. One man who had finished a course was enrolled in a basic photography course running 25 May through 12 June. He was also enrolled in an audio surveillance equipment course for 23 through 26 June. The second course was suggested by the officer he would work with. Testing was set for that Friday, and departure was expected about 1 August.

A nuclear warfare handbook item follows, tied to earlier weekly reports. On 13 May a staff member attended an Industrial War College lecture on the psychological effects of nuclear warfare. Later pages deal with release of training materials to a desk, done at request but with detailed cautioning because the circumstances were irregular. A call also asked that such releases be cleared through the school.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00463a000100010018-7:
Senate bill S. 3552, introduced on 25 March 1958 by Mr. Saltonstall for himself and Mr. Mansfield, would amend the Foreign Service Act of 1946 to improve recruitment and training for the Foreign Service. The bill went to the Committee on Foreign Relations after two readings. Its first change lets the President appoint persons direct to class 7 where they have passed the needed examinations and qualify for class 8. The step applies when age, experience, or other qualities make it fitting.

Later sections deal with training. One passage concerns an institute for training officers and employees assigned to foreign relations work overseas. It directs other government agencies, where practical, to avoid duplicating the Secretary of State's institute and its training. The bill as printed is short, with numbered lines and the act's section numbers cited for each change proposed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00463a000100040024-7:
An untitled transcript of a training gathering opens with a speaker passing the blame for budget cuts, with a joke, to Colonel White, the host. He quotes White at a recent training meeting as willing to go to most any extreme to make a program succeed, and answers: just give us another five dollars. White then speaks for himself, raising two complaints at the start and explaining his notes. White recalls that the hit of the previous year's day was Matt tearing up his script, which is why he came prepared.

Later in the transcript the talk turns serious. Courses had been cancelled for lack of enough students. The speakers argue that the training office must bring home to the rest of the Agency a duty to sharpen priorities. Names of other speakers are given in the transcript headings as the session moves on.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000100230003-7:
An annex to the 4 June 1956 brief for information agency membership in the Intelligence Advisory Committee describes the agency's own Office of Research and Intelligence. Its mission is threefold. It covers analysis of Communist propaganda in all its aspects, and analysis of foreign public attitudes on issues touching the United States interest. It also covers measurement of the effect of overseas information operations. Each phase, the annex stresses, needs specialist work.

Propaganda analysis alone must cover the apparatus, its staff, methods, money, and fronts, plus output across press, books, radio, film, and exhibits. Attitude work rests on surveys abroad. Top American professionals, George Gallup among them, serve as consultants, and spending on polls ran to 350,000 dollars a year. Polls had been taken in most European countries, a few Latin American ones, and one Far East country.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200030022-7:
A memorandum dated 23 January 1959, coordinated with Intelligence Board representatives, reviews trends in the Philippines. Recent months, it says, had borne out the rather gloomy view of estimate SNIE 66-58, approved in May 1958. That estimate stressed an atmosphere of decline under the Garcia administration and a loss of public confidence. It also stressed growing nationalist feeling that could press for a more independent foreign policy and take on an anti-American color if open issues stayed unsettled.

The political situation, the memo continues, had kept worsening, and the government's efficiency had declined. A money passage notes that credits granted fell well short of what the administration had led the Philippine people to expect, and that some credits were still under negotiation. Those sums would not give the exchange relief needed for a critical balance of payments position, and a request to the International Monetary Fund is noted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200030040-7:
A position paper built on a single assumption defines its terms at the start. A change of status for Formosa means any change in international standing short of joining the Chinese People's Republic. Purely internal changes, such as new leaders or a new character of government, do not count. Those fall under a weakening of the Chinese Nationalist position instead. The paper then asks how Communist Chinese aims and actions might shift under each case.

Long term Chinese aims in the Far East and South East Asia are listed as three. They are to dominate the region and remove Western influence, and to set up Communist or pro Communist governments in other countries there. The third is to regain control of areas held to be Chinese, naming the offshore islands, Formosa, Macao, Hong Kong, and parts of Burma. No fixed timetable is expected.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200080009-7:
A situation paper dated 5 March 1957 reports fresh moves in Indonesia. On 2 March the commander of Territory VII in eastern Indonesia proclaimed martial law. He named military governors for the four provinces in his command: Celebes, the Moluccas, the Lesser Sundas, and West New Guinea. He also sent an ultimatum to the Djakarta government. His demands included greater regional autonomy and keeping seventy percent of provincial revenues for local development.

On 5 March he demanded that Prime Minister Ali resign and stated that Communists would not be tolerated in the government. These events are placed as the latest in a run of bloodless takeovers. Army commanders, apparently backed by civilian elements, had seized North, Central, and South Sumatra in defiance of Djakarta. All had made demands of the same kind. A later passage turns to President Sukarno's February concept for a new form of Indonesian democracy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200080018-7:
An Army intelligence paper, from the Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, Intelligence, examines the position of the French Army in Algeria. The revolt, it says, has grown in intensity since it began in the Aures Mountains of eastern Algeria on 1 November 1954. That growth is best shown by the marked growth of the French effort against it. A strength table compares June 1954 with 25 January 1957.

French Army strength in the table rises from tens of thousands to 340,000 men, organized in thirteen divisions. Gendarmerie, naval, and air elements bring the total French force to about 400,000. Rebel organization, tactics, strength, and arms kept improving despite heavy losses, with armed regulars of the National Liberation Army put at ten to twenty thousand. Later pages warn that coming United Nations debate could trigger an eight-day general strike call, with violent French reaction likely.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300050010-7: Paper IAC-D-102, dated 6 February 1956, circulates membership lists for the Intelligence Advisory Committee and its standing and ad hoc subcommittees, sent for information by the committee secretary. Allen W. Dulles heads the roster as chairman in his role as Director of Central Intelligence, with his building, code, and extension given. Member entries follow the same pattern for each agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300070009-7:
Paper IAC-D-122, dated 18 June 1958, forwards the intelligence requirements of the Net Evaluation Subcommittee for review, with the matter proposed for the committee meeting set for 24 June. The attachment is a memorandum dated 12 June 1958 from the subcommittee's director to the Director of Central Intelligence. Its purpose is to help the intelligence community by setting out, early, what coordinated intelligence the subcommittee needs for its 1958-59 exercise. An outline of specific needs follows.

The first head covers Soviet nuclear delivery capability in mid-1962. It lists numbers of operational intercontinental and intermediate missiles, heavy and medium bombers and tankers, and naval and tactical aircraft. Guided missile submarines and performance data for each complete the head. The subcommittee notes that a current estimate on Soviet capabilities and policies would serve part of its need, and the outline continues by subject from there.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300040056-7: A short form dated 30 October 1956 lists adjustments to be made to a monthly report, under a project heading rendered in the scan as a PCS-DCI project for October 1956. The first item corrects an allotment symbol: a debit to one 6-1004-10 account and a credit to a 6-1004-50 account, in the amount of 153.56 dollars, with the remark that the change adjusts a charge to the proper project. Further debit and credit pairs follow in the same form, and distribution is noted to the addressee and to an IBM reconciliation address.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300050019-7: A voucher listing with cost current 57 columns pairs dates and voucher numbers with Aquatone account entries. Accounts shown are 100410000 and 100410001 in a 6002 group, with small costs in cents and dollars and one larger entry in the twenty-thousand dollar range, partly garbled. Balance forward rows repeat through the print. The sheet is a raw accounting listing for those project accounts, with no narrative text and many digits unreliable in this OCR.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300050037-7: A voucher listing pairs voucher numbers in 07086 and 17086 series with coded references and costs, and a balance forward row names Aquatone in capitals in the middle of the print. Column heads in later sections repeat date, voucher, description, allotment, and cost current 57. The sheet is a raw project account print with no narrative text and heavy digit garbling, grounded only in its voucher structure and the Aquatone balance line.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080052-7: A May IBM reconciliation worksheet for an account in the 7-1004-10 group survives as handwritten figures and short number strings, rendered almost wholly illegible by the scan. The title's account suffix is blank in the catalog record itself. No figure or remark can be read with confidence from this copy. The sheet can be grounded only as the May machine-accounting reconciliation in the monthly series; its workings cannot be recovered here.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00901a000100050017-7:
Maker's brochure for the Model CL-1 Series Rolor Color Laboratory presents a compact colour processing unit. The seller is the Rolor Industrial Corporation. In under five feet of floor space, the unit handles colour negative and positive film. It takes roll or sheet film up to 8 by 10 in size. It also handles colour print paper and print film up to 16 by 20. Small solution volumes are stressed as a saving.

The film tanks hold up to nine 120 reels and fifteen 35 mm reels at a time. One run can instead take thirty-two 4 by 5 sheet films. Listed features include two gallon film tank inserts and red brass chemical tanks. A fast drain wash tank and automatic drain controls round out the list. The brochure is sales material kept in Agency files, aimed at colour shops weighing space and labour costs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00901a000300050006-7:
Survey comments on the Agency's OCR Administrative Staff describe simple, informal procedures, with little logging or record keeping and paper handling cut to a minimum. Some duties, such as controlling promotion consideration money, sat with the operating divisions. Since the survey, a new Assistant Chief had been appointed and the staff had been told to give more time to records management and training.

Remaining problems centre on how staff time was used and where duties overlapped. The line between the Assistant Chief and the Budget and Fiscal Officer needed clearing up, since both dealt with wider budget and fiscal policy. Later pages work through office routines in detail, including how job notices were typed, logged by slot number, and sent out for division comment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00910a000100060007-7:
Statement of accomplishments and objectives for the Agency's Records Management Division looks back at fiscal year 1954. Records work was reorganised that year into separate branches for each phase of the program, under one division, to fix responsibility and give each phase proper leadership. The division then sat in the Management Staff under the Deputy Director for Administration.

Costs and scale are stated plainly. Pay for all Records Management and Records Center staff in 1954 came to 203,555 dollars, set against the filing and space costs the program held down. The Records Center had outgrown its temporary space, with only 1,482 cubic feet left for new material, and 275 record transfers were processed in the year covered.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00910a000100060025-7:
Records Management Program Guide, issued in September 1953 by the General Services Office, Records Management and Distribution Branch, is marked Restricted. Its contents run from an introduction and definitions through the creation of records, covering reports, forms, and correspondence management. Later sections deal with organising, keeping, and using records, then disposition and the vital materials program.

Practical guidance fills the middle pages. Offices are told to use pattern paragraphs, letter guides, and form letters, to keep quality standards for letters, and to cut nonessential copies of communications. Mail control aims at prompt, systematic handling. The guide gives a new staff member the full shape of the Agency's records system in one short brief.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100070060-7:
Filled Agency form reports training taken at government expense, addressed to the Director of Training through a Training Liaison Officer. The trainee, an analyst in the Industrial Division of ORR, attended a course held at an aircraft plant. The program is praised as well organised, concise, and highly profitable, with direct plant observation giving a practical angle that classroom work could not supply.

Training aims were to learn the processes and methods used in aircraft production and how an aircraft company programs its work. A related paper in the file asks for production cost data on commercial airliners, broken into airframe, engines, propellers, electronics, accessories, and furnishings, for use as comparison data on similar Soviet aircraft.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100110010-7:
Report in the Agency's files on Soviet shipbuilding techniques describes how Soviet yards changed after the Second World War. From about 1946 yards across the country were reconditioned, modernised, and expanded. Building berths were paved, old fixed cranes gave way to heavy travelling cranes, and paved subassembly areas were added beside them. New workshops, prefabrication shops, assembly sheds, and covered building ways became more common in major yards.

Later sections cover launching and quality control. Many yards used marine railways to launch ships rather than long building ways. Inspection methods include gamma ray testing with radioactive cobalt in place of X-ray photography, and ultrasonic resonance gauges to check plating thickness without drilling. The Soviet Sea Register is also cited for strength rules for merchant ship plating.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100140035-7:
Revision pages for the ORR code book of economic activities and factors change codes branch by branch. ORR is the Agency's Office of Research and Reports. The work is Project No. 00.1651. Each entry is marked Add, Delete, Revision, or New Title. Notes mark the spots where two branches share one subject. The Consumer Industries Branch list runs to service and household machines. It also runs to household electric goods, bicycles, watches and clocks, and cameras and photo gear.

Changes from the Medium Machinery Branch add new titles for farm machines. The titles cover planting, seeding, and fertilising machines, plus cultivators and seeders. They cover harvest machines and machines that get crops ready for market or use. A later part covers instruments for science work and for measure and control tasks. A missing page notice appears in the scan, so the file as released is not complete.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100010108-7:
Memo puts forward needs for the Agency's OCI Periodic Requirements List for 1 August to 30 November 1955. The areas covered are Western Europe and Latin America. One change asked for rewrites the background to an item on Austrian East-West trade. Under the Austrian State Treaty, signed 15 May 1955, Austria was to deliver goods worth 25 million dollars a year. The term was six years, and the goods paid for former German firms. Austria was also to hand over 10 million tons of crude oil over ten years. That paid for the return of the oil fields.

Austria was also to work out a five-year trade agreement with the USSR. The treaty barred strategic trade controls, though an escape clause was possible. Later pages add Latin American items. They include a protocol to a 1953 trade agreement. They also include Soviet motor graders ordered in Argentina.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100010162-7:
Agency memorandum dated 7 January 1955 invites economic requirements for the OCI Periodic Requirements List for March to June 1955, covering the Near East and Africa. A sample current list is attached as a guide. Offices are reminded that items should be current information targets to guide the field, not basic requirements, and that background should be added where it helps.

The list itself was built to forecast likely developments of note in the coming four months and point to the facts needed for sound reporting. Attached material in the file includes names and banking details for trading firms in places such as Basel and Hong Kong, given as reference data for trade reporting.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100010171-7:
Memo dated 11 January 1955 puts forward a project on East German transport capacity. The project is for an organisation whose name is redacted in the scan. The study is titled Capacity of Strategic West Transport Facilities in East Germany. It would fill a gap in a wider joint study of strategic port capacity. That study is run with the Weapons Systems Evaluation Group. The memo advises that the work go to ORR, the Agency's research office, part by part as it is done.

An attached supplement breaks the study down by section. Sections cover ports and waterways. They cover rail lines, locomotives, and rolling stock by type. Tractive effort and condition are covered as well. One point is the share of stock out of service for repair at any time. Highway transport closes the list. For each part, capacity is to be worked out on set working bases.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100030043-7:
Standing requirements paper dated 17 September 1957 sets out what the Agency's Construction Branch needs from graphic, or photo, intelligence. The branch produced all-source economic intelligence on building of fixed installations and production of construction materials in the Sino-Soviet Bloc. Its photo intelligence scope follows the same ground: construction operations and the making and distribution of construction materials.

Areas of interest are mainly Bloc countries and nearby areas, with strong interest in building work anywhere using Bloc staff, equipment, or materials. Commodity fields run from construction materials of all types to plants making them. Equipment lists name brick presses, brick kilns, handling gear, and precast and prestressed concrete plant gear, down to mixers, storage bins, scales, conveyors, and curing equipment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100050005-7:
Memorandum dated 3 July 1958, from the Agency's Chief, S/CST, to ORR and OCI reading panels, revises Construction Branch requirements. The branch produced all-source intelligence on building of fixed installations and production of construction materials in the Sino-Soviet Bloc, and, in this version, on civil defence activities there as well. It also helped coordinate such work across the United States government and fed National Intelligence Estimates.

Scope in the building industry covers costs, methods, capabilities, materials, and design standards of fixed installations. Civil defence scope covers organisation, tactics, and training units, with stress on shelters and related passive defence building. Installation lists in the paper include storage depots, fortifications, naval bases, shelters, training areas, airfields, and guided missile launching sites.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100150068-7:
Memo dated 27 April 1955 sets procedures for reading panel requirements in ORR. It comes from the Chief, Economic Research. It goes to all division, branch, and staff chiefs of ERA. Clear, set needs matter, the paper says, for a plain reason. The flow of incoming facts from OCD to ORR is routed largely on their basis. Routing inside ERA to single branches rests almost wholly on them as well.

Each Agency division chief was to run a system of regular review and updating. A fresh basic set of needs for each reading panel was due at least once a year. The best time was right after branch program approval. No set was to be over a year old. The needs should name wanted publications in three groups. The first group holds those needed on a lasting basis. The last holds those that might prove fruitful.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100150103-7:
Memorandum of Understanding dated 5 October 1954 sets working relationships between the Agency's ERA and D/E offices on commodity intelligence for economic defense. It builds on a 27 May 1954 understanding between the two research chiefs and on ERA procedures of 5 March 1954, and is meant to conflict with neither. A memorandum for the record of 20 August 1954 is also cited as rescinded in the head.

ERA takes responsibility for all research and production of commodity economic intelligence on the Soviet Bloc for economic defense support requests. Support is defined narrowly: it does not mean studies built to justify or oppose policy or action, but a fair showing of all available economic facts D/E needs. Requests D/E judged impractical or against office policy were to be settled by D/E with the requester.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100160012-7:
Paper dated 22 October, the year partly cut in the scan, states a need of the Agency's Services Division. The need is for a classified project on Communist takeover in Eastern Europe. It is on the reshaping of the economy there that would follow. The division made economic reports on the services sector of the Soviet Bloc. But no method in standard economic analysis could tie growth in that sector to the whole economy. It could not tie it to the major sectors either.

A plain case makes the gap clear. Say 10,000 workers moved from tank output in one city to cotton textile work in another. The effects on services would run far past the move itself. The division also lacked area, source, and language staff of its own. So an outside study was wanted. It would set out a theory and a worked plan for factory growth in the region.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100170048-7:
Organisation sheet for S/CST, the Agency's Construction Branch, lists the parts of the branch. The parts sit under heads for oversight. They are Industrial, Electric Power, Transportation, Housing and Utilities, and Agriculture. They are Military, Civil Defense, Building Materials, and an Economic unit for investment and labour. Names set against each post are redacted in the scan. A salary budget line for fiscal year 1955 appears below the chart, its figures redacted as well.

The mission statement on the sheet is the branch's standard one. The branch makes all-source economic reports on the building of fixed sites in the Soviet Bloc. It reports on the making of building supplies there. It works with other parts of the government on such work. It has a share in national estimates. A note on standing claims the branch was the only unit at work on building economics across the Soviet Bloc countries.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100170057-7:
Office memo dated 18 November 1954 gives briefing notes on the Transportation Branch. It goes from the Acting Chief, S/TR, to the Chief, D/S. The branch sat in the Services Division of the Agency's Office of Research and Reports. Its authority is traced to NSCID Nos. 1, 3, and 15. It is traced to DCID 15/1 of 14 September 1954 as well. Its mission covered the whole Soviet Bloc.

The mission wording is set out in the notes. The branch made all-source economic reports on transport work and transport sites in the Bloc. Rail, road, air, and water transport all fall in that scope. Military aircraft and pipelines fall outside it. The branch worked with the rest of the government on such work. It had a share in national estimates. A table for 1 May to 31 October 1954 splits branch hours by head. The heads are research, talks, upkeep of intelligence, training, office work, and other tasks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180001-7:
Structure paper for the Economic Defense Advisory Committee lists EDAC membership at Assistant Secretary level. It is marked Official Use Only. The members named are the Departments of State, Defense, Commerce, and the Treasury. They include the International Cooperation Administration and the Central Intelligence Agency. They include the Office of Defense Mobilization and the Atomic Energy Commission. The Department of Agriculture and the Export-Import Bank are named as well. The United States Information Agency sits as observer. The chairman could invite other agencies when their interests were touched.

EDAC took policy direction from the NSC and the CFEP. It advised agency heads on matters under United States economic defense policy and the MDAC Act. Working groups under it handled the detailed work. A standing Panel on Research Planning, set up under one working group, handled basic planning and the drafting of the United States position.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180010-7:
Lecture transcript kept in the Agency's files is titled Economic Warfare. It records a talk given on 26 March 1956 at the Industrial College of the Armed Forces in Washington. Colonel B. R. Nyquist, of the faculty, introduces the speaker. The speaker is a chief of economic coordination. His name is redacted in the scan. The opening words recall lessons of the last war. Wars can be fought well by means other than the Army, Navy, and Air Force. Economic warfare stands high among those means.

The lecture and the discussion that followed run to many pages. They fill Industrial College Publication No. 156-119. One passage works through the Battle Act by way of a concrete case. Ceylon had agreed to ship rubber to Communist China. Rubber is named there as a strategic good. On that ground, Ceylon was found not fit for aid under the terms of the Act.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180029-7:
Minutes in the Agency's files, ED/EC M-232, record a meeting at 10:30 a.m. on 18 April 1957. The meeting sat in Room 1213, Maiatico. The minutes were issued on 23 April 1957. Agenda items open with statements from the CHINCOM meeting of 12 April. They turn then to more work on material for EDAC. That work covers items proposed for decontrol, a Defense appeal on machine tools and electric melting furnaces, a work program for NSC 5705/1, and the Paris meeting of 7 May.

One decision opens the notes. The chairman was to draw up a memo on the CHINCOM statements. Talk on the EDAC material turned to the listing of differentials without sectors. It turned to delay as well. The chairman proposed that one attachment go before EDAC with pencilled deletions, made on the Executive Committee's word. The paper would then be redone clean once EDAC had decided.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180047-7:
Minutes ED/EC M-260, issued 31 July 1957, record the meeting at 2:00 p.m. on Thursday, 25 July 1957, in Room 1213, Maiatico. A note covers Norwegian aluminium. Numbered items take up the second revision of economic defense policy, EDAC D-135/1a, and requirements for EDAC under a Joint Chiefs of Staff memorandum attached to EDAC D-135. Attendance included a CIA member with the usual agency group.

On aluminium, the chairman said he had lately approved a joint agency telegram to the embassy in Norway. The United States had once given Norway assistance and agreed to take aluminium in repayment for the stockpile, and the telegram dealt with that standing arrangement. On policy, the chairman was to draft a transmittal explaining the changes in the revised draft and its paragraph 9 work program.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180056-7:
Minutes ED/EC M-271 in the Agency's files, issued 19 September 1957, record the meeting at 2:00 p.m. on Tuesday, 17 September 1957, in Room 1213, Maiatico. A note covers cables exchanged between USRO Paris and Washington. Numbered items are List II quotas for 1958 and comments on paragraphs of the work program for paragraph 9 of the revised policy. State, Commerce, Defense, ICA, Treasury, CIA, and MDAC members attended.

State questioned the theory of complete interchangeability within the Bloc and wanted it tested against the List II items one by one. Commerce, Defense, and ICA did not agree with the State proposal. The ICA member said intelligence evaluations had held fairly consistently that interchangeability inside the Bloc was real, which cut against reopening the point item by item.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180065-7:
Minutes ED/EC M-279 in the Agency's files, issued 13 November 1957, record the meeting at 10:30 a.m. on Friday, 8 November 1957, in Room 814 of the District National Building. A note covers proposed talks with a redacted party. Numbered items are embargo of copper wire and the work program for paragraph 9 of economic defense policy. Mr. Hale chaired, with MDAC, Commerce, Defense, ICA, and State members present.

On the work program, the committee decided to meet again on Tuesday, 12 November, to begin framing its recommendations to EDAC. First issues for discussion would be criteria, administrative principles, and changed concepts of List II. The chairman warned that a major problem would be pulling the most important elements out of the mass of material for EDAC, including the Ad Hoc Subcommittee's D-126 series reports.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180128-7:
Draft dated 24 July 1957 gives a work program for paragraph 9 of the new draft policy statement. It is filed as EDAC D-135/1a in the Agency's papers. As a basic task, Working Group I would keep the joint control system under steady review, and put changes to the Executive Committee as conditions changed. Changes from other member countries would be covered as well, so the system stayed effective.

A prompt full review of the Sino-Soviet strategic situation is also assigned, on grounds given in the draft. One ground is the recent de facto change in controls toward Communist China. One is the need to judge the Bloc as one body, while allowing for the marked gap in factory and military growth between the main European Bloc countries and China. A test of the current International Lists is also expected. Sector studies follow, from chemicals and plastics to ships and electronics.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200080047-7:
Study in the Agency's files describes the transport situation in the USSR and the Eastern European Satellites. It shows a Bloc transport system carrying heavy loads under tight capacity. Yearly freight traffic plans were usually met, and often topped. Longer hauls had commonly been put in place of capital imports that fell behind schedule. The system took such demands in its stride, showing spare capacity and much give. Rail capacity use ran far higher than in Western countries.

One central problem is named in the study. The problem is supply of Communist China. The Trans-Siberian Railroad and its links to China now carried heavy tonnages for that supply. The cost was very high, set against the natural movement of the same goods. Spending on transport had been high in the first postwar years. It was small in 1951 to 1955, set against the growth in freight moved.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120033-7:
Agency Current Support Memorandum No. 564, dated March 1958, reviews Soviet foreign trade in 1957. Recent Soviet statements seemed to show one picture of that trade. Trade with the Bloc in 1957 rose little, if at all, over 1956. Trade with the Free World rose by upward of 55 percent. The paper tests those statements against partner country figures. It finds the picture mixed rather than flat.

Early estimates by East Germany, Czechoslovakia, and Poland pointed one way. Their trade with the USSR pointed to increases, not decreases, against 1956. Hungary's trade with the USSR also seemed to have risen in 1957. Trade between the USSR and its major Bloc partner, China, had by contrast fallen. If the Soviet statements were largely right, one share is left over. Free World trade would make up the remaining 33 percent share the paper discusses.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200140095-7:
Agency capacity study of lines in northeast Hungary works line by line through a border railway district. One main line had once been double track, but material shortages had reduced it to a single track line at present. Plans completed in 1956 to relay a second track had been held up by the same shortages, and the line was believed still single with completion expected in a later period. Other lines in the district are described as single track throughout, with a second track under construction in places but progressing very slowly.

Yard and siding detail fills much of the paper: lengths of sidings in metres, a passing loop of 150 metres at one point, and a yard reported with about 80 tracks. Bridge and loading facts are added where sources gave them, so a planner could judge what weight of traffic each line could bear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100080095-7:
Memo from the Director of Central Intelligence, signed Walter B. Smith, goes to seven intelligence heads. They are State, the Army, the Navy, the Air Force, the Atomic Energy Commission, the Joint Staff, and the FBI. Its subject is intelligence deficiencies revealed in SE-27. The Office of National Estimates had reviewed them with IAC representatives, and they are set out in an enclosure.

The deficiencies lie mainly in economic matters. So the Director asked Mr. Amory to take two steps urgently. Amory was chairman of the Economic Intelligence Committee. The first step was to review standing guidance to collection agencies in that field. The second was to fill the gaps named on page four of the enclosure, which relate in part to seaborne trade. A parallel inquiry by the Assistant Director for Intelligence Coordination was to report to the Director and the IAC within six weeks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100120171-7:
Proposal dated 14 October, the year partly garbled in the scan, addresses one funding question. How can intelligence activities be strengthened through funding? The problem is stated plainly in the paper. The Director must find ways to ensure the parts of the federal intelligence system obtain sufficient funds for intelligence activities essential to national security. The paper rests on the National Security Act and NSCID No. 1, under which the Director recommends on such matters, with the concurrence or dissent of the IAC.

The discussion holds that the IAC agencies are meant to operate as a system, interrelated and interdependent, while still meeting their own departmental duties. Later pages work through single funding cases. One case is Agency reimbursement of the State Department for the National Intelligence Survey. Another asks where coordination of external research could best sit for the good of the whole system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100140197-7:
Memo dated 24 May 1954 goes to the Special Assistant to the Director for Planning and Coordination. It reports external research coordinating activities for 7 to 21 May 1954. The first item is research on exploitation of foreign documents. One office held a continuing interest in three related projects. Mechanical translation leads the items. Of the several active experimental projects in the country, the Agency had followed one group's work most closely. A version of its translating machine had been shown to Agency and defense personnel.

Agency policy on the subject rested on one 1953 memo. General Cabell wrote to the Deputy Secretary of Defense on 12 May 1953. His memo welcomed Defense interest in sponsoring research and development in mechanical translation. A second section lists research proposals from outside the Agency. One is a proposed current digest of the East Asian press. It is modelled on a digest produced for years by another office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100160005-7:
Companion draft on budget presentation for the intelligence community works one problem. Should a coordinated community budget be drawn up, and presented to the Bureau of the Budget and to Congress? The draft reaches toward a model for doing so. The views of the IAC would go to the Bureau of the Budget as a body. They would include any items on which members could not identify a sufficient community interest.

A step in the draft concerns the Bureau's allowances. The Bureau would be asked to earmark one amount in them. That amount is the sum approved for intelligence activities. It would be earmarked in the allowances granted to single IAC agencies. That step would let the coordinated total survive the budget process. In that process each agency is funded on its own. The draft notes practical difficulties, but still carries the machinery toward an actual presentation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000200030099-7:
Staff paper reexamines the Agency's reimbursement practices in two cases. One case is reimbursement to the Department of State. It is for National Intelligence Survey production. The second case concerns arrangements for external research. The paper links both cases to a wider question. That question is a coordinated budget for intelligence activities important to the Agency and to national security.

A governing principle is stated at the start of the paper. Each agency bears responsibility for obtaining its own funds. The funds are to carry out its own duties. Yet reimbursements are encouraged in one case. That is where another agency can perform a needed service more competently, or more efficiently. Care is needed on one point. Reimbursement must not subvert the intent of Congress. That intent is shown in appropriations acts. The legality of reimbursement, and the objections to it, are argued in an attached tab.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000200080094-7:
Draft memo dated 17 July 1957 in the Agency's files goes to the Special Assistant to the Director for Planning and Coordination. Its subject is program analysis. The study had been assigned by General Cabell. Its initiative came from an Inspector General report, and the IG office had drafted Cabell's memo, Tab A. The real stimulus came from the Comptroller's Office, during an IG survey.

A final draft had gone to the Comptroller on 26 April 1956, lacking only one tab, now Tab E, and the final views of the DD/S office. The writer had chased them at irregular intervals since then. The study's conclusions doubt the proposed arrangement: an analysis staff attached to the addressee and available to the PRC would tend to buttress the PRC, whose need all parties doubt. They doubt the minimum proposed staff could really perform the analysis asked of it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400100008-7:
Untitled message in the Agency's files from a commander, cite message number Whiskey Zero One Four Nine, is a photographic frame log. Numbered items list frame pairs by camera side and number, each rated for quality and geometry. Early entries read 9R 1579, good, medium oblique; 9R 781, good, near vertical; 9L 1032, good, near vertical; and 9L 778, good, near vertical. Later items pair right and left frames covering the same ground, with ratings of vertical, near vertical, medium oblique, and far oblique.

The log runs past fifty numbered items, nearly all rated good. It is the quality record for one mission's film: which frames exist, how they were taken, and whether the photography was fit for the reporting that would be built on it. No place names appear in the text; targets are identified by frame number alone.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400100053-7:
Confirming message in the Agency's files, cite Whiskey-0092, carries photo report No. 1382. Its date of information is 21 June 1957. It covers Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria. Jordan has a single item in the report. Irbid military installation showed 16 possible tanks and 40 vehicles. Lebanon items are short as well. Estabel and Metulla airfields showed no aircraft. Riyaq Airfield showed 3 possible aircraft.

Syria items open with Afisse North Airfield. It showed no aircraft, but unidentified objects lay along the airfield access road. Aleppo Airfield showed 11 T-6 and 10 liaison type aircraft. Bab el Haoua Airfield was unserviceable. An Ealunah rail freight station entry reports unidentified material in open storage. The report covers ground sites of that kind alongside the airfields.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000500030131-7:
A top secret target list for the western USSR fills the file, marked TS-164204. Entries run in alphabetical order by place name. Each entry gives an installation, its coordinates, a category code, and a level of interest. Airfields appear often, alongside complexes, ports, naval bases, and industrial sites. Early pages move from Anisovo Gorodishche and Arkhangelsk through Baku, Baltiysk, and Bobruysk, with cross references that send the reader from one place name to another.

Later pages reach Moscow in detail. Separate entries cover Moscow airfields such as Ostafyevo, Ramenskoye, Shchelkovo, and Tushino, plus a guided missile plant at Khimki. Other entries cover Murmansk and Severomorsk, Nikolayev, and Novosibirsk. The list served as a reference for planning photographic coverage. It shows the range of Soviet sites of interest in the west, and the basic facts recorded for each one before any flight was tasked.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600020005-7:
A secret plan, marked Tab B, calls for shared national needs and joint assignment of collection tasks. Priority national objectives under DCID 4/4 frame the argument. Needs now vary widely by originator, office, and agency, the paper notes. It urges stating, jointly and in precise terms, what intelligence must be produced and what raw facts must be gathered to meet those objectives.

Chief among its proposals, the Intelligence Advisory Committee should set up a joint requirements board. That body would frame national needs tied to the priority objectives. Agreed needs would guide planning and the division of collection tasks, and would be revised as objectives changed. A smaller panel would decide what extra, more detailed needs were required.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600090071-7:
War plans of the deputy directorate offices are summarised here with a note on shared ground. Planning rests on set premises: services of common concern will go on, the top committee stays in place, and the estimates process keeps its present form. Costs are met from the current budget. No added funds or staff are sought yet, and the plans remain tentative without the deputy director's approval.

Office entries then follow the same ground as a companion summary. Estimates would shift toward narrow, fast papers. Science work would stress war-making power. Current intelligence would add a centre and a situation room and move to extra shifts. Later entries add fresh detail: one office asks for more film and kit at the relocation centre. An industrial office expects fresh demands from wartime agencies, and wants overseas government files brought back for study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600130003-7:
A memo dated 14 December 1955 sends a draft war plan annex to the deputy director for intelligence. It comes from the Assistant Director for Basic Intelligence. The draft answers a request sent to assistant directors on 1 July 1955. Its core claim stands early: the National Intelligence Survey program, run by its joint committee, is the right tool to coordinate basic intelligence work in a global war.

Support for that claim fills the next pages. Published survey volumes already give a broad, well joined base of basic facts. The memo contrasts that base with the grave gaps of the Second World War. Output continues at a pace and order set by the Joint Chiefs of Staff. More than forty government activities feed their skills into the program. Special wartime needs of the Joint Chiefs and theater commanders would still be met through the same survey machinery.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600130012-7:
A draft annex from the estimates office to the deputy directorate war plan is sent with a covering memo. The memo agrees that, while two offices each produce a form of national intelligence, their problems differ sharply. Separate annexes therefore make sense. How long would the opening phase of war last? Would that phase call for current situation reports, or for full estimates as well?

In almost any opening wartime case, the memo argues, coordinated estimates will be needed at once. Early disruption should hit estimates work no harder than current intelligence work. The office also stresses its deep reliance on member agencies when national estimates are prepared. It opposes any wartime scheme that cuts those agencies down or sets CIA work against theirs. Later pages urge that a committee link for estimates survive in war, with agency liaison officers placed with the board.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700010005-7:
A long report reexamines how CIA pays and gets paid back between agencies. A covering memo sends it to the Director of Central Intelligence. The study was built with the deputy directors and the Inspector General. It answers a Director's letter of 23 September 1954, which set a fresh look at payment methods with the Budget Bureau and the State Department. Findings were due by 15 February 1955, in time for the 1957 budget.

The team ranged wider than that one case. Past disputes over payments, raised by General Cabell and the Budget Bureau, pulled in more ground. A 1954 note by Mr Amory, on joining up intelligence budgets, widened it further. The memo asks the Director to approve the report's findings and advice. It also flags fresh problem areas for prompt study. Mid pages weigh what the law allows, noting that the Security Council set no firm limits on such payments.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700020004-7:
A second orientation talk by James Reber survives as a transcript, again on the Office of Intelligence Coordination. He opens with a complaint played for laughs. The prior day's speakers stole his thunder, he says. The first twenty minutes of his speech must be laid aside, so the class will win an early break.

His core puzzle follows. The Director holds chief duty for coordinating the member agencies. Each functional assistant director also coordinates in his own field. Reber does neither job, which raises a fair question: why does his office exist? His answer is support. The office helps the Director carry a very large coordination load. It also helps assistant directors do their own parts of that shared work. Later talk turns to problems still not clear, and to output that falls short of what the time demands. He closes by taking questions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700020022-7:
Speaker's notes for a talk on services of common concern fill the file, set out as a numbered outline. Background comes first: Pearl Harbor as the spur to fix intelligence bodies, and the choice against one single agency. The need was for leadership, weighing of work, and a true federal system.

The outline then lists the Director's five chief duties under law. Advising, urging coordination, and producing national intelligence come first. Running shared services judged better done at the centre comes fourth. A section on the term itself notes it had no precedent, though a Central Intelligence Service unit existed in the old Group. Limits follow: the Council must direct, the committee must approve, and department needs must win support. Closing points draw lessons from practice, then turn to a contact office case reaching back to a 1946 State suggestion.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070054-7:
A progress report on the Interagency Clandestine Collection Priorities Committee reaches members in a single copy each. Its work is sensitive, so spread is tight. The committee was set up on 30 July 1951. By the time of writing it had run about two years. Its first formal report goes to a committee meeting set for 14 July 1953.

Three duties define the body. It decides which foreign needs call for secret collection. It keeps a live list of secret targets holding priority rank in the broad United States interest. It also speaks for member agencies on target choice and ranking. In October 1951 the committee agreed eighteen top targets across the whole Soviet orbit. Seventeen sat inside it, most in fact out of near reach. Means were thin and risks high, members knew. By report time, work on four targets had passed planning into active steps.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100160002-7:
An abridged translation carries a Soviet piece on synthetic materials in aircraft construction. Major-General A Tumanov, of the engineering services, wrote it. The piece ran in Sovetskaya Aviatsiya on 25 May 1956. Plastics of many kinds, it argues, now serve widely in building aircraft. Weight saving is the sharp prize, since cutting weight is a keen problem in flying.

Foam plastics draw long praise. They weigh far less than the loads they replace, and they block heat and sound well. Self-foaming types bond fast to metal and stiffen a frame. Glass cloth plastics earn a place too. Mixed with face layers or honeycomb fill, they suit radio gear and radar housings well. The piece claims some builds cut body weight by twenty to twenty-five percent. Named Soviet aircraft types appear as cases where such materials add stiffness and strength while shedding pounds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100170001-7:
A covering memo dated 14 April 1958 sends round a CIA summary on phthalic anhydride. The Economic Defense Intelligence Committee chairman signed it. Commerce had opened the case on 25 March. The study asks how much of the chemical the Sino-Soviet bloc makes, and how much it needs. Members had till 25 April to call a meeting, or the summary would stand approved and the case close.

Commerce wanted the facts for a live control question. Its own task group was weighing whether the chemical mattered enough for the United States Positive List, and perhaps the international list. The summary finds the bloc a net buyer. Imports of the chemical and its kin from the West trend upward. The USSR buys most, taking at least several thousand tons in 1957. Shipments from lands such as Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, and Britain are poorly tracked, so the full import picture stays incomplete.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470017-7:
Minutes of the tenth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee record a long session on 2 June 1955. Pending cases open the record. First is the pattern of Soviet bloc strategic exports to the West. A paper dated 27 April, on bloc exports of capital goods and industrial materials, had gone to members. They were asked for views and fresh examples. Commerce and the aid agency promised more material.

Once all views land, that paper goes to the Executive Committee. It will judge whether deeper study would help. Trade in freed goods follows. Defence has begun work on a Commerce list of deleted items, and G-2 will carry it forward. Later items turn to borax products, boric acid and borates. Traders and the joint committee sought facts to judge the strategic weight of those goods for rocket fuel and jet use.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470026-7:
Minutes of the first meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee are dated 16 November 1954. The group met on 4 November. Work in hand opens the record. A member reviewed West Germany's plea to put some copper wire types back under embargo for Soviet buyers. A joint body had asked this committee on 12 October for backing facts. Those facts should cover bloc needs and orders placed in the West.

State's research office had taken up a study of copper wire and cable, by deal with two other offices. It would come here for review once done. A cable of 2 November added fresh facts. Members agreed not to open a case of their own, but to judge that study when it lands. Next came indium. A case paper of 29 October, laying out a mutual defence request for a study of bloc and West European indium output and uses, was handed round.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510021-7:
A second copy of the phthalic anhydride summary fills the file, sent under the same memo of 14 April 1958. Commerce opened the case on 25 March. The question was whether the chemical earns a place on control lists. Members had till 25 April to call a meeting, or the summary would stand approved and the case close.

Findings match the first copy in the main. The bloc buys more of the chemical and its kin from the West each year. The USSR is the largest buyer. In this copy the 1957 figure reads clearly: at least five thousand tons imported. Gaps in the data are admitted again. Shipments from lands such as Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, and Britain are not fully known. With them, the import picture would be fuller. The study exists to back a Commerce task group review of the chemical's military and industrial weight.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100530001-7:
A case record of the Intelligence Working Group, dated April 1954, logs cases in a table. Columns give number, title, start date, outcome, and paper. Early cases date from June 1952. One tracks a planned shipment of 2,000 tons of copper from Turkey to Communist China. Others cover Soviet bearing output and buying, prior commitments, and a Greek shipping cartel.

Most cases close within months. A Danish tanker case ran till March 1954. One case on collection needs for East-West trade sits inactive. Ships recur often: Greek flag ships trading with the Communist Far East, a Polish ship's oil cargoes, a Finnish antimagnetic schooner for the USSR. Later rows reach 1953: a China-French barter deal in nitrogen fertilizer, and a plea for facts on hides and leather. One case still stands active: Soviet bloc financial operations in the free world, tied to report IWG/R-16.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200160029-7:
A case summary dated 30 November 1953 tells the Villach copper wire diversion in full. Copper wire forms the goods: electrolytic wire, seven millimetres thick. Orders ran to 575 metric tons in all, worth 495,000 dollars across May to December 1953. The supposed buyer sat in Italy. The real end was the Soviet bloc, by way of Vienna.

Results split three ways. A block at Villach held 173 tons, where twelve rail cars were detained. A Zurich block held 45 tons more. Thirty-six tons, though, certainly reached Rumania. The route is traced town by town, from Belgium through Luxembourg and Switzerland into Italy, then to Austria. Papers were switched at Chiasso on 29 May, with the load renamed as a metal fill good bound east. British staff detained the cars at Villach on 2 June. Later sections name the firms and men in the chain, and log how a tonnage figure on one paper was altered.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200010012-7:
A letter dated 18 August 1958 answers an inventor who wrote to the Director of Central Intelligence. John Warner, Acting General Counsel, signed it. The writer, John Langan, had raised his past work. His letter went to the Strategic Services Unit, as heir to the OSS and keeper of its archives. A search there found a fat file.

That file, the reply states, holds much on his inventions, patent bids, and patents. It can be made open to any government agency that asks. An inside memo of 12 August fills in the rest. The files give a full record of his inventions and of his deal with the wartime OSS, where some rights passed to the government. Staff agreed by phone that no outside agency had yet asked. So a bare acknowledgment was all that was owed for now. File numbers are kept on hand in case a query comes later.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200010021-7:
A letter to Mr Brundage at the Bureau of the Budget survives in a rough scan. Much of its text is garbled, and names in the heading read poorly. The legible core is plain enough. It concerns a proposed executive order under section 181 of Title 35. That order would name the Department of State a defence agency for patent secrecy work.

A draft of the order, dated 9 November 1955, rides with the letter. The writer reports talks with Patent Office and Defense Department officials on the draft. Informal concurrence, he states, has been won. The point of such naming is set by the law itself: a defence agency chief can call for secrecy orders on patent bids whose spread would harm national security. Because so much of this copy is scrambled, only the plan, its legal base, and the state of talks can be stated with care.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200010030-7:
A memo from the Director of Logistics to the General Counsel sorts patent work born of buying contracts. Agency buying follows the Armed Services Procurement Regulation as its guide. Contracts thus carry the standard patent, royalty, and copyright clauses. The patent clause wins the government royalty-free licences and other rights. The royalty clause sets duties to judge whether royalty charges are proper.

Four tasks stand out as the weightiest. Staff must review royalty-free licences from contractors and file them with the Patent Office. They must build and file patent bids for the government. They must judge whether an older government right kills a royalty charge, and whether a royalty rate runs too high. All four, the memo argues, are legal work fit for the General Counsel. A look back over many past contracts may also be owed, to check that every right was in fact reviewed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300150007-7:
A file from August 1959 tracks a planned cut in the Agency's size. Its first note logs a phone call from Roger Jones on 20 August. He raised his past talk with Lawrence Houston on section 12 of the Veterans' Preference Act. Could the matter wait a short time, he asked. Word back was that the Agency itself meant to wait for Houston and Gordon Stewart to return.

Involuntary firings should wait for Stewart, and most likely Houston too. A longer memo to the Director then thinks the cut through. It starts from the deputies' talk of 15 July. Say the on-duty force must fall by a set floor by the next 30 June, it posits, with more to come after. Some of that fall can come from sharper work, from natural loss, or from dropping tasks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300220018-7:
A file from 1959 weighs how far CIA print should spread. The Inspector General, Lyman Kirkpatrick, routes the core memos to the publications side in November. He has also sent them to the General Counsel. Counsel is asked for his view of the legal snags in wider spread. 

The Board's own memo to the Director, dated 19 March 1959, sits at the heart of the file. It asks him to bless a set policy on spread. The push came from the deputy director in December 1958. He asked the Board to study wider spread for some kinds of Agency print, in a few cases to the plain public. The Board finds the door part-way open. Open Agency work can go out under the flag of other state bodies. Up to two thousand copies of one piece could be handed free to the public in law.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400050025-7:
A note for the record, dated 5 August 1957, tracks a frail man's papers. Otto Doering had rung with word on General Donovan. The old OSS chief was a shade better, he said. Talk turned to the stock of papers Donovan held.

Houston had raised the stock in past talks. Some sheets in it look stamped and secret, he had said. Doering pushed back, in a soft way. A book on the birth of OSS and CIA is planned for print once Donovan dies. Mr Dulles backs that plan, he noted. The stock also holds plain sheets of a man's own life. Those do not belong to the Agency. Time must be given: the will's men should sort the man's own sheets from state stock first. One pledge is logged firm. The book, when built, will be shown to the Agency before it goes to print.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100040005-7:
A memo dated 3 November 1959 sends a fresh area study plan up for a nod. The Language and Area School chief writes to the training chief. It states a line and a scheme for area study, in step with a shift of weight the top men have called for.

Three first moves are named. One: rework the course stock, on lessons from the course to date and on word from men who used it in the field. Stock lent by an overseas craft scheme, on how to make the most of day-to-day touch with a land's own folk, feeds that rework. Two: build new ways to teach small bands who turn up at odd gaps: one-to-one hours, mail study, self-study kits, and a blend of broad and tight scope. Three: widen the map to lands not yet taught.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100080047-7:
Training wives of Agency staff for contract jobs overseas is the subject of a 9 October 1959 memorandum to a deputy training officer. The memo notes a long practice of hiring wives locally at stations, bases, and projects abroad. Many brought stenographic, clerical, technical, or language skills, yet most learned Agency procedure only after reaching the field.

Headquarters training before departure is proposed as the fix, so working wives could serve more effectively from the start. The plan sketches a training contract that would not count against a personnel ceiling, run for up to one year, and end when the trainee left for overseas. Field work would then continue under a new local contract arranged by the station.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100080065-7:
A participant's critique reviews the first running of a new Office of Training course called Personal Effectiveness Abroad, held from 30 March through 28 April 1959. Thirteen student-consultants took part, twelve of them with wide overseas experience. Their shared task was to help shape a course that would make Agency staff better at dealing with other cultures and at settling into life in foreign societies.

The writer explains how the course idea grew from concern about staff contact with people such as the Japanese, and from worries over family adjustment abroad. Judged as a pilot study, the course is found well planned and well presented. The critique offers it as a sound starting point for a formal basic course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000100010028-7:
Geographic intelligence reports are catalogued in a long index arranged by report number, place, and date. Entries run from March 1953 onward under the G/I series. Early entries cover the Soviet Union, Saint Paul Island in the Indian Ocean, Czechoslovakia, Austria, and China, each tied to its report number and month of issue.

The index keeps going through 1954 and 1955, ranging over Guatemala, Dien Bien Phu, the Salla Railroad, Tibet, Spain, and repeated work on the Antarctic. South China, Burma, Indochina, and Malaya appear as a cluster, with general geographic references listed beside the reports themselves. As a finding aid, the list shows the breadth of places the Agency's geographic analysts were tasked to cover in the early Cold War years.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000200090001-7:
Writing guidance for analysts who produce National Intelligence Survey chapters is circulated as NIS Memo No. 8, dated 25 August 1959. The guidance was written by W. Stewart Lester Jr., a survey coordinator at the State Department, from long experience with survey production. The Central Intelligence Agency's Office of Basic Intelligence sent it to all survey contributors as advice of general use.

Writing, the memo argues, is the main way analysts discharge their duties, and the chief basis on which their usefulness is judged. Deep knowledge of a country's parties, banks, or payments balance counts for little if it cannot be conveyed well. Later sections explain how introductory survey sections give readers a broad view of a society alongside the detailed chapters that follow.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000200160049-7:
A proposed geography project on irrigated farming in Soviet Central Asia is set out in an initiation memorandum dated 18 June 1959. The study would judge the feasibility of expanding irrigation in the region and weigh what wider irrigation would mean for the Soviet economy. Maps and help from other Agency offices were listed among the support wanted.

An attached outline breaks the study into parts. It starts with the present state of irrigation, then covers the share irrigated farming holds in the Soviet economy, past patterns, and the present spread of irrigated land and crops. Closing sections treat relief and soil factors that limit irrigation. The form estimates two hundred man-hours of work and a finished report in September 1959.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000200260002-7:
Map and chart output fills the Cartography Division's monthly report for January 1959. Requests came in from across the Agency. The plans directorate and the research offices sent the most. In the month the division finished eighty-five maps and charts. Most went to the Agency itself. A small number went to the Department of State.

Work still in hand at the end of January came to four hundred twenty-five maps and charts. The work was spread across branches for the Soviet bloc, the Far East, Europe, and Africa. Other branches covered special support and new methods. A survey coordinator handled proofing, printing, and rerun traffic at the same time. Notes at the end track special map series then in production.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000500040021-7:
Inspection of the Personnel Office is reported to the Director of Central Intelligence in a memorandum dated 30 November 1953. The inspector worked personally, asking each staff and division chief in the office to present his unit's organisation, duties, and chief problems. Every office of the Agency, including clandestine staffs and foreign divisions, was asked to judge the service the Personnel Office gave.

Annexes cover a separate survey of personnel posts held outside the office and a study of Agency regulations for fitness and completeness. One finding stands out in the discussion of placement. Staff returning from overseas, except at high grades, in effect had to shop for a job, and returnees should know their next post before leaving their station. Fault is shared between the Personnel Office and the operating offices.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200010005-7:
Release of systems and know-how developed under a secret project to the Department of Defense is governed by a policy memorandum sent to all suppliers. Access to the project, the memo stresses, had been limited from the start to people who were both security-acceptable and had a true need to know. Rank, clearances, and a general official interest did not by themselves earn admission.

Rules for disclosure follow. Information on a subsystem would normally carry a confidential marking to keep it out of print. A supplier passing on subsystem information had to be ready with a plausible account of how it was developed, one that revealed nothing of the wider system. Use of project information for a purely commercial chance required clearance in advance, while government use stood on different footing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200110040-7:
Equipment for exploiting CORONA photography is discussed in memorandum COR-0244, dated 1 December 1958. Acting on a trip report's recommendation, an officer had gone to Rochester in November to judge a live dispute: how ITEK's film processing equipment stacked up against Eastman Kodak's. Mr. Green of Eastman already knew of the ill feeling between the two firms over the processing gear.

Practical troubles fill the report. Rollers in the ITEK processor had worn and been replaced again and again until every spare ITEK held was used up, and making suitable new rollers would take time and money. When the processor was delivered, Green had asked ITEK for engineering drawings or written instructions to run it by. The memorandum shows a secret program caught between two rival suppliers, each doubting the other's kit.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100020078-7: A list of fund documents to be deposited in the Vital Materials Center gives document numbers only, with no subjects or summaries attached. Numbers run in long columns under letter prefixes such as RM, R, and P, covering a wide span of report numbers. A star against some entries marks them for indefinite retention.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100030040-7:
Plant needs for the Soviet Union and its satellites are set out in a paper dated 30 July 1958. The needs feed a standing list kept by the Office of Current Intelligence. They cover 1 September to 31 December 1958. Air needs open the list. Output of the main bomber types is tracked. Tanker planes for the long-range air force are tracked too. The entry of new light bombers into units is also watched.

Civil air work appears as well. One plane type has flown with Aeroflot since 1956. It flies foreign routes too. Questions ask how many serve with the airline and with the armed forces. They also ask how many are being built. At least three forms of the AN-10 transport are reported. The first was shown at Moscow's Vnukovo airfield in July 1957.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100110050-7: A declassified CIA monthly report for April 1959. The month's work. The document holds the report. The file remains. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120013-7:
November 1959 is covered in an Industrial Division monthly report dated 3 December 1959. The division chief gave most of his time to supporting a national estimate on Soviet capabilities for strategic attack through the mid-1960s. A meeting with the Eastern European branch decided to resume economic coverage of the Eastern European provincial press, dropped the previous spring.

Khrushchev's missile statement of 14 November produced two support papers: a comment for presentation at an Operations Coordinating Board meeting, and a comment for transmission onward. Staff also joined a study weighing whether collection and analysis on the Soviet rail network needed to grow in selected areas. A recommendation about clandestine study of ICBM production under disarmament had been approved. Division views were also gathered on a proposed Czech-American exchange program.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120103-7:
Overdue projects of the Industrial Division are listed in a status report giving each project's number, title, and stage. Several studies sat in final typing and review, with completion expected by a date in August. Titles show the division's range: production of Soviet casting machine tools, justification work on a Soviet building materials subject, and recent developments in the agriculture industry of Communist China.

Further entries cover the construction equipment industry, the growth of a named Soviet plant's freight car production, industrial capital investment in Communist China, investment in the power industry of Communist China. Industrial manpower policy in East Germany. The list form gives no findings; it is a manager's snapshot of a research queue, showing which papers were late and how close each stood to done.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100130058-7:
Collection requirements for a Moscow aircraft plant open with twenty-one numbered questions about final assembly of the Coot, the Il-18 airliner. Describe the final assembly operation, the paper asks, then give the number of assembly positions in use, workers per position, time in final assembly, time from the assembly building to first flight. Time from first flight to acceptance by the customer.

Production rate per month and cumulative production of the type are wanted, along with the number of prototypes built and of aircraft destroyed in static or water tank tests. Labour questions cover total and direct labour force, shifts, and hours per week. The engine used and the aircraft's selling price and break-even point close the Moscow list. A second part turns to a plant at Tbilisi on the north bank of the Kura River, reported to be involved in production of a new jet fighter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100160019-7:
Military production in East Germany is surveyed in a long report on plants and output. The summary is unflattering. East German military production has not increased noticeably, output in 1957 still fell short. Total production seems to have run considerably short of the annual plans, a pattern that appears to continue into 1958.
