Central control through the ATT, the body first set up to control and coordinate military production, may itself be a basic reason for poor performance at some plants. Cases of poor design and inferior materials in military vehicles are noted, along with shortages of raw materials and late delivery of plans and blueprints. The Soviets are said to hold first priority on materials and plant facilities for repair of their forces in Germany. Plant profiles follow, including one works turning out military engineering equipment, trailers, portable steel radio masts, and sectional steel bridges.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100160046-7: A declassified CIA file with comments on a draft project about defense expenditures. The draft, critiqued. The document holds the comments. The file remains. Those who study the era will use it. Declassified files like this open a window on the past.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100170009-7:
A reply to comments on Project 30.2043, from the Chief of the Far East Branch, is sent on 30 April 1959 by the Chief of the Manufacturing Sectors Branch. Machine building received the largest single share of industrial investment in Communist China, the reply notes, so whether those resources were well allocated matters greatly. They should have been allocated to maximise production and to provide the products that would most advance Chinese economic development.

Allegations that the report underestimates Chinese advances in machine building, and the vital role of Soviet aid in them, are denied. The regime is given credit for flexibility in presenting new ideas. The reply presses the critics in return: why did the regime need new economic policies to meet new economic problems, what are the problems. How did they arise from rapid, forced growth?
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00346a000100110035-7: Time taken to process reports in one office is measured in a study. The copy that survives is badly garbled. Only its frame and a few figures can be read. Reports are tracked stage by stage. The stages are typing, proofing, revision, clearance, and review approval. They run inside the office and outside it. One clear result gives a mean of eighty-six and a half days per report. The period studied runs from September 1955 onward.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00346a000100110044-7:
Soviet bloc standing on rolling mills and presses is weighed in a paper dated 5 January 1958. The paper comes from a working group of the Economic Intelligence Committee. Rolling mills come first. Steel growth across the bloc has slowed since 1955, most in the Soviet Union. The cause is traced to a lack of capital gear. The bloc could not supply the gear its first goals needed from its own stores.

Modern rolling and finishing gear had long been neglected. Under the fifth five-year plan, the Soviet steel ministry put its funds into primary iron and steel capacity. Its goal for new iron ore capacity fell short by thirty-six million tons. Presses over one thousand tons follow. The bloc had built twenty-five types of mechanical presses. It had built twelve types of hydraulic forging and bending presses. One extrusion press of twenty-five hundred tons is also named.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00346a000100250003-7: Zinc output in the Sino-Soviet bloc is shown as a bare table of figures, with no text. Output is given in metric tons, by country, for the mid-1950s. The rows run from the Soviet Union and Communist China down to the smaller states of Eastern Europe. Notes cover the metal content of ores mined. They also flag estimates that rest on imports. A second table extends the same series to world zinc output by country.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100020115-7:
The Economic Research Area's contribution to the Agency's annual report, submitted 18 July 1958, opens on a mixed note. Intelligence on the economic performance of the Sino-Soviet bloc kept improving during the year, thanks to a greater volume of material. That gain was offset by uncertainty from growing experimentation with economic policies and institutions, above all in the Soviet Union.

Research now centres on measuring what the Soviet changes will do to growth and productivity: regional councils substituted for industrial ministries, the machine tractor stations abolished. A new agricultural procurement policy adopted. Economic intelligence also fed appraisals of the size and meaning of bloc aid and trade in the underdeveloped countries of the free world. Of the bloc's growing wish to trade with the West. Serious deficiencies in direct information on bloc military programs are admitted in the same breath.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100040087-7:
Short letters dated 27 November 1959, filed in several copies, send a journal reprint to professors outside the Agency. The enclosure is an article by one of the writer's senior analysts, printed in the September 1959 issue of The American Economic Review. The article gives a critical discussion of the paper on Soviet industrial production delivered by G. Warren Nutter at the 1957 meetings of the American Economic Association.

Each letter makes the same two points: the recipient will be particularly interested in the critique, and the writer hopes to see him in Washington for the December meetings. The distribution list shows copies kept by the chief of economic research and the analysis staff. The file is a small record of how the Agency's economists kept up an open professional exchange with academic specialists on the Soviet economy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090019-7: This declassified CIA document has no surviving title. The nameless pages wait. Their story is kept. The archive holds the file. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090028-7:
Twelve years separate two speeches by Allen W. Dulles to the National Association of Manufacturers. This text of the second, delivered in New York City on 4 December 1959, opens by looking back. His 1947 subject, like the present one, was the Soviet challenge. He had defined it as a challenge to prove that the system of free men under law can survive.

In 1947 the Soviet Union based its hopes on the imminent collapse of free enterprise, not on the might of its own system. Stalin, Molotov, and Vishinsky warned that the Marshall Plan was merely a means of unloading excess goods and capital to escape an impending crisis. The old Soviet leaders have gone, and many of their arguments with them. What has not changed is the mix of economic penetration, political warfare, and subversion, pressed mainly by measures short of war. Khrushchev's recent speeches state the objectives more bluntly than ever.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090037-7:
Closing remarks to the National Strategy Seminar at the National War College are given by Allen W. Dulles on 24 July 1959. His intelligence on the seminar is good, he jokes: the officers had covered Soviet strategy and tactics, the Communist threat, East-West military strength, and war in the nuclear age.

Two errors in judging the Soviet threat are set against each other. Some experts magnify all aspects of Soviet power and become prophets of gloom. Others discount Soviet accomplishments and magnify internal difficulties, risking unhealthy complacency. The first class is the larger. Recent magazine articles have tried to discredit recognised Soviet accomplishments, particularly in outer space, on the flimsiest evidence. It is more dangerous to underrate than to overrate, he concludes, though overrating can be expensive in budget terms. Communist competition, if carried on openly and peacefully, could be accepted: let the peoples choose which system is better.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090046-7:
A lecture on the Soviet economy, delivered 11 September 1958, is built round eight questions put by the general who invited the speaker. The Soviet economy is shaped to serve the needs of the state, not the people, the lecture begins. To grasp its structure, one must start with the aims of the Communist leadership, from which its governing priorities flow.

The long-range aim is world domination. Communism is above all a revolutionary force, striving for a victory shown by the end of capitalism and the rise of a Sovietised world order. Military outlays have kept first priority in Soviet planning. Yet direct large-scale military action seems ruled out in the age of the hydrogen weapon. Education spending in the two countries is compared as quite close. Soviet stress falls much more on the physical sciences. The Soviet Union is said to be graduating about ninety thousand engineers a year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090109-7:
Soviet Economic Problems; Labor Productivity is a declassified Agency talk that names labor supply as the Soviet economy's most serious problem. For the first time, the speaker says, the Soviet Union faced a shortage of workers. Two causes are given: low birth rates during and just after the war, and a farm sector that could spare no more hands.

The talk puts new workers entering the force from 1957 to 1962 at about 5.7 million. That is a sharp drop from the prior span. It weighs cures such as moving soldiers into civil jobs and raising output per worker. Farm promises by Khrushchev may force funds toward farming and slow industry, the speaker warns.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090118-7:
Production of Selected Food Items in the USSR is a declassified Agency data table with source notes. It sets Soviet output of eight food items in 1913 beside output in 1956. All figures are in million metric tons. Grain rose from about 84 million tons to 115 million. Potatoes rose from about 32 million to about 96 million.

Meat, milk, sugar, fish, vegetable oils, and vegetables fill out the table. Long footnotes explain how each figure was built and where it came from. Several notes warn that official Soviet figures for meat and milk looked too high. Those figures were cut down in the table to match international usage. The sources for each line are listed at the end.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100008-7:
The Role of Intelligence in Forming National Security Policy Within the Executive Branch is a declassified article kept in Agency files. Its author writes from direct service in that machinery. He served as Deputy Director of the Psychological Strategy Board in 1951 and as an administrative assistant to President Eisenhower in early 1953.

The article argues that sound policy rests on the latest and best intelligence bearing on the question at hand. It explains how papers should reach the National Security Council in time to be studied before debate. Work at the Planning Board level, where this practice had stood since 1953, gets close attention.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100044-7:
Report of the Committee on World Economic Practices is a committee report kept in declassified Agency files. Its members, chaired by Harold Boeschenstein, were drawn from major United States firms. They were asked to propose a joint government and private program against the Sino-Soviet Bloc economic offensive.

The contents run from private enterprise in foreign development to the United States image abroad. Sections cover how aid should be given, world trade, East-West trade, and civil aviation. One theme runs through the middle pages: aid works best when its terms do not spoil the local gains it aims to create. Recipient nations' own use of their resources is treated as a test of sound aid.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100020007-7:
Ruble Dollar Ratios is Appendix B of a declassified Agency study, built around a table of selected 1950 price ratios. The notes stress that the figures show price ratios only. They do not directly show how real costs compare between the Soviet Union and the United States.

Group averages open the table, with total output at 8 rubles per dollar and total goods output at 10. Farm production stands at 11 and primary non-ferrous metals at 16. The notes explain that ruble prices were changed only to strip out the turnover tax on farm goods and oil products. A planned study of prices against true costs is named as the next step.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100080001-7:
Uniformity of Participation in Free World Controls is Staff Study No. 7 in the CFEP Drafting Group's Economic Defense Policy Review. The file holds the draft of June 6, 1955 with revised pages of June 23, 1955 laid in. Pages 2, 4, 6, 7, and 8 were replaced in that revision.

The study asks whether all free world nations must apply trade controls on the same terms. Its core case concerns special latitude, where one nation eases controls for its own reasons. Such easing can blunt the controls kept by others, the study warns. It also makes strict controls harder to win in talks, and invites other nations to seek the same freedom. The Agency's CREST files preserve the study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100120006-7:
Economic Penetration of the Area by the Communist Bloc is a paper prepared for the OCB Inter-Agency Working Group on NSC 5506, titled Future Economic Assistance for Asia. It asks what stance the United States should take when Asian nations accept Soviet Bloc offers of trade and development aid. Trade controls as such are left to a review then under way.

The paper notes that growth had barely begun in south and southeast Asia. That fact shapes its caution. The United States, it argues, must not bid against Moscow offer for offer. Doing so would hand the direction of United States aid programs to the Soviet Union itself, a result the paper treats as a trap.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100160002-7:
U.S. Policies on Enforcement of Controls is Staff Study No. 16 of the CFEP Drafting Group, revised draft of June 20, 1955. Its first section covers present control arrangements in COCOM. Primary controls over exports of strategic goods are explained, along with the understandings that backed them among partner nations.

Enforcement aids take up much of the later text. Confidential lists served to screen requests for export licenses before goods moved. The BFC Special Check List, called the Watch List by officials who used it, heads that account. It warned officers abroad about firms or persons whose work might need more than routine attention, including checks on end use. The Agency's CREST files preserve the study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100160011-7:
U.S. Policies on Enforcement of Controls is Staff Study No. 16 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 7, 1955, prepared in consultation with the State and Commerce Departments. It opens with COCOM enforcement: present arrangements, understandings, and where primary controls over strategic exports lay.

Practical cooperation fills the later pages. Technical teams from all but three COCOM nations had visited the United States. United States expert teams had in turn visited seven of the most prominent COCOM nations. Those exchanges built shared knowledge of control policy, licensing practice, and enforcement method on both sides, the study reports. The Agency's CREST files preserve the study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000200100025-7:
An enclosure in declassified Agency files gives supplemental facts on Diversion Control Panel cases. Case 384-A covers mercury: a Hague firm, Mexican Products Trading Company, offered Spanish mercury of 99.99 percent purity to the East Berlin trade body DIA. About 1,500 bottles were in play, priced at 325 dollars a bottle.

Delivery was offered in small rail shipments every two to four days, with payment on arrival in free United States dollars. A second case covers 35 tons of nickel tied to a Stockholm firm. Later pages return to copper: a Danish firm, Tradevox of Copenhagen, appears as the proposed recipient of 3,000 tons of Chilean copper.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100020070-7:
Draft comments in declassified Agency files pick apart an Inspector General survey of Agency training, point by numbered point. An early note questions the survey's own base: many senior officers asked to judge training had never taken Agency courses themselves. Their grasp of the courses and facilities is thus doubted.

Recruiting figures for 1960 draw close replies. The junior officer intake goal had been cut after the survey was written, so no firm share of needs met through the program could be stated. One hiring taste is also challenged: officers hired ready trained in a subject still lack intelligence training. The Overseas Training Branch is defended as working at top capacity.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100040032-7:
Course Reports is a memorandum dated 30 September 1960 to the Chairman of the OTR Educational Committee. It records how each training school reported its courses, after a briefing of the Director of Training on the same day. The Director, Mr. Baird, is reported as content with the practices in place.

The Operations School sent a detailed report after each course for staff employees, in a set format. Special briefings, tutorial work, and covert training went instead into the Weekly Activities Report. The Intelligence School followed a like pattern. One standing wish closes the memo: the Director wants close, detailed word on new courses and on courses changed in any large way. The memo survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200060011-7:
Concept of an Advanced Officer Training Program for DD/P is a declassified Agency staff study. Its problem is stated at the head: should DD/P start a formal mid-career program of five to eight months? The current practice sent single officers to set courses of two to five weeks at a time.

The study finds for the longer program. Gains in officer performance and wider freedom to reassign officers to priority work are expected to repay the time away from the desk. A start could be made with as few as thirty students. Classes would grow by steps to ninety a year from 1965, with a table of course blocks drawn mostly from existing training office courses.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00313a000500010063-7:
Historical Revue, Lockheed Aircraft Corp. is a set of outline charts in declassified Agency files tied to Project CHALICE and Contract No. 313. Handwritten heads sketch the background first: the parties and the path from a letter contract of December 1954, signed by the DCI, toward a full contract.

The definitive contract is dated 2 March 1955 in the notes. Its type is given as fixed price, open to later redetermination, with no ceiling price set. Basic scope lists twenty U-2 aircraft complete, with provision for varied configurations and spares. Wind tunnel, static, and flight tests, plus engineering reports, follow. Added scope covers a test site survey, guards and fire protection, and depot set up help.
clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of-a-you:
Clarissa Harlowe — Volume 7 of Richardson's novel in letters shows the circle closing around Lovelace. Clarissa, in the contents' summary, will consent to prosecute him in a court of justice rather than leave Miss Howe living in terror. Lovelace writes that he has no subject worth writing on, now he has lost his Clarissa.

His family moves against him. Lady Sarah Sadleir and Lady Betty Lawrance engage Lord M. and the two Montague cousins to press him. The cousins must try to win Miss Howe's help in persuading Clarissa to accept him on his repentance. Miss Howe does advise the marriage. Belford, more practically, offers himself as Clarissa's banker, in secret from Lovelace.
dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-7:
Tiberius, Caligula, and Claudius rule in books fifty-six through sixty of Dio Cassius, given here in Earnest Cary's Loeb translation. This seventh volume runs from the last years of Augustus through the reign of Claudius. Dio wrote around 230 CE, and for these books his text survives in full.

Readers get the gloom of Tiberius on Capri, the wild turns of Caligula, and the odd rise of Claudius. Dio also covers the takeover of Britain under Claudius. His senate tales mix fact, gossip, and shrewd reads of character. The volume bridges the founding of the principate and the age of Nero.
establishing-relations-odd-craft-part-7:
W. W. Jacobs spins a Wapping courtship in Establishing Relations, the seventh part of his Odd Craft stories. Mr. Richard Catesby, second officer of the steamship Wizard, comes ashore in high good humour for an evening. Bashford's Lane, a retiring street facing a blank dock wall, holds one sight worth stopping for: a fine girl at the window of No. 5, with dark eyes much discussed by neighboring matrons.

Catesby walks back past the window, pretending he has forgotten something. Later scenes bring a constable, a frightened visitor, and Mrs. Truefitt's sharp verdict that she never heard of such a thing. Prudence judges the man only a little weak in the head. Jacobs keeps the tale at short-story length, dockside and droll.
evan-harrington-volume-7:
The seventh and final volume of George Meredith's Evan Harrington runs from chapter thirty-nine to the end. It opens in the domain of tailordom, at peace in Mr. Goren's honest shop. The Countess still scents game as plots by the brothers Cogglesby come to light. Juliana, Rose's watchful aunt, guards the family's honour.

Evan's long concealment breaks at last, and lovers part under the shadow of the shop. A year later, a letter from the Countess de Saldar to her sister Caroline closes the tale. Meredith resolves his comedy of class with candour about work and worth. Evan stands or falls as himself, not as a borrowed gentleman. Readers who followed the seven volumes reach the reckoning toward which every cricket match, letter, and dinner has been steering.
family-cares-deep-waters-part-7:
Jacobs's Family Cares is the seventh part of his Deep Waters story set. W. W. Jacobs opens in a grocer's shop during a lull in business. Mr. Jernshaw weighs sugar packets when a tall, bronzed man enters. Quizzical blue eyes give the stranger away as Harry Barrett.

Barrett has come home after fifteen years, covered with moss like a rolling stone. He made his pile in Melbourne and can live on it, he says. At forty-three he calls this the evening of his life. Smithson has let him the house in Webb Street, Jernshaw learns. The two old friends settle in the parlour behind the shop. Jacobs builds the tale from return, pride, and village talk.
following-the-equator-a-journey-around-t:
Following the Equator, Part 7, by Mark Twain, closes the world voyage with some of his sharpest essays disguised as sightseeing. Twain opens Chapter LXI with a calendar maxim claiming that God made idiots for practice, then made school boards. The chapter argues from the teaching of deaf, dumb, and blind children, whose teachers measure each child's capacity exactly and set tasks that keep pace with its growth.

Against that rational method Twain sets the average public school, which, in his caricature, teaches a child to spell cat and then asks it to calculate an eclipse. The exaggeration carries a real charge about hurried, one size schooling near the end of a long imperial tour. Part 7 brings the traveler home by way of South Africa and the long sea roads, with education, race, and empire all argued over in the diary's last stretch.
four-pigeons-captains-all-book-7:
Jacobs opens this Captains All tale outside the Cauliflower inn, where an old man angles for ale. His hearing, he hints, might fail just as a second mug is offered. The landlord obliges, and the old man grows talkative.

The talk turns to a shooting party and Bob Pretty's pigeons, which gentlemen pay eighteen-pences to shoot. On Friday the birds grow scarce and the sportsmen grow reckless past the keepers' warnings. Sam Jones is hit in the leg and Peter Gubbins in the arm at the corner of the wood. W. W. Jacobs keeps the comedy dry as the guns blaze away.
froude-history-england-vol-7:
Conspiracy besets Elizabeth in the seventh volume of Froude's History, from 1863. The Northern Rebellion of 1569 raises the Catholic earls in revolt. The Ridolfi plot then schemes to seat Mary Stuart on England's throne by foreign arms.

Froude turns secret history into high drama in these pages. Spies, coded letters, and informers fill the shadow war he recounts. The scaffold waits at the end of each failed design. He shows a regime learning to survive by vigilance and ruthlessness. The volume reads like a thriller of the Tudor age, yet rests on hard digging in state papers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-7:
An editorial note in volume two of the Potsdam papers covers a lunch on July 17, 1945, with no official record. In place of minutes, the editors print Secretary Stimson's diary entry for that day. Stimson had returned to Potsdam and lunched with Churchill, Attlee, and Lord Leathers.

Stimson records talk of ships, above all the sharing out of the German merchant marine. Coal supplies for Britain and the U.S. were discussed too, both facing a short winter. As Churchill walked to the gate, Stimson told him of Harrison's message. Churchill had heard nothing of it from his own people. He was, Stimson writes, intensely interested and greatly cheered, but strongly inclined against any disclosure. The editors note the secrecy likely concerned the Soviet Union. Stimson argued against Churchill's view at some length.
gao-gaoreports-b-292995-7:
Costs claimed by CourtSmart Digital Systems, Inc., form the subject of GAO file B-292995.7, a decision of March 18, 2005. CourtSmart had won its protest against the Social Security Administration and sought its costs back. It claimed $189,748.50 for outside legal work. GAO recommended that the agency reimburse $187,108.50. The test applied was whether the hourly rates claimed matched the going rates for like services. Where the proof of a rate fell short, GAO applied the rate the record did support.

The firm had won its earlier protest on the merits. The agency's scoring of quotes and its source choice were found improper under the Federal Supply Schedule rules.
gao-gaoreports-b-294530-7:
American Floor Consultants, Inc., a small business, brought the protest in GAO file B-294530.7, decided on June 15, 2006. The Air Force had awarded FloorPro, Inc., a contract to apply chemically resistant urethane on floors at Air Force sites. The firm argued that its own past performance had been judged unfairly. It also claimed the award as the lowest-priced acceptable offeror. GAO denied the protest. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release.

The digest states the ground in short form: the references the firm supplied were incomplete or not relevant. On that record, the agency's judgment on its history was fair.
gao-gaoreports-b-294604-7:
Logistics Solutions Group, Inc., protested an Army cancellation in GAO files B-294604.7 and B-294604.8, dated July 28, 2005. The solicitation had sought training on the Standard Army Management Information Systems and support for automation offices. The Army cancelled it and planned to resolicit. GAO denied the protests in part and dismissed them in part. This copy is a redacted version cleared for public release.

The digest gives the ground in one line: the original document no longer matched the agency's real needs. Where that is so, starting over is a fair course. The needing activity was the Coalition Forces Land Component Command.
gao-gaoreports-b-296946-7:
University of Dayton Research Institute sought protest costs in GAO decision B-296946.7, dated October 23, 2006. The Air Force had fixed the buy after the first protest. The fight now was over proof of costs. Some sums dealt with the choice to protest. Some dealt with a pact to end the fight.

GAO limited the pay to proved costs. Costs need clear proof of sums spent. Time spent to choose to protest is not paid. Costs tied to a pact to end the fight are not paid. Time spent to chase the cost claim was also cut. Delay there came from the firm's own thin claim. Proof rules thus cut the claim in three ways.
gao-gaoreports-b-298694-7:
Kellogg Brown & Root Services, Inc. again protested the Navy's global contingency construction awards. The three contracts went to Fluor International, URS-IAP, and Atlantic Contingency Constructors. The work spans disaster aid and conflict-zone building. GAO decided B-298694.7 on June 22, 2007.

This round targeted the technical scoring of the firm's proposal. The Navy put forward a deep and full record. That record backed each strength and weakness it had marked. GAO found the review tracked the stated tests. The depth of the file set this round apart from the firm's prior win. The new attack did not hold up. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-7:
Cleanup of polluted development sites gets little grant money, GAO found in GAO-06-7, a report dated October 27, 2005. Brownfields are properties whose reuse is clouded by real or feared contamination. More than 450,000 such sites are scattered across the United States. A 2004 law required GAO to evaluate brownfield grants from the Economic Development Administration. GAO measured how much grant funding went to cleanup itself.

GAO found that remediation work took only a small share of total brownfield grant funding. Grants paid for many kinds of development instead. Some regional offices had built steps to check compliance with cleanup standards. GAO also found that data on the projects' impact were largely unavailable. The report questions whether grant goals and grant spending line up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-7:
Storms and quakes can wipe out home insurance markets, leaving owners bare. GAO-08-7, dated November 26, 2007, weighs the roles of private insurers, states, and Washington in covering such losses. It counts how many owners lack cover and what Washington paid after the 2005 hurricanes.

Public plans often charge less than the true risk, so they run short after big storms and refill from taxpayers. Many owners skip cover by choice or carry too little for a full rebuild. Washington paid about $26 billion to such owners after the 2005 storms. GAO lays out seven options to reshape the federal role, with no single pick.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FordGeraldR10-7:
Carl Bernstein and Bob Woodward reported for the Washington Post that the Watergate special prosecutor had closed an investigation of President Gerald Ford's finances. The office announced it lacked evidence on mishandled campaign funds. With that finding, the inquiry into the sitting president's money ended.

Ford had inherited the presidency from the Watergate scandal itself, so any probe of his finances carried weight beyond the sums involved. A closing for lack of evidence cleared him on the record. The article preserves the announcement by the two reporters most tied to Watergate's exposure.
history-of-the-world-war-volume-3-of-7:
Francis A March wrote this third volume of his seven-volume History of the World War. Richard J Beamish, a war correspondent, worked with him. General Peyton C March, the army's chief of staff, wrote the introduction. The New York edition is dated 1919.

Photographs by James H Hare and Donald Thompson fill the volume. Official pictures from five allied governments add to the set. A plate shows a Scots stirrup charge in the old style. The text follows the eastern front, where Hindenburg gathered a great army at Thorn by rail. Readers get a rich, immediate record of the war's vast middle years.
humboldt-personal-narrative-williams-vol:
The seventh volume of Humboldt's Personal Narrative, in Williams's translation, closed the English set in 1829, fifteen years after it began. The expedition's last stages stand here: Mexico, the voyage to the United States, and the return to Europe in 1804. Humboldt's American journey ends where his fame begins.

In Mexico he mines the archives for maps, population counts, and the wealth of the silver mines. He visits Washington and talks with Jefferson before sailing home. The volume's surveys of New Spain fed statesmen as much as scientists. Across seven volumes, the Narrative set the pattern for the scientific travel book: exact, wide-ranging, and alive to wonder.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-7:
Nora Helmer slams a door at the end of A Doll's House, and the sound echoed around the world. Archer's seventh Ibsen volume, from 1908, pairs that play with Ghosts, its darker twin. Together they remain the most famous double bill in the English Ibsen.

A wife walks out on a doll's marriage in the first play, demanding a life of her own. Ghosts then traces inherited sin through a widow's house, as a son pays for his father's hidden life. Both plays outraged their first audiences and rewrote what drama could discuss. Archer's translations kept their power in English. No volume better explains Ibsen's fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-7: Aaron, an amora, or Talmud teacher, is named in this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He is mentioned twice in the Babylonian Talmud, in Bava Kamma and in Menahot, the entry states. In both places he gives Rabina information on Baraitot, tannaitic traditions not embodied in the Mishnah. Rabina headed the academy at Sura from 488 to 499 and was one of the editors of the Babylonian Talmud. Nothing more of Aaron's life is recorded here.
lecky-england-18th-vol-7:
Ireland takes the whole stage in the seventh volume of Lecky's History, from 1891. Penal laws crush Catholic life while Grattan's parliament wins a brief, bright season of self-rule. The road then runs downhill toward the Union of 1801 and the parliament's extinction.

Lecky, an Irishman, writes his own country's tragedy with unmatched knowledge. Deep feeling moves beneath his measured, careful prose on every page. He blames misrule in London and faction in Dublin alike. Many readers call this the finest single volume on Ireland's saddest century, a work of love and grief by its ablest modern historian.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-7:
Part Seven opens near Napoleon, Arkansas, in Chapter 31. Twain ponders an errand best done at night, not noonday. Inquisitive eyes make daylight wrong for his purpose. He persuades his friends to leave luggage ashore and stop over.

Their disapproval comes prompt, loud, and mutinous in language. They argue that an earlier decision binds him to the boat. Twain mocks that logic as compounding one unwise act. The chapter title promises a thumb-print and what came of it. Muttons, he tells readers, await after the twenty-one-year absence. The plain question and plain answer settled his perplexity fastest.
memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-montesp:
Book seven of Madame de Montespan's memoirs opens at chapter thirty seven. The King takes Luxembourg because it is his will, the head says. Waste of the Electorate of Treves and the Marquis de Louvois follow.

Crequi took Luxembourg with thirty thousand men in a week. Treves owned the King of France as lord with no fight at all. Its fine walls were levelled at once by his troops. Louvois gets a full portrait here, as a man of vast range and drive. How one manages not to bow stands in the later heads. Money makes fat, she jokes, in a court that ran on gold.
merivale-romans-empire-vol-7:
Golden years return in the seventh and final volume of Merivale's History, from 1865. Merivale looks back over the Antonine age, from Nerva to Marcus Aurelius. The philosopher emperor on the throne crowns his meditation on power, peace, and their limits.

He closes his great work with Rome at its wisest hour. Good rule, he argues, rests on character more than on systems. The volume reflects on all that came before it in the set. It forms a fitting end to a classic history. The tone is elegant, learned, and quietly sad throughout the closing pages.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-7:
Augustine's homilies on the Gospel of John fill most of volume seven of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, from 1886. Homilies on the First Epistle of John follow, and the early Soliloquies close the volume. Philip Schaff edited the series.

The John homilies are sermons, preached over years to a North African congregation, verse by verse through the most mystical gospel. Augustine lingers on love: the epistle talks became a classic on charity, urging readers to love, and do what they will. The Soliloquies, a dialogue with his own reason, were written just after his conversion. The volume spans his whole career in one binding.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-7:
Cyril of Jerusalem and Gregory Nazianzen share volume seven of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890. Cyril taught new converts in Jerusalem itself around 350. Gregory, Basil's friend, was the poet-theologian of the Trinity. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

Cyril's catechetical lectures walk baptism candidates through the creed, article by article, in the church of the Holy Sepulchre. His talks on the sacraments are our earliest full witness to the Easter rites. Gregory's five theological orations then defend the divinity of the Holy Spirit with unmatched polish. The volume pairs the classroom of the early church with its highest pulpit.
roughing-it-part-7:
Part 7 of Mark Twain's Roughing It, in an 1880 printing, opens at Chapter LXI with Dick Baker, a pocket-miner of Dead-House Gulch. Baker was forty-six, gray as a rat, plain in dress and clay-soiled from work. Twain calls him one of the gentlest spirits he knew, a man whose heart was finer than any gold his shovel ever found. Eighteen years of hard toil and blighted hopes in exile had not soured him.

When luck ran low, Baker mourned a fine cat he once owned, named Tom Quartz. Where women and children are not, Twain notes, kind men take up with pets, for they must love something. Baker held that the cat had more plain sense than any man in camp. Tom Quartz never caught a rat and cared for nothing but mining.
samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-7:
Part 7 of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren, written as Josiah Allen's Wife, opens at Chapter XXVI with a plea for money. A man sat counting out his money before putting it away in his tin box. Samantha laid the subject before him strong and eloquent. She laid out just the wants and needs of the meeting house. She told how hard the female sisters were working, and how much money they needed to buy ingredients for the fair. He sat still, counting, but she knew he heard her. There were four fifty dollar bills, a ten, and a five. At the very least reckoning, she felt, he would hand her the ten or the five, maybe both.

Instead he laid the bills carefully in the box, pulled out his old pocket-book, and handed her a ten cent piece. A picture in the passage is captioned with that act.
sandra-belloni-volume-7: George Meredith's Sandra Belloni, Volume 7, marked v7, appears here only in header matter, as number 25 in a series by the author. A release date of September 2003 is given, and the file was first posted on January 4, 2002, as Etext number 4419, in Edition 10, in English and ASCII. Pat Castevans and David Widger are named as the producers of the electronic text. The portion shown here contains no title page and no text from the novel itself.
sketches-new-and-old-part-7:
Mark Twain's sketches new and old close in this seventh part, opening with his first interview with Artemus Ward, written about 1870. Ward arrived in silver country with letters from shared San Francisco friends, and Twain breakfasted with him by invitation. Custom there called for whisky cocktails before such a meal, near a religion, Twain states.

Twain begged off, fearing the drink would cloud his head within ten minutes. Ward gently insisted, and Twain drank under protest. Ideas duly clouded as Ward, with superhuman earnestness, posed an astounding question. The sketch honors a fellow humorist's deadpan art at close range.
symonds-renaissance-italy-vol-6-7:
Volumes 6 and 7 close Symonds's Renaissance in Italy in one Gutenberg text. The sixteenth-century aftermath fills these final parts of his vast work. A late flowering blooms, then the long sunset of the age begins.

Symonds surveys the decline with the same care he gave the rise. Foreign armies, church discipline, and tired courts drain Italy's lead. Yet art and letters leave a harvest all Europe still gathers. His seven volumes form the most bold English account of the age. No later single author has matched its scope and sweep in English. The close is elegy, audit, and praise in equal parts.
the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-volume-: Only a Project Gutenberg header covers volume seven here. The book is The Adventures of Harry Richmond by George Meredith. No chapter text follows the header. The header numbers the part 56 in the Meredith run. It files the part as 4450. First posting is dated January 31, 2002. David Widger is credited with its making.
the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-7:
Part seven of Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer opens at chapter twenty-eight, on a night when Tom and Huck are ready for their boldest errand yet. They hang about the tavern till after nine, one watching the alley and one the door.

No one like the Spaniard comes or goes, and the clear night spoils their plan to try the keys in the dark. Huck gives up the watch at twelve and sleeps in an empty sugar hogshead. Tuesday and Wednesday bring the same bad luck, but Thursday night looks better, and Tom slips out with his aunt's old tin lantern. Readers follow the boys toward the tavern room where a treasure chest waits.
the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-7:
Jesus walking on the water opens volume seven of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations. Mark's text tells how the disciples rowed against the wind at night and cried out at a shape on the sea. Jesus bids them be of good cheer, steps aboard, and the wind drops. Next comes Christ's entry into Jerusalem on a colt, with crowds strewing clothes and branches.

Each scene pairs a Gospel text with a Doré plate and short notes. Storm, faith, and triumph crowd this volume, which follows Christ through the height of his work among the people.
the-gilded-age-part-7:
Part 7 of The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today is dated 1873. Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote the novel. This part opens with Chapter LV. Henry Brierly takes the stand at a trial. He tells the jury what he knows of a killing. He went with Laura Hawkins to New York. He thought her trip dealt with a bill in Congress.

He tells how Laura fired twice at Colonel Selby. She then turned the gun on her own breast. He snatched it away. Mr. Braham cross-examines him. Braham draws out his name to mock him. He states his work as civil engineer. The court scene mixes grief, shame, and sly court craft. The jury smiles even in a case of death.
the-great-conspiracy-volume-7:
John Logan wrote The Great Conspiracy: Its Origin and History. This record is Part 7 of that work. It opens with Chapter XXVIII, Freedom at Last Assured. Logan first gives the military situation. Hood had marched north with some 50,000 men toward Nashville, Tennessee. Sherman left Thomas with some 35,000 men to thwart him. Sherman then abandoned his base and marched south from Atlanta, through Georgia, toward the sea.

On November 30, 1864, General Schofield made a stand at Franklin, in the angle of the Harpeth River. He commanded the 4th and 23rd Corps of Thomas's army. His aim was to give the Union supply trains time to cross the river. With fewer than 20,000 troops behind hasty works, he met Hood's assault. At first the attack threatened a bloody rout. A brilliant counter-charge and stubborn defense repulsed the Rebel forces.
the-guardian-angel-ship-s-company-part-7:
W. W. Jacobs wrote The Guardian Angel, in his Ship's Company. A night-watchman tells it. He has never met any philanthropists, he says. Kindness, he holds, is often only another name for artfulness. A stranger once stood him eight half-pints, then borrowed five shillings off him. 

The three sailors had just come back from a voyage and taken a room in Wapping. Then, in a small public-house down Poplar way, they fell out over a joke of Ginger's. Ginger bet Sam a level half-dollar that he would not drink a pot of beer without taking breath. Twice Sam raised the mug and set it down, asking what the game was. The third time he started. Halfway through, Ginger asked the landlord, in a loud voice, whether he had caught it in the mouse-trap, or had it died of poison?
the-history-of-sir-charles-grandison-vol: Samuel Richardson wrote The History of Sir Charles Grandison, shown here as Volume IV of seven. The contents of the volume summarize letters in order, most from Miss Byron to Miss Selby and built around letters from Dr. Bartlett. Summaries track Sir Charles with the Porretta family at Bologna, Clementina's wish to see him once more before his departure from Italy, her ill-treatment by her aunt, and his arrival at Naples. Only the title page and letter summaries are present here, so the letters themselves do not appear.
the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-7:
Part 7 of Mark Twain's The Prince and the Pauper opens at Chapter XXII, A Victim of Treachery. King Foo-foo the First is roving again with the tramps, a butt for coarse jests. Only Canty and Hugo truly dislike him. The others admire his pluck and spirit. Hugo, who has charge of the boy, makes him uncomfortable as he covertly can, even stepping on his toes as if by accident.

The third time Hugo tries that trick, the King fells him with a cudgel. A ring forms, betting and cheering begin, and Hugo springs up in fury. He stands no chance. The small King's arm was trained by Europe's first masters in single-stick and swordsmanship. He turns aside the rain of blows and lands lightning raps on Hugo's head. Battered and ridiculed, Hugo slinks away. The rabble crowns the boy King of the Game-Cocks.
the-toll-house-sailor-s-knots-part-7:
W. W. Jacobs opens The Toll-House, from his 1909 Sailors' Knots, over tea at the Three Feathers Inn. Jack Barnes dismisses ghost talk as nonsense: people die in every house, and noises are wind and rats. Meagle, presiding over the tea, admits a half-and-half belief in the supernatural. Lester and White chime in with an aunt and an uncle who each saw a ghost, drawing Barnes's retort that it is always somebody else who sees them.

Meagle then names a large, suspiciously cheap house that no one will take, said to have claimed a life from every family living there. White bets Barnes a sovereign he will not spend a night there alone, and Lester matches him. Jacobs sets his trap with pub talk and a wager, his favourite road into a haunted-house tale.
the-unknown-night-watches-part-7:
W. W. Jacobs opens The Unknown with his night-watchman musing that handsome is as handsome does. Good looks, he claims, bring a man little else, and they often push him into early marriage. The handsomest fellow he knew married five times and got seven years for it.

His main example is Captain Bill Smithers of the schooner Wild Rose, a quiet, well-behaved skipper on the London river. Smithers waited until nearly forty, then married a widow who decided he was too handsome to trust alone. She made him log every trip in a book, then took to sailing with him each voyage. The watchman's dialect telling keeps the comedy dry and gossipy.
thirlwall-history-greece-vol-7:
Volume 7 of Thirlwall's History, from 1845, covers Thebes and rising Macedon. Epaminondas frees Greece from Sparta's grip with bold new tactics. Then Philip of Macedon looms from the north, patient and strong.

The city-states play their last acts of freedom in these pages. Leagues form and break while Macedon's power grows year by year. Thirlwall moves his long history toward its climax with quiet force. He honors Thebes' brief glory without hiding its swift fade after. Freedom's old forms can no longer hold against a kingdom united. Readers feel an old world ending as the volume closes.
un-ga-res-a-69-7:
Yearly work by the world's atomic watchdog comes before the General Assembly in Resolution A/69/7, from its sixty-ninth session. The Assembly had the report of the International Atomic Energy Agency for 2013, and heard its chief lay out the main turns of 2014. The agency checks that atomic work stays peaceful, and helps states use the atom for power, health, and farms.

The Assembly takes note of the report with thanks. It lists the agency's own 2014 votes: on joint work for atomic safety, on atomic security, and on aid to states that need skills. The text also recalls the 1957 deal that ties the agency to the UN family.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: The annual report of the International Atomic Energy Agency is taken up in Resolution 69/7, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014. The Assembly takes note of the Agency's report for 2013. It takes note of the resolutions adopted at its fifty-eighth General Conference in September 2014. Those cover nuclear safety and security, safeguards, and the application of safeguards in North Korea and the Middle East.
un-sc-res-7: Spain under Franco stayed on the Security Council's watch list under Resolution 7 of 1946. A team of the Council had probed the state of Spain that spring. Its work, the text holds, bore out in full the facts behind the Franco regime's fall from grace. Those facts had led the Potsdam and San Francisco meets, the General Assembly, and the Council itself to condemn it. The Council rules to keep the Spanish question under steady watch, on its list of live matters, ready to act if peace needs it.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Spain under the Franco regime stood condemned by the world conferences of 1945, and the Council kept it under watch in 1946. A sub-committee named on 29 April 1946 had looked into the situation in Spain. Its findings confirmed the facts behind that blame. Resolution 7, from the first year of the United Nations, does one thing. The Council decided to keep Spain under constant watch. Spain stayed on its list of open matters. The Council could then act at any time, if its duties required it.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s17-7:
Section 17.7 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets the tests for the deferred schedule for documents. It sits in Part 17, on filing for public inspection and publication schedules. Part (a) states when a document may be placed on that schedule. One ground is a technical problem with the document. Long or odd tables and figures are named as such a ground.

A document of a size that calls for out-of-the-way handling time is a ground as well. A second ground is a request by the agency at stake for a later publication date. Part (b) adds that the staff of the Office of the Federal Register will tell the agency if its documents must take that path, as the text goes on to state. The text is drawn from the eCFR.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s21-7: Section 21.7 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers titles and subtitles in the Code. It sits in Part 21, on the preparation of documents subject to codification. Part (a) states what a title is in that scheme. The major divisions of the Code are titles, and each brings together functions of government that are broadly related. Part (b) states what subtitles may be used for. They may split the matter of a broad agency from the matter of its parts, or group chapters within a title.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s22-7: Section 22.7 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations is a rule on the shape of drafts of rules. It sits in Part 22, on the prep of notes and of drafts of rules. Any part of a draft that holds the full text of a draft law must keep a set of marks. Those marks are the marks set in Part 21 of the chapter, the part that bears on the shape of such texts.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s5-7:
Title One of the Code of Federal Regulations, in the section numbered five point seven, deals with how the Federal Register is sent out. The section sits in Part Five, which covers general rules for the Register. It sets the duty for the Government Printing Office, the office in charge of the work. That office must get each issue out on the day it is due.

The office must hand the issue over for delivery, or leave it at a post office, by nine in the morning on the day it comes out. A clear rule covers the issue dated for a Monday. That Monday issue must be left at a post office by nine in the morning on the Saturday just before it.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s603-7:
Section 603.7 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets the steps to guard Records. It sits in Part 603, the Privacy Act rules of the National Capital Planning Commission. The Commission is to put the steps of the section in force. The aim is to make sure that guards of three kinds are in place. They are guards in the way work is run, guards in the tools of the work, and guards in the flesh. Those guards are to keep the safety and the private nature of Records.

The steps set out are also to guard against a set of harms. They are to guard against threats or risks, of a kind that can be seen in advance, to the safety of the Records. The part of the text shown is cut off at that point in the list of ends.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s8-7: Section 8.7 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations deals with the aid that agencies must give in the work of the Code. It sits in Part 8, on the Code of Federal Regulations. The rule is one line. Each agency is to join in the work of keeping the printing of the Code up to date. It is to do so by a prompt meet of the dates set by the Director of the Federal Register and by the Public Printer.
vittoria-volume-7: Number 47 in the Project Gutenberg series of George Meredith's works is volume seven of Vittoria. Its pages here consist of the familiar old header, which tells readers the words are carefully chosen and must not be changed without written permission. That header is the whole of what is present; the novel's text is not shown. Readers seeking the plot can turn to the companion record whose contents run from Monte Motterone to the tobacco riots of the revolt.
